section: Can two exhausted empires choose peace over one more round of war?
text: This lesson turns to Anatolia and the Aegean world just across the sea from it. This lesson meets the Hittites, whose empire grew to rival Egypt itself, clashed with it at the largest chariot battle in history, and then did something rarer than winning a war: signed the oldest surviving peace treaty in world history instead of fighting again.

section: BY THE END OF THIS LESSON YOU WILL BE ABLE TO…
text: This lesson turns to Anatoliaan-uh-TOH-lee-uhthe large peninsula making up most of modern Turkey, home to the Hittite kingdom., the peninsula that makes up most of modern Turkey, and the Aegean world of Crete and mainland Greece just across the sea from it. Three civilizations rose here during the same centuries Egypt's New Kingdom pharaohs were fighting abroad, roughly 1600 to 1200 BC: the Hittites in Anatolia, and the Minoans and Mycenaeans further west. This lesson introduces the Hittites. The Minoans and Mycenaeans were two related but separate peoples with stories of their own.
📚 ANATOLIAN BEGINNINGS

Anatolia had been farmed since long, long ago. Einkorn wheat, the world's very first tamed grain, was grown in this same region as far back as 9000 BC, part of the Fertile Crescent story of early farming. The Hittite state itself would not exist for thousands more years. Around 1650 BC, a Hittite kingdom began to pull power together across central Anatolia. It centered on the heavily fortified city of HattusaHAT-oo-sahthe massively fortified capital city of the Hittite Empire.. Hittite scribes borrowed **cuneiform** from Akkadian scribal custom, as cuneiform spread beyond Mesopotamia. They used it to write the Hittite language, the oldest known member of the Indo-European language family. That same broad family later includes Greek, Latin, and English.
📚 AN EMPIRE BUILT BY CONQUEST

Hittite power reached its height under kings like Suppiluliuma I🔊soo-pih-loo-lee-OO-maha powerful Hittite king, ruling around 1350 BC, who expanded Hittite power deep into Syria., who around 1350 BC pushed Hittite rule deep into Syria. He beat the strong kingdom of Mitanni. This brought the Hittites into direct, sometimes hostile contact with Egypt's own sphere of power in the Levant. Hittite kings ruled as both political and religious heads of their state. They dealt with Egypt's pharaoh as self-declared equals. Both used the title "Great King." Only a small handful of the era's most powerful rulers could fairly claim that title for themselves. Historians sometimes call this small circle of rulers the Amarna system, named for a cache of clay letters found in Egypt. Those letters record the "Great Kings" of Egypt, Hatti, Babylon, Assyria, and Mitanni. They wrote to each other almost as equals, even while they were rivals and sometimes fought.
🌐 FOREIGN LANGUAGE VOCABULARY

**Suppiluliuma I** 🔊soo-pih-loo-lee-OO-maha powerful Hittite king, ruling around 1350 BC, who expanded Hittite power deep into Syria. opens this lesson. Later in the lesson: **Ramesses II** 🔊RAM-uh-seezpharaoh of Egypt from about 1279 to 1213 BC, who led Egypt's army at Kadesh and later signed peace with the Hittites., **Muwatalli II** 🔊moo-wah-TAH-leethe Hittite king who commanded Hittite forces against Ramesses II at Kadesh., and **Hattusili III** 🔊hah-too-SEE-leethe Hittite king, and Muwatalli II's younger brother, who later signed the peace treaty with Ramesses II..
👤 HISTORICAL FIGURE · SUPPILULIUMA I

Photo: via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 2.0. (This relief actually depicts the later king Tudhaliya IV; no confirmed portrait of Suppiluliuma I himself survives, so this image stands in as a representative example of Hittite royal relief art.)

Suppiluliuma Isoo-pih-loo-lee-OO-maha powerful Hittite king, ruling around 1350 BC, who expanded Hittite power deep into Syria. ruled the Hittites around 1350 to 1322 BC, expanding Hittite power deep into Syria and setting up the empire that would later face Egypt at Kadesh.

section: KADESH: THE LARGEST CHARIOT BATTLE IN HISTORY
text: 📚 KADESH: THE LARGEST CHARIOT BATTLE IN HISTORY

section: KADESH: THE LARGEST CHARIOT BATTLE IN HISTORY
text: That rivalry between Hatti and Egypt came to a head in 1274 BC. The two powers clashed at the **Battle of Kadesh**, fought in modern Syria. Egypt's army was led by Ramesses II🔊RAM-uh-seezpharaoh of Egypt from about 1279 to 1213 BC, who led Egypt's army at Kadesh and later signed peace with the Hittites., only in the fifth year of a reign that would eventually last sixty-six years. The Hittite army was led by Muwatalli II🔊moo-wah-TAH-leethe Hittite king who commanded Hittite forces against Ramesses II at Kadesh.. Both sides sent out thousands of horse-drawn chariotsCHAIR-ee-uhta light, two-wheeled cart pulled by horses, used in war for fast attacks and quick movement., with modern estimates for the two armies combined reaching five to six thousand chariots in all. This likely makes Kadesh the largest chariot battle ever fought in world history. Both empires' own records claim victory, a useful reminder that royal writings rarely give a fair, two-sided account of their own wars. What really followed the battle was neither a clear Egyptian win nor a clear Hittite one. Years of tension followed. At last came something neither side had won through years of fighting.
👤 HISTORICAL FIGURE · RAMESSES II
Photo: via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 2.0.

Ramesses IIRAM-uh-seezpharaoh of Egypt from about 1279 to 1213 BC, who led Egypt's army at Kadesh and later signed peace with the Hittites. ruled Egypt from about 1279 to 1213 BC, one of the longest reigns in Egyptian history. He personally led Egypt's army at Kadesh as a young pharaoh and, decades later, signed the peace treaty that ended the long rivalry with the Hittites.
⚔️ BATTLE · KADESH
Relief carving, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

Fought in 1274 BC, the Battle of Kadesh pitted Ramesses II's Egyptian army against Muwatalli II's Hittite forces, each fielding thousands of chariots. Neither side won a clear victory on the field, but the battle's real legacy came fifteen years later, in the peace treaty it eventually produced.
📚 A DIFFERENT KIND OF ENDING

In 1259 BC, Ramesses II and the new Hittite king Hattusili III🔊hah-too-SEE-leethe Hittite king, and Muwatalli II's younger brother, who later signed the peace treaty with Ramesses II. signed a formal peace deal. It was the **Egyptian-Hittite Peace Treaty**, the oldest surviving peace treatyTREE-teea formal written agreement between two states, often ending a war or setting the terms of peace. in world history. Rather than one side simply beating the other, both empires chose to talk out a deal instead. Years of costly fighting neither side could clearly win had worn them both down. The treaty set out clear rules. Neither side would attack the other. Both sides promised to help defend each other against outside threats. Each side agreed to send back people who had fled to it. Years later, Hattusili III's own daughter married Ramesses II, sealing the peace between the two empires with a royal marriage as well as a written deal. This is worth holding up as a real case study in how lasting peace really gets made. Two worn-out great powers, having fought as much as either could stand, chose the harder, less exciting work of talking out peace over the costs of more war. Both judged that peace served them better than any further fighting could.
👤 HISTORICAL FIGURE · HATTUSILI III
No verified public-domain image of Hattusili III (a seal impression or relief bearing his name) could be located during this reconciliation pass. Flagged rather than substituting an uncleared photo.

Hattusili IIIhah-too-SEE-leethe Hittite king, and Muwatalli II's younger brother, who later signed the peace treaty with Ramesses II. ruled the Hittites after taking the throne from his own nephew. He is best remembered for signing the Egyptian-Hittite Peace Treaty with Ramesses II in 1259 BC, ending decades of rivalry between the two empires.
👥 PEOPLES · THE HITTITES
Photo: via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 2.0.
Hittite relief carvings show soldiers and officials in pointed shoes, short kilts, and conical caps. Charioteers wore bronze scale armor for protection in battle.
🏙️ CITIES · HATTUSA
Photo: via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

HattusaHAT-oo-sahthe massively fortified capital city of the Hittite Empire. was ringed by massive stone walls more than four miles long, pierced by gates decorated with carved lions and a sphinx. Thousands of cuneiform tablets found in its ruins recorded the Hittite Empire's laws, treaties, and religious rituals.
📚 IRON, RECONSIDERED

One more Hittite feat deserves a closer look: early ironworkingthe skill of heating and shaping iron into tools and weapons, a harder and eventually more common metal than bronze.. For decades, popular stories described the Hittites as guarding a strict monopolymuh-NOP-uh-leetotal control over making or selling something, with no real competition. on iron-making skill. In these stories, iron was a closely held state secret, kept hidden from rival kingdoms. More recent study has changed this picture a good deal. Iron-working knowledge during the Hittite period seems to have grown more slowly than that old story claimed. It also seems to have spread more widely across the region than the "secret monopoly" story allowed. One striking example, a dagger with an iron blade and a gold handle, was found in a royal tomb at Alaca Höyük in central Anatolia, dating to around 2500 BC, centuries before the Hittite state itself existed. This shows iron was already known and prized as a rare, precious metal long before anyone learned to make it in any real amount. Iron did not fully replace bronze until later, once the shocks of the Bronze Age Collapse cut off the long-distance tin trade that bronze production depended on. The Hittites deserve credit as early, skilled ironworkers, but not for a tightly guarded monopoly the evidence no longer supports.
⚙️ TECHNOLOGY SPOTLIGHT · IRONWORKING
Photo: via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.5.

Iron has one big advantage over bronze: it does not need tin, a metal that had to be hauled in from distant mines and made bronze production dependent on long, fragile trade routes. Early Hittite smiths worked with iron by at least 1400 BC, though it stayed rare and costly, more a prestige metal for gifts and ceremonial objects than an everyday replacement for bronze weapons. Turning raw iron ore into usable metal took much higher furnace heat than bronze-making required, along with repeated hammering to drive out impurities. Only after the Bronze Age Collapse cut off the tin trade did iron slowly become the practical, everyday metal of choice across the ancient world.
💪 KEEP THIS IN MIND
Kadesh and the treaty that followed it show two great powers choosing the harder, less exciting work of peace over more war neither could clearly win.

section: How does a king from outside Egypt end up becoming its truest defender?
text: Egypt's New Kingdom survived the Bronze Age Collapse, but only just, and a century later it had quietly split into rival kingdoms. This lesson follows Piye, a king of Kush from far up the Nile, who marched north not to seize Egypt for its own sake, but, in his own telling, to restore the order and respect for Amun that Egypt's own divided rulers had let slip.

section: BY THE END OF THIS LESSON YOU WILL BE ABLE TO…
text: Egypt's New Kingdom lived through the Bronze Age Collapse, but only just. Its treasury shrank. Its land grew smaller. This lesson picks up about a hundred years later, in a stretch historians call the Third Intermediate Periodthe long stretch of Egyptian history, about 1077 to 664 BC, when Egypt broke apart into rival kingdoms instead of standing as one country. (about 1077 to 664 BC). During this time, Egypt split apart. The one, single Egypt that Narmer first united came undone. Then a king from the far south marched north to put it back together, on his own terms.
📚 A KINGDOM IN PIECES

By the ninth century BC, Egypt was not one country in any real sense. Rival dynasties ruled from different cities at the same time. Local princes in the Nile Delta acted like kings in all but name. The high priests of Amun at **Thebes** held power that could rival any pharaoh's. No single big crash caused this, unlike the sudden fall of the Bronze Age collapse. It was a slow drift instead. A kingdom quietly came apart at the seams, even while most people still called themselves Egyptian and still honored Egyptian gods. This is worth pausing on. Unity is not a natural state that a civilization just falls back into on its own. Someone has to build it, and rebuild it, on purpose. In other words, a country does not stay whole by accident. It stays whole because real people keep doing the hard work of holding it together, year after year. When that work stops, or when no one is left strong enough to do it, a kingdom can come apart even without a single big war or disaster to blame.

section: PIYE AND THE KINGDOM OF KUSH
text: 📚 PIYE AND THE KINGDOM OF KUSH
🌐 FOREIGN LANGUAGE VOCABULARY

**Piye** 🔊PEE-yaythe Kushite king who conquered Egypt around 727 BC, founding what historians call Egypt's Twenty-fifth Dynasty., the Kushite king who conquered Egypt around 727 BC, founding what historians call Egypt's Twenty-fifth Dynasty.

That someone came from far to the south. Along the upper Nile, past Egypt's old border, in the region called NubiaNOO-bee-uhthe wider region south of Egypt along the Nile, home to the kingdom of Kush., a kingdom called **Kush** had grown for centuries around the city of Napatanuh-PAH-tuhthe capital city of the kingdom of Kush, far south along the Nile, near a stretch of rocky river rapids called the Fourth Cataract.. Kush had taken in Egyptian religion, Egyptian writing, and worship of the god Amun so fully that its own kings saw themselves as the true keepers of Egyptian ways, maybe even more devoted than Egypt's own divided rulers. Kushites even believed a holy mountain near Napata, called Jebel Barkal, was one of Amun's true homes on Earth. Around 727 BC, the Kushite king Piye🔊PEE-yaythe Kushite king who conquered Egypt around 727 BC, founding what historians call Egypt's Twenty-fifth Dynasty. marched his army north. By his own account, he came not to grab land for its own sake, but to punish a northern prince named Tefnakht for showing no respect to Amun, and for upsetting **ma'at**, Egypt's own idea of cosmic and social balance, the same idea found in the Old Kingdom.

Piye's own Great Triumphal Stele tells this campaign in striking, personal detail. It tells a story quite different from a simple tale of conquest. Piye orders his generals to purify themselves before battle. He tells them to make proper offerings at Thebes before marching further, treating the war as a religious duty first, and only a war second. City after city surrenders to him. Again and again, the stele shows Piye showing mercy to defeated princes who submit and show proper respect. He lets many keep their thrones as his vassalsa ruler who keeps his own throne and people, but agrees to obey and pay tribute to a stronger king., ruling their own cities but now paying him tributegoods, money, or gifts a weaker ruler sends to a stronger one to buy peace or show loyalty. and owing him loyalty. Yet he saves his sharpest anger not for a defeated human rival, but for finding out that a surrendered prince's horses had been left to starve during a siege. Piye's own words show a king more upset by cruelty to animals than by the shame of his human rivals. Maybe this reflects Piye's real character. Maybe it reflects the stele's own careful public image making. It is likely both at once. Either way, it is a striking piece of evidence for how a real historical figure wanted to be remembered. In short, this stele lets us see how Piye wanted people to remember him: as a king who fought for order and fair play, not just for land and power.
👤 HISTORICAL FIGURE · PIYE
Image: after Auguste Mariette, 1872, via Wikimedia Commons, public domain.

PiyePEE-yaythe Kushite king who conquered Egypt around 727 BC, founding what historians call Egypt's Twenty-fifth Dynasty. ruled the kingdom of Kush from about 744 to 714 BC. Around 727 BC, he marched north and conquered Egypt, founding the line of kings historians call Egypt's Twenty-fifth Dynasty.

section: VICTORY, AND A KING WHO GOES HOME
text: 📚 VICTORY, AND A KING WHO GOES HOME

section: VICTORY, AND A KING WHO GOES HOME
text: Piye won submission from nearly every rival prince in Egypt. Then he did something a reader used to conquest stories might not expect. He marched back south to Napata. He seemed content to let local rulers keep running Egypt's different regions under his own rule, rather than staying in Egypt to rule it directly himself. This is worth sitting with as a real choice, not an obvious or forced one. A different king, or the same king on a different day, might have stayed instead. Many conquerors have chosen to stay in the land they won and rule it up close. Piye chose a different path. That choice tells us something real about what he wanted most: order restored, not a new home in a new land. Piye's own line of kings, the Kushite pharaohs later historians number as Egypt's Twenty-fifth Dynasty, would go on to rule as far north as the Nile Delta for decades. Piye's successors, kings such as Shabaka and Taharqa, kept building temples and fixing up old Egyptian monuments, proud to present themselves as keepers of a tradition older than their own kingdom. Kush's own kings would go on ruling from Napata, and later from a city called Meroe even further south, for many centuries after Piye's own reign ended.

section: VICTORY, AND A KING WHO GOES HOME
text: That rule would not last in peace for long. A much larger power was rising in Mesopotamia during these same decades, and it had its own reasons to want Egypt weak. In 663 BC, an Assyrian army would sack Thebes itself, Egypt's ancient religious capital. It was a shock so severe that a prophet writing more than a century later could still point to it as a warning to Assyria's own future enemies. In other words, Egypt's story does not stop here. It only pauses, before an even bigger power arrives on the scene.
👥 PEOPLES · THE KUSHITES
Photo: Museo Egizio, Turin, via Wikimedia Commons, CC0.

The **Kushites** ruled a kingdom along the upper Nile, south of Egypt. They took in Egyptian religion and writing so fully that their own kings saw themselves as the truest keepers of Egyptian tradition, shown here in the close-cropped wig and headdress favored by Kushite kings.
🏙️ CITIES · NAPATA
Photo: via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

Napatanuh-PAH-tuhthe capital city of the kingdom of Kush, far south along the Nile, near a stretch of rocky river rapids called the Fourth Cataract., capital of the kingdom of Kush, stood far south along the Nile near a stretch of river rapids called the Fourth Cataract, beside the sacred mountain of Jebel Barkal. From here, Piye ruled both Kush and, for a time, all of Egypt.
💪 KEEP THIS IN MIND
Piye restored Egypt's unity, but chose to rule it from a distance rather than staying to hold it directly. Egypt's story does not stop here.

section: Can a pharaoh win greatness through trade and peace instead of war?
text: Can a pharaoh win greatness through trade and peace instead of war?

section: Can a pharaoh win greatness through trade and peace instead of war?
text: Egypt's Old Kingdom eventually gave way to a Middle Kingdom, a period of foreign Hyksos rule, and finally the New Kingdom, an age of empire and bold pharaohs. This lesson meets one of its most unusual rulers: Hatshepsut, a woman who took the full throne and held it for two decades. Rather than building her name through conquest, she is remembered for a great trading expedition to the land of Punt. This lesson asks whether that kind of greatness counts for as much as a warrior-king's.

text: Egypt's Old Kingdom, the pyramid-building age, did not last forever. Around 2181 BC, central power grew weak. Local governors grew stronger than the pharaoh in Memphis. Egypt broke apart into a time historians call the First Intermediate Period. Egypt came back together under the **Middle Kingdom** (about 2055 to 1650 BC). This was a time of new order, growing trade, and some of Egypt's finest writing. That order broke down again in the Second Intermediate Period. A Semitic-speaking people called the **Hyksos** took control of Lower Egypt from their capital at Avaris. They ruled as outsiders, though partly in the Egyptian style, from roughly 1650 to 1550 BC. The Hyksos are remembered for one key import: the horse-drawn chariot and the composite bow. Egypt would soon turn these into the backbone of its own New Kingdom armies. Egyptian princes later drove out the Hyksos. They joined the country back together under the **New Kingdom** (about 1550 to 1150 BC), the age of Hatshepsut and Thutmose III. It was an age of empire and bold pharaohs. In this lesson, it is also the age of a queen who ruled as king.
🌐 FOREIGN LANGUAGE VOCABULARY

**Hatshepsut** 🔊hat-SHEP-soota female pharaoh of Egypt's New Kingdom, ruling in her own right from about 1479 to 1458 BC. is this lesson's central figure. Later in the lesson: **Senenmut** 🔊SEN-en-mootHatshepsut's chief steward and architect, who oversaw her building projects and tutored her daughter..

section: AN UNUSUAL PATH TO THE THRONE
text: 📚 AN UNUSUAL PATH TO THE THRONE

section: AN UNUSUAL PATH TO THE THRONE
text: Hatshepsut🔊hat-SHEP-soota female pharaoh of Egypt's New Kingdom, ruling in her own right from about 1479 to 1458 BC. came to power around 1479 BC. She first ruled as regent for her young stepson and nephew Thutmose III. Within a few years, she ruled as pharaoh in her own right. She took on the full royal titles, regaliarih-GAY-lee-uhthe special clothes, crowns, and objects that mark someone as a king or queen., and even the old false beard of Egyptian kingship. Still, carvings and statues sometimes show her with female features alongside these male royal symbols. This was, by any measure, a rare path. Egyptian kingship had never shut women out by rule. But almost no woman before Hatshepsut had claimed the full throne and held it for roughly two decades, as she did.

section: AN UNUSUAL PATH TO THE THRONE
text: Her advisors worked to explain her rule through careful writings. They called her chosen by the god Amun himself. This divine-selection story is not unlike the "divine kingship" claim made for earlier pharaohs, now stretched to cover a truly new case. Carvings at Deir el-Baharidayr el-ba-HAH-reethe site near Thebes where Hatshepsut built her mortuary temple, cut into the cliffs. go even further, showing Amun himself as Hatshepsut's true father, visiting her mother in the form of the reigning pharaoh. This was a bold claim for any pharaoh to make about their own birth. It was even bolder for a female ruler seeking to hold power in her own name. Only one earlier woman, Sobekneferu near the end of the Middle Kingdom, had ever ruled Egypt as pharaoh in her own right, and her reign lasted only about four years. No queen before Hatshepsut had ever ruled anywhere near as long as her two full decades on the throne.
👤 HISTORICAL FIGURE · HATSHEPSUT
Photo: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons.

Hatshepsuthat-SHEP-soota female pharaoh of Egypt's New Kingdom, ruling in her own right from about 1479 to 1458 BC. ruled Egypt as pharaoh from about 1479 to 1458 BC, one of the few women in Egyptian history to hold the full throne. She is remembered for her trading expedition to Punt and for the grand building projects of her reign.
📚 TRADE INSTEAD OF CONQUEST

Rather than building her name mainly through war, Hatshepsut is best remembered for a different kind of feat: a major trading expeditionek-spuh-DISH-una journey made by a group of people for a clear purpose, such as trade or exploration. to the land of Punta land likely along the Red Sea coast of modern Eritrea, Sudan, or Somalia, a source of incense, gold, and other prized goods.. She sent this expedition out around the ninth year of her reign. Carvings that record the trip show a fleet of about five ships, each roughly seventy feet long, sailing down the Red Sea coast. The writings Hatshepsut had carved at her mortuary temple at Deir el-Bahari, near Thebes, survive. They record the voyage in vivid detail: ships loaded for the return trip with incense trees dug up with their root balls whole, ebony, ivory, gold, myrrh resin, leopard skins, and even live baboons.

Egypt's own land could not make many of these luxury and ritual goods at home. Incense above all was burned nonstop in temple rituals across Egypt. This made a steady supply from Punt a real need, not just a show of royal wealth. This is a useful case study in scarcitySKAIR-sih-teenot having enough of something people want or need.: Egypt lacked certain resources it needed. Rather than simply doing without them or seizing them by force, Hatshepsut's government organized a large, carefully planned trading trip to get them through fair exchange.
⚙️ TECHNOLOGY SPOTLIGHT · TRADE AND SCARCITY
Photo: Olaf Tausch, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

Every civilization faces the same basic problem: scarcity, not having enough of something people want or need. Egypt had plentiful grain and stone, but it lacked incense, ebony, and other goods its temples and elites demanded. Hatshepsut's Punt expedition shows one common answer to scarcity: organized trade. Rather than seizing goods by force or simply doing without, her government sent ships, sailors, and trade goods on a long journey to exchange for what Egypt needed. This same basic pattern, a society identifying what it lacks and organizing to trade for it, will reappear across ancient history, from Phoenician traders to Persian roads.

Hatshepsut also spent resources on building projects at home. At the great temple of KarnakKAR-naka huge temple complex at Thebes, dedicated mainly to the god Amun., she raised a pair of tall granite obelisksOB-uh-liska tall, four-sided stone pillar that narrows to a point at the top, often set up in pairs at a temple entrance., four-sided pillars carved from single blocks of stone, built for the god Amun. One still stands today, nearly 97 feet tall, among the tallest ever raised in Egypt. Cutting and moving a single block of stone that size took hundreds of workers. It likely also took barges built strong enough to carry the stone down the Nile without breaking apart. Her mortuary temple at Deir el-Bahari, cut into cliffs across the river from Thebes, was designed by her chief steward and architect, a trusted official named Senenmut🔊SEN-en-mootHatshepsut's chief steward and architect, who oversaw her building projects and tutored her daughter., who also served as tutor to her young daughter.
👤 HISTORICAL FIGURE · SENENMUT
Photo: Rijksmuseum van Oudheden, Leiden, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

SenenmutSEN-en-mootHatshepsut's chief steward and architect, who oversaw her building projects and tutored her daughter. served as Hatshepsut's chief steward and architect, likely overseeing the design of her mortuary temple at Deir el-Bahari. He also tutored her daughter, Neferure, and left behind more statues of himself than almost any other non-royal official of the New Kingdom.
🏙️ CITIES · THEBES
Photo: Chris Devers, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

Thebestheebza major city in southern Egypt, the New Kingdom's religious capital and home to the temple of Karnak., in southern Egypt, served as the New Kingdom's religious capital and the site of the great temple of Karnak. Hatshepsut's mortuary temple at nearby Deir el-Bahari still stands today, cut into the cliffs across the river from the city.
📚 A DIFFERENT KIND OF GREATNESS

Compare Hatshepsut's approach to what you might expect from a bold New Kingdom pharaoh eager to prove himself through war. Hatshepsut's Punt expedition, and the peaceful building projects that filled much of her reign, stand for a real, clear choice: greatness reached through careful rule, careful peace-making, and strong trade, rather than through the battlefield. Whether this made her a lesser pharaoh than a conquering warrior-king is a real question worth thinking about, not one with a clear answer already settled. Her stepson, Thutmose III, chose a very different path to greatness once the throne became fully his own.
💪 KEEP THIS IN MIND

Hatshepsut reached two decades on the throne, and left behind obelisks, a temple, and a famous voyage, without building her name mainly through war. Whether that counts as a lesser kind of greatness than a warrior-king's is a real question, and her stepson Thutmose III offers a warrior-king to compare her against.

📖 TODAY'S FOCUS
How do you read a source honestly when it mixes careful reasoning with tall tales?

Most ancient sources come from the civilizations themselves. One source is different: it comes from Herodotus, a Greek outsider writing about Egypt roughly two centuries after Piye. This lesson teaches you to read Herodotus the way a careful historian does, telling apart his own reasoned judgment from the stories he repeats while openly doubting them.

section: BY THE END OF THIS LESSON YOU WILL BE ABLE TO…
text: Most ancient sources come from the civilizations themselves: royal writings, law codes, king lists, and office records. One source is different. It comes from an outsider, a Greek traveler writing roughly two centuries after Piye, who set out to describe Egypt for readers who had never seen it.
📚 MEET HERODOTUS
🌐 FOREIGN LANGUAGE VOCABULARY

**Herodotus** 🔊heh-ROD-uh-tusa Greek writer of the fifth century BC, often called the Father of History for his careful, questioning approach to the past., a Greek writer of the fifth century BC, often called the "Father of History" for his careful, questioning approach to the past.

Herodotusheh-ROD-uh-tusa Greek writer of the fifth century BC, often called the Father of History for his careful, questioning approach to the past., born in the Greek city of Halicarnassus in the fifth century BC, is often called the "Father of History." That title is not because he was the first person ever to write about the past. It is because he was the first to approach it the way modern historians try to. He traveled to see things for himself. He asked more than one source. He told his readers plainly when he was unsure or doubtful, rather than just repeating whatever he had been told as settled fact. This careful, questioning approach to the past is the start of what historians today call historiographyhis-tor-ee-OG-ruh-feethe study of how history gets written, and of which sources deserve trust.. Historiography is the study of how history gets written and which sources deserve trust. In other words, it asks two questions at the same time: what happened, and how do we actually know that? His book, the *Histories*, gives an entire section, Book II, to Egypt.

Herodotus deserves careful reading, not blind trust. He really did travel, and he really did question Egyptian priests and other local sources. Much of what he reports about Egyptian customs, worship, and the Nile's flooding holds up well against what archaeology and Egypt's own sources confirm. In other words, when we can check his work against other evidence, he usually comes out looking honest and careful. But he was also a foreigner working through translators. He wrote centuries after some of the events he describes. He was willing to pass along stories he found amazing, even when he openly doubted them himself. Reading him well means learning to tell these two kinds of things apart.
📚 TWO KINDS OF CLAIM

Consider two examples from his own text. Herodotus lists three different Greek ideas for why the Nile floods every year on a steady summer schedule. One idea blamed strong seasonal winds pushing the river back on itself. A second blamed melting snow far to the south. A third pointed to a great ocean Greeks believed circled the whole world. Herodotus argues against the first two ideas. He leans toward a version closer to the third. He weighs each one and offers his own reasoned judgment, a truly historical way of handling a real puzzle. Modern science instead credits heavy summer rains falling on the Ethiopian highlands, far south of Egypt, feeding the river until it rises and spreads across its banks each year. But he also repeats a story about a phoenix bird that is said to carry its dead father's body, wrapped in sweet-smelling resin, from Arabia to the temple of the sun once every five hundred years. This is a story he tells his readers he does not fully believe. He adds only that this is what the Egyptians themselves say. That one small word, "say," carried honestly through a whole text, is itself a piece of historical method worth noticing. Herodotus is not lying to us. He is showing his work. In other words, he lets his readers see the seam between what he checked himself and what he only heard from someone else. That seam is exactly what good historical reading looks for.
🎯 TRY IT: READING HERODOTUS Sort two of Herodotus's own claims by the kind of evidence behind them. "It is said to carry its father's body, wrapped in sweet-smelling resin, all the way from Arabia to

Photo: Palazzo Massimo, Rome, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

Herodotusheh-ROD-uh-tusa Greek writer of the fifth century BC, often called the Father of History for his careful, questioning approach to the past. was a Greek writer of the fifth century BC, born in Halicarnassus. His book, the *Histories*, is one of the earliest surviving works of history in the Western tradition, and its Book II is a main window into ancient Egypt as an outsider saw it.

section: A DYNASTY THAT LOOKED TO THE PAST
text: 📚 A DYNASTY THAT LOOKED TO THE PAST

section: A DYNASTY THAT LOOKED TO THE PAST
text: Egypt's own story continues past the Kushite pharaohs. After Assyria's sack of Thebes in 663 BC weakened Kushite rule, a new Egyptian dynasty rose from the Delta city of **Sais**, a period historians call the Saite DynastySAY-itethe family of Egyptian kings who ruled from the Delta city of Sais, about 664 to 525 BC, known for reviving old Egyptian art styles. (664 to 525 BC). Saite kings, unlike most earlier pharaohs, welcomed Greek traders and soldiers into Egypt. They even let Greek merchants build their own trading town, called Naukratis, in the Nile Delta. This new openness to outsiders is likely a real reason Herodotus, a Greek himself, could travel through Egypt so freely two centuries later. His own visit to Egypt likely came during or just after this era, which helps explain how much he was able to see and record for himself.

section: A DYNASTY THAT LOOKED TO THE PAST
text: The Saite pharaohs are worth noticing for a reason that runs through ancient history: not everything in history moves forward. Saite artists and builders studied and copied the styles of the Old Kingdom on purpose. That was the pyramid age of the Old Kingdom. They copied ancient tomb writings on purpose. They brought back nearly thousand year old art styles by choice, down to fine details of pose and dress found on tomb walls far older than their own time. This was not laziness or a lack of new ideas. It was a planned choice: a civilization looking to its own deep past for the right to rule and a sense of steadiness during an uncertain present. It is exactly the kind of pattern worth remembering. History is not one long climb toward something better. Sometimes a civilization's most confident move is to look backward rather than forward. In other words, the Saite kings were not stuck in old habits by accident. They chose to look backward on purpose, because Egypt's own deep past gave them a kind of strength that a brand new style never could.

section: A DYNASTY THAT LOOKED TO THE PAST
text: Egypt's own freedom, however, was not built to last. Beyond its borders, first Assyria, and later a much larger power still, was changing the whole Near East. Egypt would soon be pulled into that story directly, when Persia conquered it. For now, the story turns north and east, to the empire whose rise Egypt's own weakness helped make possible. In other words, as Egypt grows weaker at home, somewhere else, a new power is quietly growing stronger.
💪 KEEP THIS IN MIND

Herodotus rewards careful reading precisely because he shows his own work, letting readers see the seam between what he checked himself and what he only heard. As Egypt's own freedom fades under a much larger power's rise, the story turns to that power directly.

section: Why did Egypt unify almost overnight, while Mesopotamia took centuries?
text: Why did Egypt unify almost overnight, while Mesopotamia took centuries?

section: Why did Egypt unify almost overnight, while Mesopotamia took centuries?
text: Mesopotamia offers a useful contrast. It was a land built from two rivers that could flood without warning. It had dozens of cities fighting for power, with centuries of shifting rule between them. Egypt tells a nearly opposite story from its very start. One river, the Nile RiverNYLEthe long river running through Egypt from south to north, flooding its banks every year and making farming possible in an otherwise dry land., floods on such a steady schedule that Egyptian farmers could set their whole year by it. One long strip of farmland, boxed in by desert on both sides, made outside attack harder. It also made it easier to picture the land as one single place. Sumer took centuries to slowly crawl toward kingship. Egypt's story is not like that. It opens with one sharp act of unity that historians can almost point to like the starting shot of a race.

section: A RIVER THAT KEEPS ITS PROMISES
text: 📚 A RIVER THAT KEEPS ITS PROMISES

section: A RIVER THAT KEEPS ITS PROMISES
text: Every year, snowmelt and rains far to the south sent the Nile rising over its banks. It rose each summer, then fell back each fall. This flood, called the inundationin-un-DAY-shunthe yearly flood of the Nile River, which covered nearby farmland with rich, dark soil., left behind a fresh layer of dark, rich soil across the farmland. Egyptians called their own land Kemet, "the black land," for that soil. They called the desert beyond it deshret, the "red land." This steady pattern mattered a great deal. A Mesopotamian farmer faced a river that might flood too hard, or fail to rise at all, in a given year. A Nile farmer, for most of Egyptian history, could count on the flood arriving close to the same weeks each year. It usually began in June and peaked by September, then pulled back in time for planting.

section: A RIVER THAT KEEPS ITS PROMISES
text: Egyptian officials even built stone gauges called nilometers along the riverbank to measure the flood's height each year and guess how good the harvest would be. One famous nilometer still stands today on the island of Elephantine, near modern Aswan, marked with lines that once tracked flood heights year after year. Farming itself did not begin in Egypt on its own, though. It reached the Nile Valley from the Fertile Crescent, the region where farming first took hold. It spread south and west by around 5200 BC. Egypt's true skill was not inventing farming. It was fitting farming, with real success, to a kind and steady river.
📚 TWO LANDS BECOME ONE

For centuries before it became one kingdom, Egypt was really two lands. Upper Egyptthe southern half of Egypt, a narrow strip of farmland along the river valley. lay to the south, a string of towns strung along the narrow river valley. Lower Egyptthe northern half of Egypt, centered on the wide, marshy Nile Delta. lay to the north, centered on the wide, marshy Nile Deltathe fan-shaped area where the Nile splits into many smaller channels before reaching the Mediterranean Sea., where the river fans out toward the Mediterranean Sea. Around 3100 BC, a ruler most historians call Narmer🔊NAR-merthe ruler most historians credit with joining Egypt's two lands into one kingdom, around 3100 BC. brought these two lands under one crown.

This event is shown on the **Narmer Palette**, a carved stone slab found at Hierakonpolishy-air-uh-KON-poh-lisa city in Upper Egypt where the Narmer Palette was found. in Upper Egypt. It shows a king wearing the White Crown of Upper Egypt on one side and the Red Crown of Lower Egypt on the other. On both sides, he is shown striking down a bound enemy in a formal pose of conquest. The Palette also carries one of the very first known cases of a king's name written down in Egypt, framed inside a small box above his figure. Some historians think an earlier ruler, known only as Scorpion from a second carved macehead, may have begun the work of joining Egypt that Narmer later finished, or simply claimed credit for. Whether the Palette records one clear war, a longer process of joining squeezed into one single picture, or something in between is a real debate among historians today.
🌐 FOREIGN LANGUAGE VOCABULARY

**Narmer** 🔊NAR-merthe ruler most historians credit with joining Egypt's two lands into one kingdom, around 3100 BC. is credited with uniting Upper and Lower Egypt. Egyptian kings were charged with protecting **cosmic order and justice** (*ma'at* 🔊mah-AHTthe truth and balance that ancient Egyptians believed kept the whole world working the right way, a duty every pharaoh had to protect.).
👤 HISTORICAL FIGURE · NARMER
Photo: anonymous ancient Egyptian carver, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

NarmerNAR-merthe ruler most historians credit with joining Egypt's two lands into one kingdom, around 3100 BC. is the ruler most historians credit with joining Upper and Lower Egypt into one kingdom, around 3100 BC. Almost everything known about him comes from a single carved stone slab, the Narmer Palette, found at Hierakonpolis.

section: MEMPHIS AND A KING FROM THE START
text: 📚 MEMPHIS AND A KING FROM THE START

section: MEMPHIS AND A KING FROM THE START
text: After Egypt was joined, a new capital, **Memphis**, was built near the border of Upper and Lower Egypt. This choice was meant to stand for the joining of the two lands. From nearly this same starting point, Egyptian kingship took a shape unlike anything Mesopotamia had built. Sumerian and Akkadian kings built their power slowly. They often still had to answer to priests or councils of elders. Kingship itself only slowly pulled apart from temple rule in Mesopotamia.

section: MEMPHIS AND A KING FROM THE START
text: Egypt's king, called pharaohFAIR-ohthe title used for the king of Egypt in later periods of its history. in later times, was treated from a very early point as a living god. He was seen as an image of the falcon god Horus on earth, in charge of keeping cosmic order and justice🔊MAH-aht (ma'at)the truth and balance that ancient Egyptians believed kept the whole world working the right way, a duty every pharaoh had to protect.: the cosmic order, truth, and balance that kept the whole world running the right way. The word pharaoh itself first meant "great house," a name for the royal palace, before it later came to mean the king himself. Dynastic Egypt, once begun, would go on to last more than three thousand years, one of the longest runs of any civilization in world history. This is a truly different idea of kingship. It is not a man chosen by the gods to rule, as Hammurabi would later claim. It is a man who was, in some real sense, seen as divine himself. Egyptian writing, called hieroglyphicshy-ruh-GLIF-iksEgypt's early writing system, made of small pictures that stood for sounds, words, or ideas., appears on royal monuments like the Narmer Palette from this same early period. It records the names and titles of kings almost from the moment Egypt was joined.
👥 PEOPLES · THE EGYPTIANS
Tomb painting, unknown ancient Egyptian artist, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

Early Egyptians wore simple linen clothing suited to a hot, dry climate: kilts for men, close-fitting dresses for women, and wide bead collars for the wealthy. Eye makeup made from ground minerals was common for both men and women, worn to guard against sun glare and eye disease as much as for looks.
📚 A QUESTION WORTH HOLDING ONTO

This difference is worth sitting with rather than rushing past. Why might one river valley civilization arrive at total, sudden divine kingshipdih-VYNE KING-shipthe belief that a ruler is not just chosen by the gods, but is in some real way a god. almost from its first united moment? Why did another spend centuries working out the pull between kings and priests, cities and empires? Geography answers part of the question. Egypt's desert walls on both sides gave a joining king fewer rivals to answer to than a Mesopotamian ruler ringed by rival cities and open plains. But geography alone does not settle the matter.
🏙️ CITIES · MEMPHIS
Photo: Daniel Csörföly, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons. (Ruins at the site of ancient Memphis today.)

**Memphis** stood near the point where the Nile Delta begins, chosen as Egypt's first capital because it sat right on the border between Upper and Lower Egypt. For centuries afterward, it remained one of Egypt's most important cities.
💪 KEEP THIS IN MIND

Egypt's sudden unity under Narmer, and the total divine kingship that followed almost right away, look nothing like Sumer's slow centuries of city-states and priest-kings. Geography explains part of that difference, but not all of it.

📖 TODAY'S FOCUS
What did it really take to build the Great Pyramid, and who built it?

Roughly five centuries after Narmer joined Egypt, the Old Kingdom's pharaohs turned their new power into the boldest building projects the ancient world had yet tried. This lesson looks at what building the Great Pyramid actually took, and at who really built it, since the popular picture of whip-driven slaves does not match the evidence. It also turns to a very different kind of Egyptian text: not a king's boast, but real advice for living well.

section: BY THE END OF THIS LESSON YOU WILL BE ABLE TO…
text: Roughly five centuries after Narmer joined Egypt, it entered a time historians call the Old Kingdomthe period of Egyptian history, about 2686 to 2181 BC, when strong pharaohs ruled a unified Egypt and built its greatest pyramids. (about 2686 to 2181 BC). This was an age of strong, centered pharaoh rule. It was also the age of the boldest building projects the ancient world had yet tried. This lesson looks at the Old Kingdom's most famous monument. It also looks at what building that monument really took, and at a very different kind of Egyptian text: not a king's boast, but real advice for living well.
🌐 FOREIGN LANGUAGE VOCABULARY

New this lesson: **Khufu** 🔊KOO-foothe pharaoh under whom the Great Pyramid of Giza was built, ruling roughly 2589 to 2566 BC. and **Ptahhotep** 🔊tah-HOH-tepa vizier whose collected wise sayings, the Instructions of Ptahhotep, are among the oldest surviving wisdom writing in the world..
📚 THE GREAT PYRAMID

Around 2560 BC, under the pharaoh Khufu🔊KOO-foothe pharaoh under whom the Great Pyramid of Giza was built, ruling roughly 2589 to 2566 BC., workers finished the **Great Pyramid of Giza**. It first rose about 481 feet high. It was built from more than two million blocks of limestone and granite. Some granite blocks, hauled from quarries at Aswan far to the south, weighed as much as 80 tons each. The Greek historian Herodotus later claimed the pyramid took twenty years to build, though modern experts still debate the exact number.

For a long time, popular stories pictured this as the work of huge crowds of enslaved workers driven by the whip. Evidence dug up from workers' villages near the pyramids tells a new story. Diggers found bakeries, breweries, and animal bones nearby. These finds show that pyramid workers ate a solid diet that included beer and meat. They lived in planned camps, not scattered huts. The workforce seems to have included skilled full-time builders. Alongside them worked changing crews of Egyptian farmers. These farmers were likely called up for a set season each year. This was likely during the months of the inundationin-un-DAY-shunthe yearly flood of the Nile River, which covered nearby farmland with rich, dark soil., when Nile floodwaters left the fields underwater anyway. Some work crews even carved their own team names into the stone blocks they moved. Names like "Friends of Khufu" turn up on blocks today, a small, human trace of pride left behind by common laborers.

None of this means the work was easy or freely chosen the way a modern job is. But it was organized, paid, state labor. It was not simple mass slavery, and that popular mistake is worth correcting plainly rather than letting it stand. In 1954, workers clearing rubble near the pyramid found a complete wooden boat, taken apart and sealed inside a pit. It had likely been built for Khufu's own journey through the afterlife. Once put back together, the boat stretched more than 140 feet long, its ancient cedar planks still sound enough to fit together again.

Building the pyramid took great skill and precision. Its sides line up with true north within a tiny fraction of a degree. Khufu's engineers had no compass or telescope. They used only careful eyesight, surveying tools, and star sightings to reach that precision. Ramps, levers, and copper tools, not any wheeled machine, moved and shaped the stone. Whatever else can be argued about the Old Kingdom, one thing stands out. Its power to organize labor, supplies, and exact engineering skill on this scale, kept up across decades of rule, was real. Nothing else on Earth matched it at the time.
👤 HISTORICAL FIGURE · KHUFU
Photo: Prof. Mortel, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

KhufuKOO-foothe pharaoh under whom the Great Pyramid of Giza was built, ruling roughly 2589 to 2566 BC. ruled Egypt around 2589 to 2566 BC. He is remembered today almost entirely for one achievement: ordering the building of the Great Pyramid of Giza, the largest pyramid ever built and one of the most massive structures in human history. Ironically, this small ivory statuette, only a few inches tall, is the only confirmed image of him that survives.
📚 PTAHHOTEP'S ADVICE

Not every Old Kingdom text is a royal monument. The **Instructions of Ptahhotep**, one of the oldest surviving wisdom texts anywhere in the world, is written as advice from an aging viziervih-ZEERa pharaoh's top official, in charge of running the day-to-day business of government. to his son and successor. The full text survives today mainly through a later copy called the Prisse Papyrus. Historians are not fully sure just when Ptahhotep🔊tah-HOH-tepa vizier whose collected wise sayings, the Instructions of Ptahhotep, are among the oldest surviving wisdom writing in the world. lived. The text names him as vizier to a king called Djedkare Isesi, which would place him late in the Old Kingdom, well over a century after Khufu. Egyptian tradition later said Ptahhotep lived to the legendary age of 110 years, a symbol of the wisdom his advice claimed to offer.

Rather than boasting of conquest or divine favor, Ptahhotep's advice is about everyday virtue. It covers how to listen well. It covers how a powerful man should treat those below him without pride. It covers how to control one's temper, and how to remember that wisdom can come from anyone, no matter their rank. Some of that advice survives, written down long ago in hieroglyphicshy-ruh-GLIF-iksEgypt's early writing system, made of small pictures that stood for sounds, words, or ideas. on papyrus. Notice how different this text feels from a pharaoh's grand monument. Where Narmer's Palette and a pyramid's huge size show power outward, Ptahhotep's instructions look inward. They point at the private, personal virtues, courtesy, self-control, and patience, that Egyptian culture expected even from its most powerful men.
👤 HISTORICAL FIGURE · PTAHHOTEP
Photo: Gary Todd, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons. (A papyrus scroll, the same kind of material that preserved Ptahhotep's Instructions.)

Ptahhoteptah-HOH-tepa vizier whose collected wise sayings, the Instructions of Ptahhotep, are among the oldest surviving wisdom writing in the world. served as vizier, a pharaoh's top official, during the Old Kingdom. He is remembered today for a collection of wise sayings on courtesy, self-control, and good leadership, among the oldest surviving wisdom writing anywhere in the world.
📚 DIVINE KINGSHIP, HELD IN TENSION

Taken together, the evidence presents a pharaoh who was two things at once. On one hand, he was treated as a living god in charge of keeping **ma'at** across the entire universe. On the other hand, his own officials wrote guidance on ordinary human virtues like patience and self-control. These do not have to be opposites. A king understood to stand for cosmic order might be expected, just because of that role, to model the same personal order and self-government at every level. That standard would run from the pharaoh's own household down to the humblest farmer's.

Compare this again to Mesopotamia. Hammurabi backed his rule with a promise of justice enforced through law. Egypt's Old Kingdom pharaoh backed his rule with a claimed link to the divine itself. This lesson suggests that claim was backed up by a call for personal virtue, not law alone.
⚙️ TECHNOLOGY SPOTLIGHT · DIVINE KINGSHIP
Photo: Jon Bodsworth, copyrighted free use, via Wikimedia Commons.

Egyptian kingship claimed something Mesopotamian kingship never quite claimed for itself. A Sumerian or Akkadian king ruled with the gods' favor, chosen and backed by them, but still a man set apart from the gods themselves. Egypt's pharaoh, from the very start of the unified kingdom, was treated as an actual living god on earth, an image of the falcon god Horus, responsible for keeping ma'at, the truth and balance holding the whole universe together. This is a truly different idea of kingship, one worth comparing against Mesopotamia's model.
💪 KEEP THIS IN MIND

The Old Kingdom shows Egypt's pharaoh from two directions at once: a living god who could organize a workforce and an engineering feat unmatched anywhere on Earth, and a man whose own vizier still wrote that patience and courtesy mattered. Keep watching whether that divine claim holds steady as Egypt's story continues.

text: 📖 GLOSSARY OF SUBJECT VOCABULARY
There are some vocabulary words in this lesson worth reviewing. Tap or hover any highlighted word in the text for a quick reminder, or use the list below.
Bronze Age Collapse🔊the sudden, poorly understood breakdown of many great powers across the eastern Mediterranean and Near East, roughly 1200 to 1150 BC.
Sea Peoples🔊a shifting coalition of seaborne raiders and migrants, named by modern scholars, blamed for attacks on Egypt and other powers during the Bronze Age Collapse.
systems collapse🔊a breakdown in which several linked problems (drought, war, broken trade routes) combine and make each other worse, rather than one single cause bringing down a whole civilization.

🗺️ MAIN MAP · THE EASTERN MEDITERRANEAN IN CRISIS Map: via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0. This map traces likely Sea Peoples' raiding routes across the eastern Mediterranean, marking Medinet Habu in
📖 TODAY'S FOCUS
What could bring down almost every great power at once, in just a few decades?

Civilizations across the ancient Near East and beyond had long been rising, growing, and fighting. Then, nearly all of it comes apart at once. Between roughly 1200 and 1150 BC, the Hittite Empire collapses, Mycenaean Greece is devastated, and Egypt barely survives an assault by a shifting coalition modern historians call the Sea Peoples. Historians still do not agree on a single cause, and this lesson will not pretend the question is fully settled.

text: **I will be able to** explain why a good historian resists inventing a tidy explanation the evidence does not support.

section: BY THE END OF THIS LESSON YOU WILL BE ABLE TO…
text: Civilizations across the ancient Near East and beyond had long been rising, growing, and fighting: Sumer, Akkad, Babylon, Egypt, the Indus Valley, Shang China, the Hittites, and the palace worlds of Crete and Mycenae. Then, nearly all of it comes apart at once, and no single city or kingdom of that world is left fully untouched by what follows. Between roughly 1200 and 1150 BC, in the span of just a few decades, the eastern Mediterranean world went through one of the most dramatic collapses in recorded history. Historians still do not agree on just why, and this lesson will not pretend the question is fully settled.
🌐 FOREIGN LANGUAGE VOCABULARY

**Ramesses III** 🔊RAM-uh-seezpharaoh of Egypt from about 1186 to 1155 BC, who repelled a major Sea Peoples assault. and **Merneptah** 🔊MER-nep-tahpharaoh of Egypt from about 1213 to 1203 BC, whose victory stele contains the earliest known mention of "Israel." both appear later in this lesson.
📚 WHO WERE THE SEA PEOPLES?

Egyptian records from this period describe repeated attacks by a shifting group of seaborne raiders and migrants. Modern historians call them the Sea Peoplesa shifting coalition of seaborne raiders and migrants, named by modern scholars, blamed for attacks on Egypt and other powers during the Bronze Age Collapse.. This is a label invented by nineteenth-century scholars, not a name these groups used for themselves. Egyptian writings name several distinct peoples within this coalition. Egyptian scribes called them the Peleset, Sherden, Shekelesh, Denyen, and Weshesh. The Peleset most of all are widely thought to be the ancestors of the Philistines. Their exact origins are still debated among historians today. They may have come from the Aegean, Anatolia, the central Mediterranean, or several places at once. What is not in doubt is the timing. These attacks grow sharply worse in these very same years. This is exactly when the Hittite Empire, Mycenaean Greece, and Kassite Babylon all collapse or suffer heavy damage.

Around 1208 BC, shortly before this wider crisis, the pharaoh Merneptah🔊MER-nep-tahpharaoh of Egypt from about 1213 to 1203 BC, whose victory stele contains the earliest known mention of "Israel." had already fought off a coalition of enemies. It included Libyan raiders and groups later linked to the Sea Peoples. He marked his win on a stele. That stele happens to hold the earliest known mention anywhere of a people called "Israel," living in CanaanKAY-nunthe region along the eastern Mediterranean coast, roughly modern Israel, the Palestinian territories, and Lebanon.. But the more serious crisis was still to come. The Medinet Habu inscription of Ramesses III🔊RAM-uh-seezpharaoh of Egypt from about 1186 to 1155 BC, who repelled a major Sea Peoples assault., describes a much larger Sea Peoples attack reaching Egypt's own borders roughly a generation later, one Egypt survived, but at lasting cost.
👤 HISTORICAL FIGURE · MERNEPTAH
Photo: via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

MerneptahMER-nep-tahpharaoh of Egypt from about 1213 to 1203 BC, whose victory stele contains the earliest known mention of "Israel." ruled Egypt from about 1213 to 1203 BC. His victory stele, celebrating a win over Libyan raiders, contains the earliest known writing anywhere naming "Israel."
📚 A CASE STUDY IN HISTORIOGRAPHY

This is a moment where being honest about the evidence matters more than telling a tidy story. It would be tempting to tell this story as one clean tale: one cause, one villain, one clear turning point. The evidence will not support that kind of story. Historians have proposed drought and long-lasting famine, weakening royal treasuries and pushing groups to migrate and raid. Others point to political failure at home, revolts, and breakdowns in the complex trade networks that bronze production itself depended on. Bronze needs tin, and tin had to travel huge distances to reach Bronze Age workshops. Fragile palace economies depended on steady tribute and trade flowing in all the time. They may have been quick to fall apart once any one link in that chain snapped. Still others describe a kind of systems collapsea breakdown in which several linked problems (drought, war, broken trade routes) combine and make each other worse, rather than one single cause bringing down a whole civilization., in which several of these pressures combine and feed each other. In this picture, no single cause alone would have been enough to bring down so much at once. Several causes together, though, proved too much to stop. The honest, current answer from scholars is that several of these factors were likely working together. Just how they combined is still not fully understood, and it may never be settled with full confidence.

This is one of the clearest examples anywhere in the ancient world of how messy real historical change can be. There is no march toward sure progress here, no plan unfolding as it should. Great powers, the Hittite Empire above all, simply stop existing within a matter of decades. Others, Egypt and Mesopotamia among them, survive, deeply wounded. They never become quite the same civilizations they were before. At the trading city of Ugarit in Syria, archaeologists found a letter from the king's own officials still baking in a kiln, a plea for ships and help that was never sent in time before the city burned. History does not owe anyone a tidy explanation. A good historian resists making one up where the evidence will not support it.
📚 EGYPT, WOUNDED BUT ALIVE

Ramesses III's forces did succeed in beating back the Sea Peoples assault, in a major land and sea battle the Medinet Habu inscription describes and celebrates in vivid detail. Egyptian carvings show ships locked in close combat, archers on both riverbanks, and captured Sea Peoples warriors bound and paraded before the pharaoh. One likely Egyptian tactic was to draw enemy ships into the narrow, shallow channels of the Nile Delta itself. There, the enemy ships had little room to turn or flee. Rows of Egyptian archers on the banks could then fire down on them at close range.
But victory came at a real cost. Egypt's New Kingdom survived the crisis, but its money, land, and standing abroad never fully came back. The following century sees Egyptian power steadily fading.
👤 HISTORICAL FIGURE · RAMESSES III
Photo: via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 4.0.

Ramesses IIIRAM-uh-seezpharaoh of Egypt from about 1186 to 1155 BC, who repelled a major Sea Peoples assault. ruled Egypt from about 1186 to 1155 BC. He repelled a major Sea Peoples invasion in his eighth year as pharaoh, though the cost of that fight left Egypt permanently weaker.
👥 PEOPLES · THE SEA PEOPLES
Photo: via Wikimedia Commons, CC0.

Egyptian carvings show Sea Peoples warriors wearing tall feathered or spiked headdresses, kilts, and round shields, arriving with entire families and ox-carts loaded with belongings, a picture of migration as much as invasion.

section: BATTLE EGYPT AGAINST THE SEA PEOPLES
text: Fought around 1175 BC near Egypt's Nile Delta borders, this combined land and naval battle is unusual for having a naval fight recorded in such visual detail. Egyptian archers on shore and aboard ships trapped the invaders' vessels, a rare surviving picture of Bronze Age naval combat.
💪 KEEP THIS IN MIND
Egypt survived the Sea Peoples, but wounded, and its power never fully returned.

section: Would you gamble your whole army on a single narrow mountain pass?
text: When Hatshepsut died, her stepson Thutmose III became sole ruler and chose a very different path to greatness: the battlefield. His first campaign, against a rebel coalition at Megiddo, produced the earliest battle in world history with a detailed surviving account, and it turned on one risky decision his own officers argued against.

section: BY THE END OF THIS LESSON YOU WILL BE ABLE TO…
text: When **Hatshepsut** died around 1458 BC, her stepson Thutmose III🔊thoot-MOH-suhpharaoh of Egypt from about 1479 to 1425 BC, Hatshepsut's stepson and successor. at last became sole ruler of Egypt in more than name. For years, he had stood as co-regent in his stepmother's shadow. Where Hatshepsut had built her legacy on trade and careful rule, Thutmose III built his on the battlefield. Over his reign he would lead as many as seventeen trips into the Levant. Later historians gave him a nickname for it: the "Napoleon of Egypt." His first campaign came almost right after he took full power. It produced the earliest battle in world history for which a detailed, clear account survives.
🌐 FOREIGN LANGUAGE VOCABULARY
New this lesson: **Thutmose III** 🔊thoot-MOH-suhpharaoh of Egypt from about 1479 to 1425 BC, Hatshepsut's stepson and successor..
📚 A REBELLION IN CANAAN

A coalitionkoh-uh-LISH-una group of separate rulers or states that join forces for a shared goal, such as a rebellion or a war. of Canaanite and Syrian rulers had gathered at the fortified city of **Megiddo**, in modern northern Israel. They were backed by the strong kingdom of Mitanni to the northeast. Together, they rose up in open revolt against Egyptian rule. Egyptian records claim the coalition included the chiefs of over 330 towns and cities across Canaan and Syria, a sign of just how big this revolt was. Thutmose III marched his army north to face them. His route took about ten days, moving up the coast road Egyptians called the Ways of Horus. The official Annals of Thutmose III, recorded on temple walls at Karnak, tell what happened next in rare detail for an ancient war record.
📚 A RISKY CHOICE OF ROADS

Three roads led to Megiddo through the surrounding hills. Two were wide, safer routes coming in from the sides. One was a narrow, direct mountain pass called the Aruna Pass. It was so tight that soldiers had to march single file, horse following horse. They would be fully exposed if the enemy chose to attack while the army was strung out along it. According to the Annals, Thutmose III's own war council argued strongly against the narrow pass. They urged him to take one of the safer roads instead. Thutmose III overruled them. He reasoned that the enemy would expect an Egyptian attack from the safer routes. He guessed the enemy would gather their own forces there, leaving the direct pass open. He himself led his army through the narrow pass at its head, sharing the same risk he asked of his soldiers.

The gamble paid off. The Egyptian army came out of the pass with no enemy in sight, just as Thutmose III had guessed. His forces formed up in the open plain before Megiddo while the coalition's forces were still spread out elsewhere. In the battle that followed, the coalition army broke and ran back into the city. The open field was now Thutmose III's. To keep help from reaching the city, Egyptian soldiers built a wooden wall and ditch all the way around Megiddo, cutting it off from the outside. Still, Megiddo itself held out under siege for seven more months before it finally gave up. Egyptian scribes later listed a huge haul of goods taken from the fallen city. The list included hundreds of horses, chariots trimmed with gold, and enough grain to fill Egypt's royal storehouses for years.

section: HELPFUL TO KNOW CONTINGENCY AT THE MOUNTAIN PASS
text: 💡 HELPFUL TO KNOW · CONTINGENCY AT THE MOUNTAIN PASS

section: HELPFUL TO KNOW CONTINGENCY AT THE MOUNTAIN PASS
text: This is worth pausing on as a real historical contingency, in the spirit of Sargon's basket and Hammurabi's late-life wars. Thutmose III's own officers thought the narrow pass was reckless. By ordinary war logic, they had a point. Suppose the coalition army had simply posted a small guard at the pass's far end. The exposed, single-file Egyptian column could have been badly hurt before ever reaching open ground. Nothing about this outcome was set in stone ahead of time. A different set of scouts, a slightly different coalition plan, or a pharaoh less willing to overrule his own generals, and the history of Egypt might record a very different first campaign for Thutmose III.
👤 HISTORICAL FIGURE · THUTMOSE III
Photo: via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 4.0.

Thutmose IIIthoot-MOH-suhpharaoh of Egypt from about 1479 to 1425 BC, Hatshepsut's stepson and successor. ruled Egypt from about 1479 to 1425 BC, spending his early years as co-regent under Hatshepsut before becoming sole pharaoh at her death. He led as many as seventeen military campaigns into the Levant, earning a lasting reputation as one of Egypt's greatest warrior-kings.

section: A LASTING GRIP ON THE LEVANT
text: 📚 A LASTING GRIP ON THE LEVANT

section: A LASTING GRIP ON THE LEVANT
text: Megiddo was only the beginning. Over the next two decades, Thutmose III returned to the Levant again and again. Local rulers who had once rebelled were now forced to send tribute to Egypt each year. Some were even made to hand over their own sons to be raised at the Egyptian royal court. Those sons, once grown, sometimes went home as rulers loyal to Egypt. This was a quiet but strong way of binding a conquered region to the empire without constant war. By the end of his reign, Egypt controlled more land than at any earlier point in its history, stretching from Nubia in the south to the Euphrates River in the north. Thutmose III kept careful written lists of the tribute he collected each year, recording exact counts of gold rings, cattle, timber, and captives from every subject city, a habit of precise record-keeping that echoes the Mesopotamian scribal traditions of Sumer, Akkad, and Babylon.
⚔️ BATTLE · MEGIDDO

Fought around 1457 BC, the Battle of Megiddo is the earliest battle in world history with a detailed surviving account. Thutmose III's risky choice to march his army through a narrow mountain pass, rather than a safer road, caught the rebel coalition by surprise and helped decide the outcome before the fighting even began.
📚 TWO PHARAOHS, TWO VIRTUES

Set beside Hatshepsut's Punt trip, Thutmose III's Megiddo campaign offers a clear contrast in what ancient greatness could look like. Hatshepsut sought careful rule, patience, and strong peace-making. Thutmose III sought a bold gamble he led in person, growing Egyptian power by force. Neither path was clearly the right one. Both rulers are remembered, in their own ways, as strong pharaohs.
💪 KEEP THIS IN MIND
Hatshepsut and Thutmose III ruled back to back, and reached for greatness in almost opposite ways. Neither path was obviously the right one.

section: Can a real civilization run its cities without a king at all?
text: The Indus Valley grew up far from Mesopotamia and Egypt, with little or no contact with either. This lesson meets the Indus Valley civilization: a river valley people with planned cities, standardized weights, and long-distance trade, but no palace, no royal tomb, and no writing that names a single king. That absence is a genuine, unsolved puzzle, not a gap this lesson will pretend to fill in.

section: BY THE END OF THIS LESSON YOU WILL BE ABLE TO…
text: This lesson steps outside the Near East. It looks briefly at two civilizations growing up farther away. One is the Indus Valley, in what is now Pakistan and northwest India. The other is Shang China, along the Yellow River far to the east. But both deserve a real look now. They are true river valley civilizations in their own right. They are also a chance to compare civilizations that grew up in very different ways, each with little or no contact with Mesopotamia and Egypt.

section: A CIVILIZATION BUILT ON A RIVER, LIKE THE OTHERS
text: 📚 A CIVILIZATION BUILT ON A RIVER, LIKE THE OTHERS

section: A CIVILIZATION BUILT ON A RIVER, LIKE THE OTHERS
text: Farming reached the region around the Indus Rivera long river flowing through modern Pakistan, along whose banks the Indus Valley civilization grew. on its own. Wheat, barley, and a local kind of cattle called the zebu were tamed by around 7000 BC. This happened at sites like MehrgarhMER-garan early farming site in the hills near the Indus plain, where wheat, barley, and cattle were first tamed in this region., in the hill country near the river plain. Over the next centuries, this early farming culture grew into a full urban civilization. It reached its height in what historians call the **Mature Harappan** period, roughly 2600 to 1900 BC. This period is named for Harappahuh-RAP-uhthe other of the two largest Indus cities, which gave the whole civilization its name., one of its two greatest cities. The other was Mohenjo-daromoh-HEN-joh-DAR-ohone of the two largest Indus cities, known for its careful street planning and covered drains.. In 1924, the British archaeologist Sir John Marshall told the world about this whole lost civilization for the first time. Marshall's own dig report describes what his team found at Mohenjo-daro. Long before Marshall's find, British railway engineers in the 1850s had already dug up ancient bricks at Harappa. Not knowing what they had found, the engineers crushed thousands of these bricks to use as gravel under new railway tracks, wrecking part of the very civilization Marshall would later announce to the world.
📚 REMARKABLY PLANNED CITIES

What Marshall's digs turned up was startling. Cities were laid out on a precise grid of straight streets. Builders used bricks cut to standard sizes across the whole civilization's land, an area larger than either Mesopotamia or Egypt at the time. Traders also used a shared system of standardized weightsa matched set of weights, built to the same sizes everywhere, used to measure goods fairly across a wide territory.. These were small cube-shaped stones, cut to matching sizes. A trader could use them to measure goods fairly, no matter where in the civilization they traveled. Mohenjo-daro's houses linked to covered brick drains running beneath the streets. Many houses even had private wells and what appear to be early bathing rooms. This level of city planning and clean water would not be matched again in much of the world for centuries.

At the port city of LothalLOH-tuhlan Indus port city with what may be one of the world's earliest tidal dockyards., archaeologists found what may be one of the earliest tidal dockyards built anywhere. This is proof of long-distance sea trade. Indus goods reached as far as Mesopotamia itself, where Sumerian texts speak of a trading partner called "Meluhha," widely thought to be the Indus civilization. Carved stone seals from Indus cities often show animals such as bulls, elephants, and a one-horned creature some call a "unicorn" figure. What these images meant to the people who made them is still unclear.
👥 PEOPLES · THE HARAPPANS
Photo: via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0.

Small clay figurines and carved seals give the best clues to how the Harappans looked and dressed: draped cloth garments, elaborate hairstyles, and layered bead and shell jewelry. This famous small bronze figure, nicknamed the "Dancing Girl," shows bangles worn stacked up one arm, a style some in the region still wear today.
📚 A GENUINE, UNRESOLVED PUZZLE

Here is where the Indus Valley becomes truly strange. It is stranger than the civilizations of Mesopotamia and Egypt. Despite years of careful digging, archaeologists have never found a royal palace anywhere in Indus territory. They have never found a grand temple or a huge royal tomb either. No writing naming a king, a dynasty, or even a single ruler has ever turned up. The Indus scriptthe still-undeciphered writing system found on small carved seals and pottery across the Indus Valley civilization. itself, found on small carved seals and pottery, remains undeciphered to this day. About four hundred distinct symbols have been found so far, usually written from right to left, but the language hidden behind them is still unknown. Scholars still argue over whether it even records a full spoken language. It might instead be something closer to a system of symbols and marks. Very little proof of warfare has turned up either: no walls built against other Indus cities, and no stockpiled weapons.

This lesson will not pretend to solve what expert archaeologists themselves have not solved. Some historians suggest Indus cities were ruled by some kind of shared body, a council of merchants or priests, rather than a single king. Others suspect proof of kingship simply has not survived, or has not yet been found. Still others wonder if Indus society worked by rules quite different from the kingdoms and empires of Mesopotamia and Egypt, with no clean match among its Bronze Age neighbors. The honest answer, at this point in the story, is that nobody knows for sure. A good historian says so plainly, rather than making up a confident answer the evidence does not support. This mature phase of Indus civilization also faded out around 1900 BC. Many experts link this decline to a shifting river system. A once-major river likely dried up over time and left some cities without the water they needed. Even here, though, scholars have not settled on one single cause.
🏙️ CITIES · MOHENJO-DARO
Photo: via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

Mohenjo-daromoh-HEN-joh-DAR-ohone of the two largest Indus cities, known for its careful street planning and covered drains. was built on a precise grid, with wide main streets and narrower side lanes. Its most famous structure, the Great Bath shown here, was a large, carefully waterproofed pool, likely used for ritual bathing rather than everyday washing.
📚 WHY THE PUZZLE MATTERS

This is worth taking seriously as its own kind of lesson. It would be easy to assume every ancient civilization must have looked something like Sumer or Egypt: a king, a temple, a monumental tomb. The Indus Valley shows that civilization does not always need the same political shape everywhere it shows up. Cities, planned streets and drains, workers with special skills, and long-distance trade can all exist without a king at their head. Keep this open question in mind when comparing it with Shang China, a river valley civilization that, unlike the Indus, left plenty of written proof naming its kings by name.
💪 KEEP THIS IN MIND

Civilization does not have to look like Sumer or Egypt to be real. Planned streets, drains, fair weights, and long-distance trade all existed at Mohenjo-daro without any proof of a king at the top. Hold that open question when comparing it with Shang China, a river valley civilization that left behind exactly the kind of written proof of kingship the Indus Valley did not.

section: How do we know what happened before anyone wrote anything down?
text: Farming spread across the Fertile Crescent thousands of years before anyone invented writing. No one alive today watched any of it happen, and no ancient author left behind a diary of the Neolithic Revolution. So how do historians know it happened at all? The answer comes from patient digging, not old books. Two real excavations, one at Jericho and one at Çatalhöyük, show exactly how archaeologists turn buried dirt, stone, and bone into real historical knowledge.
