section: BY THE END OF THIS LESSON YOU WILL BE ABLE TO…
text: By the time of King **Cyaxares** (r. 625 to 585 BC), the Medes were no longer anyone's tribute-paying frontier people. They were one of the two powers that ended the Neo-Assyrian Empire outright. Media joined Babylon in the siege and destruction of Nineveh in 612 BC. In barely more than a century, the Medes had gone from near-invisibility in the historical record to bringing down the largest empire the Near East had yet seen. Herodotus credits Cyaxares with rebuilding the Median army itself. He separated spearmen, archers, and cavalry into their own distinct units. Earlier armies often fought all mixed together instead. Whether or not this specific reform belongs to Cyaxares alone, one thing is clear. A stronger, more organized Median military is what made the siege of Nineveh possible in the first place. In other words, a stronger army is exactly what let the Medes finally settle old scores.
🌐 FOREIGN LANGUAGE VOCABULARY

**Cyaxares** 🔊sy-AK-suh-reezking of Media from 625 to 585 BC, who helped destroy Nineveh and fought Lydia to a negotiated peace., king of Media from 625 to 585 BC, who helped destroy Nineveh and fought Lydia to a negotiated peace.

section: A WAR THAT ENDED WITHOUT A WINNER
text: 📚 A WAR THAT ENDED WITHOUT A WINNER

section: A WAR THAT ENDED WITHOUT A WINNER
text: Cyaxaressy-AK-suh-reezking of Media from 625 to 585 BC, who helped destroy Nineveh and fought Lydia to a negotiated peace.'s Median kingdom soon found itself at war with another rising power to the west. This was **Lydia**, a wealthy kingdom in Anatolia, ruled by King Alyattes. Herodotus describes a war that dragged on for roughly five years with no clear winner on either side. Then, during a battle in its sixth year, something amazing happened. The day suddenly turned to night.

section: A WAR THAT ENDED WITHOUT A WINNER
text: A solar eclipsean event where the sun or moon is blocked from view, in this lesson by the moon passing in front of the sun. interrupted the fighting so completely that both armies stopped at once. Herodotus reports that the Greek thinker Thales of Miletus had predicted this eclipse in advance. Whether or not that detail is exactly true, both sides seem to have been badly shaken. To them, this eclipse was a celestial omensuh-LES-chul OH-menan event in the sky, such as an eclipse or comet, that ancient peoples often read as a sign or warning from the gods., a sign in the sky that the gods themselves were sending a warning. Neither army wanted to defy an omen this dramatic. Both sides quickly pursued peace. They sealed that peace through a marriage between the two royal families. They also agreed on a new, shared border along the **Halys River** in Anatolia. Alyattes's own son, a young prince named Croesus, grew up watching this peace hold. His own remarkable rise, and fall, is a story worth telling in full. In other words, a strange sky event ended a war that years of fighting could not.

section: A WAR THAT ENDED WITHOUT A WINNER
text: Modern astronomers have actually worked backward from this account and calculated the exact date of this eclipse: May 28, 585 BC. This is a genuinely useful tool for historians, not just a fun fact. Eclipses can be calculated exactly, centuries in advance or centuries after the fact. Because of this, a single eclipse mentioned in an ancient text can help pin down the exact dates of everything else connected to it. Assyrian records keep their own list of eclipses too, an official record scholars still use today to check and correct Mesopotamian dates across many different reigns and events. This is one of the clearest examples anywhere of science and history working together to answer the same question: when, exactly, did this happen? In other words, the sky itself can help us pin down exactly when history happened.
⚙️ TECHNOLOGY SPOTLIGHT · READING THE SKY
Photo: via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

Mesopotamian and Near Eastern observers had spent centuries carefully tracking the sky. They recorded the regular movements of the sun, moon, and stars for religious, farming, and government purposes. By the sixth century BC, this patient watching had built up real predictive power over certain celestial omenssuh-LES-chul OH-menan event in the sky, such as an eclipse or comet, that ancient peoples often read as a sign or warning from the gods., events like eclipses that most people still read as messages from the gods rather than natural, foreseeable events.
📚 A DEEP-DIVE SPOTLIGHT ON ASTRONOMY

This episode is a deep-dive spotlight on astronomy. Whether or not Thales specifically deserves credit for predicting this particular eclipse is still debated. Ancient and modern scholars have both argued about it. Either way, the underlying point stands. To most observers, this would have seemed like nothing but a terrifying omen. Instead, it became something at least some people of the time could reportedly see coming ahead of time.

Prediction, even imperfect prediction, is a truly different relationship with the natural world than pure superstition alone. It means asking what will happen next, instead of only reacting once it does. Still, the point should not be overstated. Fear of the eclipse is what actually stopped the battle that day. It was not calm scientific confidence, and it was not some shared trust in Thales's calculations.

section: SLOWLY, THEN ALL AT ONCE, ONE FINAL TIME
text: 📚 SLOWLY, THEN ALL AT ONCE, ONE FINAL TIME

section: SLOWLY, THEN ALL AT ONCE, ONE FINAL TIME
text: Consider the full arc of the Medes' rise. Four centuries of near-total silence in the record. A legendary founding king whose story cannot be fully confirmed. Then, within a single lifetime, an empire strong enough to help destroy Assyria and negotiate as an equal with a wealthy Anatolian kingdom. This is a pattern that recurs in history. It keeps happening, again and again, in very different times and places. History does not move at a steady pace. Long periods of apparent stillness can give way, with startling speed, to real, lasting change. In other words, do not expect history to move at the same speed all the time.

section: SLOWLY, THEN ALL AT ONCE, ONE FINAL TIME
text: One final piece of this pattern deserves to be named directly, since it closes the story with real irony. The same Median royal house had grown so powerful. It had negotiated so successfully with Lydia. Yet it was not destined to stay in power much longer. Within a few decades, Cyaxares's own line would be overthrown. The one who overthrew it was not a foreign invader at all. It was his own grandson, a young Persian vassal king named Cyrus. In other words, the Medes' own rise helped raise up the very man who would end their rule.
👤 HISTORICAL FIGURE · CYAXARES

No contemporary image of Cyaxaressy-AK-suh-reezking of Media from 625 to 585 BC, who helped destroy Nineveh and fought Lydia to a negotiated peace. survives, and no verifiable public-domain artist's depiction could be located this session, so none is shown here. Cyaxares ruled Media from 625 to 585 BC. He helped destroy Nineveh alongside Babylon and fought Lydia to a negotiated peace after a solar eclipse halted their war.
💪 KEEP THIS IN MIND

Slowly, then all at once: four centuries of silence, a legendary founding king, and then, within a single lifetime, an empire strong enough to help destroy Assyria and negotiate as an equal with Lydia. Its own rise, though, helped raise up the very grandson who would end its rule, a young Persian vassal king named Cyrus.

Why does the start of Cyrus's story sound like something already heard twice before?

The Medes stood at the height of their power. They ruled a kingdom strong enough to help destroy Assyria and deal with wealthy Lydia as an equal. But there was a warning in that success. The Median royal house was not going to hold power much longer. It would be overthrown, not by a foreign enemy, but by its own grandson. text: **I will be able to** explain Solon's warning to Croesus and how Croesus's own downfall bore it out.
📚 ANOTHER INFANT, BARELY SAVED

According to Herodotus, King Astyagesas-TY-uh-jeezthe king of Media whose own grandson, Cyrus, overthrew him. of Media, Cyaxares's own son, dreamed that his daughter's newborn son would someday overthrow him. Terrified, Astyages ordered the infant killed. The herdsman given this grim task instead spared the child. He raised the boy in secret as his own. The boy grew up as Cyrus, a Persian vassal youth, and Astyages never learned the truth until it was already too late to matter.

🎯 TRY IT: WHO'S WHO IN THE DREAM Match each description to the person it names in Herodotus's account. The infant secretly spared by a herdsman and raised in obscurity, who grew up to lead a revolt ag

However this story actually began, it should sound familiar right away. The same figure appears three separate times: an abandoned or endangered infant, secretly saved and raised in hiding before rising far beyond what anyone expected. It happened in Sargon's basket. It happened in Romulus and Remus's river rescue. Now it happens again in Cyrus. It is worth saying directly what has only been hinted at before. This is a known kind of story. It shows up across far-apart cultures with no contact at all. Its repeated appearance should make any student rightly careful about taking any single version as sure, word-for-word history. In other words, when the very same tale keeps showing up in unrelated places, that is itself a clue about how legends grow, not proof that the tale is true.

Whatever the truth of his childhood, the grown Cyrus led a Persian revolt that overthrew Astyages around 550 BC. This united Media and Persia under his own rule for the first time. Until this moment, the Medes had been the stronger of the two peoples, with Persia serving as a vassal state beneath them. Cyrus flipped that order permanently, and Persia never again played second to Media. This union marks the true start of the Achaemeniduh-KEE-muh-nidthe Persian royal line founded by Cyrus, and the name historians give to his empire. Persian Empire, named for Cyrus's royal line. That empire would grow larger than anything the ancient Near East had yet seen, larger even than Assyria at its own height.
👤 HISTORICAL FIGURE · CYRUS
Engraving: Charles Texier, 1852, via Wikimedia Commons, CC0.

CyrusSY-rusa Persian vassal king who overthrew his own grandfather Astyages around 550 BC and founded the Achaemenid Persian Empire. (SY-rus) overthrew his grandfather Astyages around 550 BC, united Media and Persia, and founded the Achaemenid Persian Empire, one of the largest empires the ancient world had yet seen. This engraving records the winged-figure relief at his capital, Pasargadae, long associated with Cyrus himself.

section: CROESUS, SOLON, AND A WARNING IGNORED
text: 📚 CROESUS, SOLON, AND A WARNING IGNORED

section: CROESUS, SOLON, AND A WARNING IGNORED
text: Cyrus's next target lay to the west: Lydia, a wealthy Anatolian kingdom. Lydia was now ruled by King CroesusKREE-susthe wealthy king of Lydia, defeated by Cyrus in 547 BC., whose name became a byword for riches in the ancient world. Herodotus tells a good story about Croesus, set some years before his war with Cyrus. In this account, the Athenian lawgiver Solon visited Croesus's court. The king proudly showed off his riches and asked Solon to name the happiest man alive, plainly expecting Solon to name him. Solon instead named two little-known private citizens who had each lived well and died with honor. When Croesus pressed him further, Solon offered a warning rather than praise. Count no man happy, Solon said, until his life has actually ended, since fortune can turn on anyone, however rich, at any time. In other words, do not call your own life a success until it is over and done.

section: CROESUS, SOLON, AND A WARNING IGNORED
text: Croesus, Herodotus tells us, brushed the warning aside as foolish talk. Sure of his own wealth and power, he went to war against the rising Persian empire and lost badly. His kingdom was conquered, and, in most versions of the story, his own life stood in real danger before Cyrus spared him. Whether or not this exact talk with Solon ever truly happened, and Herodotus himself was writing generations after the fact, it holds a piece of Greek moral thinking worth taking to heart on its own terms. Worldly success is not the same thing as a settled, safe happiness, and pride in present fortune has a long history of coming right before a fall. The same lesson appeared once before, in a different shape. There, the Curse of Akkad blamed Naram-Sin's own pride for his empire's fall. Here, a Greek lawgiver offers almost the same warning about one overconfident king.
👤 HISTORICAL FIGURE · ASTYAGES AND CROESUS
Vase painting: attributed to Myson, c. 500 BC, Louvre, via Wikimedia Commons, public domain.

Astyagesas-TY-uh-jeezthe king of Media whose own grandson, Cyrus, overthrew him. was the Median king overthrown by his own grandson, Cyrus. CroesusKREE-susthe wealthy king of Lydia, defeated by Cyrus in 547 BC. was the fabulously wealthy king of Lydia, defeated by Cyrus in 547 BC after ignoring Solon's warning about the fragility of fortune. This Greek vase painting, made not long after Croesus's own lifetime, shows him upon the pyre from a later stage of his legend.
📚 CLOSING

Lydia's conquest in 547 BC brought the wealthy Ionian Greek coastal cities, the same cities Homer's descendants and neighbors called home, under Persian rule for the first time. Cyrus's empire, barely a few years old, had already reached from the Zagros Mountains to the shores of the Aegean Sea. In less than a decade, Cyrus had gone from a hidden infant to the ruler of the largest kingdom the Near East had yet seen, and he was not finished yet.

🗺️ SECONDARY MAP · THE EMPIRE DARIUS INHERITED Map: Ali Zifan, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0. Darius put down his rivals and carved his account of it into a cliff face at Mount Behistun 🔊 beh-hi
📖 TODAY'S FOCUS
Can a single carved cliff face unlock an entire lost language, centuries after the empire that carved it is gone?

Cambyses died in 522 BC, on his way back from Egypt, in ways no surviving source explains for sure. What followed was a real fight over the throne. The man who came out on top, Darius Iduh-RY-usthe Persian king who took the throne after a succession crisis in 522 BC and left behind the Behistun Inscription., left behind an account of his own rise carved directly into a cliff face, in a form that can still be read today.

text: **I will be able to** explain why Egypt's conquest and Darius's secure throne marked a genuine turning point for the whole ancient Near East.
📚 A CONTESTED THRONE

According to Darius's own inscription, a man claiming to be Cambyses's brother, Bardiya, seized the Persian throne while Cambyses was still in Egypt. Darius's account insists this man was actually a fake, an impostor named Gaumata. The real Bardiya, Darius claims, had secretly been killed by Cambyses's own order years earlier. Darius killed the pretender and took the throne for himself. He then spent much of his first year as king putting down a wave of revolts across the empire. An empire this large, stitched together so quickly under Cyrus and Cambyses, was never fully settled the moment a new king took the throne. Darius had to prove, by force, that it truly answered to him.

There is a real limit here. Darius's version is the only full account of these events to survive. It was carved at his own command, to defend his own right to rule. No separate Persian or Egyptian record exists to check his claims against. This does not mean Darius made up the whole story. It does mean a king's own defense of seizing his own throne cannot simply be taken as plain, checked fact. The Cyrus Cylinder's words cannot be taken at face value either, for the exact same reason. A king writing about his own rise to power is never a neutral witness to it.
👤 HISTORICAL FIGURE · DARIUS I
Photo: Patrick C (dynamosquito), via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 2.0.

Darius Iduh-RY-usthe Persian king who took the throne after a succession crisis in 522 BC and left behind the Behistun Inscription. (duh-RY-us) took the Persian throne after Cambyses's death in 522 BC, put down rival claims to it, and left behind the Behistun Inscription, the key that later let scholars read cuneiform again. This relief, carved beside the inscription itself, shows Darius standing over the defeated Gaumata.

section: A ROCK THAT UNLOCKED AN ENTIRE FIELD
text: 📚 A ROCK THAT UNLOCKED AN ENTIRE FIELD

section: A ROCK THAT UNLOCKED AN ENTIRE FIELD
text: The inscription itself is known as the Behistun Inscription. It is carved high into a cliff face at Mount Behistun, in what is now western Iran. Beside the text sits a large relief image. It shows Darius standing over the defeated pretender and a line of other captured rebel leaders. What makes this inscription truly remarkable is not just its content, but its form. The same text appears three times, carved in three different languages and cuneiform scripts. This kind of carving is called a trilingual inscriptiontry-LING-gwula single carved text written out in three different languages side by side.. In other words, one single message, carved three separate times side by side, so that no one who could read any one of the three languages would be left out. Its three versions are written in **Old Persian**, **Elamite**, and Babylonian, the same script used in the Epic of Gilgamesh, Hammurabi's Code, and Ashurbanipal's library tablets.

section: A ROCK THAT UNLOCKED AN ENTIRE FIELD
text: Because the same message appeared in three known and unknown scripts side by side, the Behistun Inscription became cuneiform's own key to deciphermentdee-SY-fur-mentthe work of figuring out how to read a lost or unknown system of writing., in much the way the Rosetta Stone had already done for Egyptian hieroglyphics. In the 1830s and 1840s, a British officer and scholar named Henry RawlinsonRAW-lin-sunthe British scholar who copied the Behistun Inscription at great personal risk and helped decipher Babylonian cuneiform in the 1830s and 1840s. again and again risked his own life climbing the steep, dangerous cliff face to copy the inscription by hand, section by section. Using the Old Persian part, already partly known, as a starting point, Rawlinson and other scholars slowly worked out how to read Babylonian cuneiform too. This is worth stating plainly, as a closing thought. Every cuneiform source, from Sumer onward, can be read today mostly because of the work this single inscription made possible.

text: 👤 HISTORICAL FIGURE · HENRY RAWLINSON
Photo: Arthur J. Melhuish, via Wikimedia Commons/BNF Gallica, public domain.

Henry RawlinsonRAW-lin-sunthe British scholar who copied the Behistun Inscription at great personal risk and helped decipher Babylonian cuneiform in the 1830s and 1840s. (RAW-lin-sun) was a British officer and scholar who risked his life scaling Mount Behistun's cliff face in the 1830s and 1840s to copy Darius's inscription, work that helped unlock cuneiform for modern readers.
📚 ONE EMPIRE, THREE RIVER VALLEYS

With Egypt conquered and Darius's throne now secure, the story has reached a genuine turning point. For the first time in this long story, Mesopotamia, Egypt, and Persia's own homeland all answer to one empire. That is an achievement no earlier power ever managed. Not Sargon. Not Hammurabi. Not even Assyria, at its height. And this empire does not stop looking outward. The Ionian Greek cities along Anatolia's coast have been Persian subjects since Cyrus's conquest of Lydia. Just across the Aegean Sea lie other Greek cities, the mainland city-states. Those cities are about to matter a great deal.
📚 CLOSING

This is where the story ends, and on purpose. One vast empire, newly joined across three river valleys, now looks west toward a scattered handful of small, feuding Greek city-states. At this exact moment, those small cities would seem to have no real chance against an empire this size at all. What actually comes next for Greece, and for Persia's own plans in that direction, is a story for another time.
💪 KEEP THIS IN MIND

One vast empire, newly joined across three river valleys, now looks west toward a scattered handful of small, feuding Greek city-states that would seem to have no real chance against it. What actually happens next is a story for another time.

📖 TODAY'S FOCUS
Can a people be building toward something big for centuries before history notices them?

Most civilizations of the ancient Near East left behind a fairly steady written record of their own rise. The Medes are different: nearly invisible in the record for four centuries, known to outsiders only as one tribute-paying frontier people among many. This lesson reads Herodotus's memorable, and possibly legendary, account of how they are said to have first united under a single king.

section: BY THE END OF THIS LESSON YOU WILL BE ABLE TO…
text: Most civilizations of the ancient Near East left behind a fairly steady written record of their own rise. The Medes are different. That difference is itself worth understanding before their story can even be told.

section: A PEOPLE ALMOST INVISIBLE IN THE RECORD
text: 📚 A PEOPLE ALMOST INVISIBLE IN THE RECORD

section: A PEOPLE ALMOST INVISIBLE IN THE RECORD
text: The Medes were an Iranian-speaking people. They settled in and around the Zagros MountainsZAG-rosa long, rugged mountain range east of Mesopotamia, home to the Medes and later the Persians., the rugged highland region east of Mesopotamia, sometime after the Bronze Age Collapse. For roughly the next four hundred years, from about 1150 to 728 BC, the Medes appear in the historical record only faintly and now and then. Mostly, they show up as one tribute-paying people among many along Assyria's eastern border. This is the same kind of relationship seen in Jehu of Israel. No Median king from this long stretch left behind writings of his own, the way Assyrian, Babylonian, or Egyptian kings did. There is simply no Median version of Ashurnasirpal's annals or Piye's stele for these centuries. It is worth being honest about that gap, rather than pretend otherwise. In other words, the Medes' story cannot be told the same way as Egypt's or Assyria's.

section: A PEOPLE ALMOST INVISIBLE IN THE RECORD
text: The Medes are not entirely silent in outside sources, though. Assyrian kings, including Sargon II and Sennacherib, record campaigns against Median chiefs in their own royal writings, from the eighth and seventh centuries BC. They call these chiefs the "Mada." These brief mentions confirm that Median communities existed. They also show that Medes sometimes resisted Assyrian power. But they tell almost nothing about how the Medes organized themselves. They also do not say who, if anyone, ruled the Medes as a single people during this long stretch of time. In other words, outsiders saw the Medes only from a distance, and only now and then.
👥 PEOPLES · THE MEDES
Photo: via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0.

The **Medes** were an Iranian-speaking people who settled the Zagros Mountains east of Mesopotamia. Nearly invisible in the historical record for four centuries, they built a kingdom that would help end the Neo-Assyrian Empire within a single lifetime. This later Persian-era relief shows Median delegates in their traditional pointed cap and belted riding coat.

This kind of near-invisibility is worth pausing on. It does not mean nothing was happening among the Medes during these four centuries. Communities were forming. Tribal and family structures were organizing local life. Slowly, something like shared political identity was taking shape. All of this happened outside the notice of nearby empires that kept written records. A people can be building toward something big for a very long time before that process becomes visible to history at all. In other words, silence in the record is not the same thing as nothing happening.
📚 DEIOCES, ACCORDING TO HERODOTUS
The Greek historian Herodotus is the main source here. His book gives the fullest surviving account of how the Medes are said to have first united under a single ruler.
🌐 FOREIGN LANGUAGE VOCABULARY

**Deioces** 🔊dee-OH-seeza Median villager Herodotus credits with uniting the Medes under a single king, becoming their first ruler., a Median villager Herodotus credits with uniting the Medes under a single king, becoming their first ruler.

Herodotus tells a truly memorable story. A Median villager named Deiocesdee-OH-seeza Median villager Herodotus credits with uniting the Medes under a single king, becoming their first ruler. was known locally for his fairness in settling disputes. He became so trusted that people from beyond his own village began bringing him their conflicts to judge. According to Herodotus, Deioces then deliberately stopped judging cases altogether. Disorder among the Medes grew worse without him. Eventually, the Medes themselves gathered and chose him as their first king. Once in power, Deioces is said to have built a grand, carefully guarded court at a new capital, Ecbatanaek-BAT-uh-nuhthe capital city Herodotus says Deioces built for the united Medes, in the Zagros highlands.. Herodotus describes this capital as ringed by seven walls, one inside another. Each wall was painted its own color: white, black, deep red, blue, and bright orange. The two innermost walls were plated in silver and gold. He surrounded himself with strict rules, even forbidding laughter in his presence. This was meant to keep the nobles from feeling too familiar with him. Not long before, after all, they had been his own equals, and he did not want them plotting against him. Herodotus also names six Median tribes that are said to have come together under Deioces's rule. One of them was called the Magi. This priestly tribe would later play a major religious role under the Persian kings. Keep that name in mind. It will come up again.

🎯 TRY IT: NAMING MEDIA'S GEOGRAPHY Match each term to what it names in this story. The rugged highland homeland of the Medes, east of Mesopotamia. Zagros Mountains Halys River The capital Deioces is s

This is a wonderful story, and it needs to be read the way Herodotus should generally be read, with care. It may preserve a real memory of how Median kingship actually began. If so, it began from below, built through a real reputation for fairness rather than conquest. That would make it a very different kind of origin story than most kingdoms of the ancient Near East. It may also be, in whole or in part, a legendary account, shaped over generations of retelling before Herodotus ever wrote it down. This is the same caution applied to Sargon's basket or Gilgamesh's flood. Modern historians still remain divided on how much of Deioces's story reflects real history. They also debate how much of it grew in the retelling. Two full centuries passed between his supposed reign and the day Herodotus wrote it all down. The honest answer, once again, is that no one can be sure. Pretending otherwise would be worse than admitting the uncertainty directly. In other words, an honest "we don't know" is better than a confident guess.
👤 HISTORICAL FIGURE · DEIOCES

No contemporary image of Deiocesdee-OH-seeza Median villager Herodotus credits with uniting the Medes under a single king, becoming their first ruler. survives, and no verifiable public-domain artist's depiction could be located this session, so none is shown here. Herodotus credits Deioces with uniting the Medes under a single king and founding their capital, Ecbatana, around the seventh century BC. Whether this story reflects real history or later legend remains genuinely uncertain, a caution this lesson discusses directly.
📚 CLOSING

Whatever its true origins, a united Median kingdom did come to exist. Its rise from a barely visible frontier people to a major regional power is one of the clearest examples of a pattern worth naming directly. That pattern is simple: slowly, then all at once.
💪 KEEP THIS IN MIND
Whatever its true origins, a united Median kingdom did come to exist, rising from a barely visible frontier people to a major regional power.

section: What can cracked bones tell us about a Bronze Age king's own worries?
text: What can cracked bones tell us about a Bronze Age king's own worries?

section: What can cracked bones tell us about a Bronze Age king's own worries?
text: Far to the east of the Indus Valley, along the Yellow River in northern China, Shang China left behind exactly the kind of written proof of kingship the Indus Valley lacked. Its kings asked questions of their ancestors by cracking heated bones, then had scribes carve the questions, and sometimes the answers, onto the very same bones. This lesson reads those oracle bones directly, meets a warrior queen named Fu Hao, and asks what a distant Bronze Age court's own day-to-day worries can teach us.

section: BY THE END OF THIS LESSON YOU WILL BE ABLE TO…
text: Far to the east of the Indus Valley, along the Yellow River in northern China, a very different kind of river valley civilization was taking shape by around 1600 BC. Historians call it the **Shang dynasty**. It is the first Chinese dynasty confirmed by both digging and its own writing. Chinese tradition remembers an earlier dynasty, the Xia, founded by the legendary flood-taming hero Yu the Great. No confirmed writing or dig evidence for the Xia has yet turned up. Historians treat it, like Gilgamesh's Uruk or the Trojan War, as legendary rather than confirmed history. The Shang dynasty is a different matter entirely. Its kings, its capital cities, and even the names of certain people are recorded in the civilization's own surviving writing. At its height, Shang territory covered much of what is now northern China, organized around a network of walled towns loyal to the king at Anyang.
🌐 FOREIGN LANGUAGE VOCABULARY

**Wu Ding** 🔊woo-DINGa Shang king, ruling around 1250 BC, under whom the earliest confirmed Chinese writing appears. and **Fu Hao** 🔊foo-HOWa wife of King Wu Ding who personally led military campaigns, a rare example of a woman with real military power in the ancient world. both appear later in this lesson.
📚 TALKING TO THE ANCESTORS

Those records take a strange form: oracle bonesOR-uh-kula bone or shell used in Shang China to ask the royal ancestors or gods a question, then carved with the question and answer.. These were the flat shoulder bones of cattle, or the underside of turtle shells, prepared by Shang diviners working for the royal court. A diviner would press a heated point against the bone or shell. This caused it to crack. The diviner then read the pattern of the crack as an answer from the royal ancestors or gods. Kings asked about the harvest, whether to go to war, a coming illness, or the meaning of a dream. Afterward, scribes carved the original question, and sometimes the answer, right onto the same bone. This practice, called divinationdiv-uh-NAY-shuna practice meant to answer questions or predict the future by reading signs, such as cracks in a heated bone., gives modern historians something rare: a huge stash of evidence. Tens of thousands of carved bones survive today. They show a Bronze Age royal court's own day-to-day worries, written in its own hand. Oracle bone writing, dated to around 1250 BC under a king named Wu Ding🔊woo-DINGa Shang king, ruling around 1250 BC, under whom the earliest confirmed Chinese writing appears., is the first confirmed Chinese writing system. It is the direct ancestor of the Chinese characters still used today, thousands of years later.

For centuries after the Shang fell, no one remembered what oracle bones were. Farmers who dug them up sold them to pharmacies as "dragon bones," to be ground up as medicine. Only in 1899 did a Chinese scholar named Wang Yirong notice strange carved marks on some of these bones. According to the most common telling, he first spotted the marks on "dragon bones" he had bought from a pharmacy to treat his own illness. He realized the marks were real ancient writing, not random scratches. That discovery was made almost by accident. It opened up a whole lost period of Chinese history for the first time. Since then, well over one hundred thousand inscribed oracle bones have been recovered, most of them from Anyang itself.
👤 HISTORICAL FIGURE · WU DING
Photo: via Wikimedia Commons, CC0.

Wu Dingwoo-DINGa Shang king, ruling around 1250 BC, under whom the earliest confirmed Chinese writing appears. ruled Shang China around 1250 BC. The earliest confirmed Chinese writing dates to his reign, preserved on the oracle bones his court used to question the royal ancestors.
📚 ANYANG AND A WARRIOR QUEEN

Around this same time, the Shang capital settled at **Anyang**, known to archaeologists as Yinxu. Large royal tombs have been dug up there. One of the most striking belonged to Fu Hao🔊foo-HOWa wife of King Wu Ding who personally led military campaigns, a rare example of a woman with real military power in the ancient world., a wife of King Wu Ding. Her tomb was found still sealed and unlooted in 1976. It held a huge store of ritual bronze vessels, jade objects, and weapons, more than 1,600 items in all. Oracle bone writings naming Fu Hao describe her leading her own military campaigns for the king. In at least one account, she commanded thousands of troops. This is a rare, well-recorded case of a woman holding real military power in the ancient world. It is worth comparing to Hatshepsut's very different path to power in Egypt.
👤 HISTORICAL FIGURE · FU HAO
Photo: via Wikimedia Commons, CC0.

Fu Haofoo-HOWa wife of King Wu Ding who personally led military campaigns, a rare example of a woman with real military power in the ancient world. was a wife of the Shang king Wu Ding, who ruled China around 1250 BC. Oracle bone writings show her leading her own military campaigns, commanding thousands of soldiers, an unusually direct record of a woman's military power in the ancient world.
📚 BRONZE AT A REMARKABLE SCALE

Shang China also made ritual bronze vessels of great skill. Craftsmen cast them using a method called piece-mold casting. A clay model was carved, then cut into separate pieces that formed a mold. This method differed from the lost-wax casting used in the Near East. It could produce some of the largest and most finely carved bronze objects made anywhere in the ancient world. One surviving vessel, the Houmuwu ding, weighs over 1,600 pounds, among the heaviest bronze objects ever cast anywhere in the ancient world. Producing bronze on this scale needed tin and copper. Both metals were hauled in from mines sometimes hundreds of miles away, proof of trade networks reaching well beyond the Shang king's direct land. Shang China's elites also wore fine silk cloth, made from threads unwound from the cocoons of silkworms raised on mulberry leaves, a Chinese skill that stayed mostly unknown outside East Asia for many centuries. These vessels were not everyday tools. They were ritual objects, used to offer food and wine to royal ancestors, whose favor and guidance, as the oracle bones show, the Shang kings sought all the time.
👥 PEOPLES · THE SHANG
Photo: via Wikimedia Commons, CC0.

Shang elites wore silk robes, a fabric first made in China from the cocoons of silkworms, along with jade jewelry believed to protect the wearer and honor the ancestors. Bronze helmets and armor equipped Shang soldiers for war.
🏙️ CITIES · ANYANG
Photo: via Wikimedia Commons, CC0.

**Anyang** served as the Shang dynasty's capital for over two centuries. Its royal tombs, packed with bronze, jade, and oracle bones, have made it one of the richest archaeological sites in Chinese history.

section: A CIVILIZATION UNTOUCHED BY DISTANT COLLAPSE
text: 📚 A CIVILIZATION UNTOUCHED BY DISTANT COLLAPSE

section: A CIVILIZATION UNTOUCHED BY DISTANT COLLAPSE
text: One more point is worth holding onto. A wave of crisis and collapse hits much of the Near East around 1200 to 1150 BC. Shang China, thousands of miles away with no direct contact with that world, is not touched by it at all. Its dynasty continues on for another century beyond that collapse, only ending around 1046 BC, when a rival people called the Zhou overthrew it. Keep this in mind as a useful check against assuming any single historical event, however dramatic, reached the whole world at once.
💪 KEEP THIS IN MIND

The Indus Valley and Shang China both grew up along great rivers with no contact with Mesopotamia or Egypt, and yet arrived at civilization by very different roads: one leaving no trace of a king, the other leaving tens of thousands of bones carved with a king's own questions.

A few words in this lesson are worth a look before you read. They show up in bold, and you can hover over any of them for a reminder.
**barter** (BAR-ter). To trade goods for other goods without using money.
**bison** (BY-sun). The large, shaggy animal of the American plains, often called a buffalo.
**enslave** (en-SLAYV). To force a person to work for you without pay or freedom.
**expedition** (eks-pih-DISH-un). A long trip taken for a purpose, such as exploring or conquering.
**healer** (HEE-ler). A person who treats sick or hurt people.
**route** (root). The path from one place to another.
**viceroy** (VYS-roy). An official who rules a colony and speaks for the king or queen. A viceroy rules a viceroyalty.

section: Eight years on foot, across a land no European had ever crossed.
text: After the shipwreck, **Cabeza de Vaca** lived among the peoples of Texas for years. He was a slave, then a trader, then a **healer**. At last he walked west with three other survivors until he reached Spanish soil again. When he finally told his story, it sent Spaniards searching for riches in the north.

📚 PART 1 · FROM SLAVE TO TRADER
A way to survive

Cabeza de Vaca spent about six years living among the peoples of the Texas coast and the country beyond it. At first he was **enslaved**. Then he found a way to change his place in the world. He escaped from his captors and became a trader. He carried sea shells and other coastal goods inland, and he brought back animal hides, flint for tools, and other things that people wanted.
🌐 FOREIGN LANGUAGE VOCABULARY
**Cabeza de Vaca** (kah-BEH-sah deh VAH-kah). Álvar Núñez Cabeza de Vaca, the treasurer of the Narváez expedition. He later wrote the story of his journey.

A trader had one great advantage. He was not a threat. A man who carried shells and flint, and who belonged to no group, was welcome in places where an armed stranger would have been driven away. This freedom let him see more of the country than any European had seen before. It also taught him how different peoples depended on each other for things they could not make or find at home.
Those years were hard. He wrote that he went hungry, worked at hard tasks like digging roots, and often had little clothing in cold weather. He was far from home with no way to send word.

This kind of trade is called **barter**. Because he was a stranger who belonged to no group, he could travel between peoples who might otherwise have kept apart. His travels took him far beyond the coast where the **Karankawa** lived.
🌐 FOREIGN LANGUAGE VOCABULARY
**Karankawa** (kuh-RANG-kuh-wah). The name often used today for the coastal peoples of the Texas Gulf coast.
The healer

People also asked him to heal them. He wrote that he and his companions prayed over the sick, made the sign of the cross, and used simple treatments. Many people recovered, or so he said. We cannot know what really happened in each case. What we do know is that word spread. Groups began to welcome the strangers as healers, giving them food and guides.

As their fame grew, crowds of people began to travel with them from town to town. Villages gave them food and gifts, and each new group handed them on to the next. In this way, a few starving strangers became honored guests.

It is worth thinking about how this looked from the other side. The people who welcomed the four men had their own ideas about sickness and healing. They saw strangers who seemed to have power, and they decided that it was wise to treat such people well. Their careful choices were part of what kept the travelers alive.
📚 PART 2 · FOUR SURVIVORS WALK WEST
The long walk

In 1532, Cabeza de Vaca met three other survivors of the **expedition**. Two were Spanish officers, **Dorantes** and **Castillo**. The third was **Estevanico**, an enslaved man from Morocco in North Africa. The four had been held by different groups. They agreed to escape together, and in 1534 they set out to the west.
🌐 FOREIGN LANGUAGE VOCABULARY
**Castillo** (kah-STEE-yoh). Alonso del Castillo, a Spanish officer who survived the expedition.
**Dorantes** (doh-RAHN-tes). Andrés Dorantes, a Spanish officer who survived the expedition.
**Estevanico** (es-teh-vah-NEE-koh). An enslaved man from Morocco in North Africa. He survived the expedition and walked with Cabeza de Vaca.

They walked for about two years across what is now Texas and northern Mexico. Historians still argue about their exact **route**. Along the way, they passed through many different groups, each with its own food, customs, and language. They had no map. They depended on the kindness of strangers and on their growing fame as healers.

The route is hard to trace because Cabeza de Vaca gave few place names, and the land has changed since then. Some historians place the travelers along the Texas coast and then across the middle of the state. Others place them farther north or south. Nobody can be sure, which reminds us how much of this story rests on a single book.

On the way, the travelers saw huge herds of animals that Europeans had never described before. Cabeza de Vaca called them "cows with humped backs." We call them **bison**. His book is one of the first European descriptions of them.

These details mattered because they were new to European readers. Nobody in Spain had ever seen a bison, so Cabeza de Vaca had to describe one using animals his readers knew. He compared it to the cattle of home. Writers who meet a strange thing often do this, and it shows how hard it is to describe something that has no name in your own language.
In 1536, they met a party of Spanish soldiers in western Mexico. Cabeza de Vaca had been gone for eight years. The soldiers could hardly believe who he was.

The Spanish soldiers they met were hunting for Native people to make slaves. Cabeza de Vaca was angry. He had spent years among these peoples, and he knew what captivity felt like. He argued with the soldiers and tried to protect the people who had helped him.

What Cabeza de Vaca had lived through changed his mind about many things. He had been treated as a slave, and he had also been treated as a guest, and he knew both feelings. He later argued that Native peoples should be won by kindness, not by force. Not everyone in the Spanish system agreed with him.

section: PART 3 THE REPORT THAT CHANGED THE PLAN
text: 📚 PART 3 · THE REPORT THAT CHANGED THE PLAN
What Spain heard

When the four reached Mexico City, they told the **viceroy** what they had seen. They described many peoples, large towns in some places, and stories of rich lands to the north. They had not seen cities of gold. But Spain was hungry for another Mexico, and people tend to hear what they hope to hear. The report led the viceroy to send out new explorers, and Estevanico would soon be one of them. The search that followed is a story of its own.
Cabeza de Vaca also wrote a book. It was printed in 1542 as **The Account** (*La Relación*). It is one of the earliest written descriptions of Texas and its peoples.
🌐 FOREIGN LANGUAGE VOCABULARY
**The Account (*La Relación*)** (lah reh-lah-see-OHN). The book Cabeza de Vaca wrote about his journey, first printed in 1542.
📚 PART 4 · READING HIS WORDS

section: What does he notice? What does he assume?
text: What does he notice? What does he assume?

section: What does he notice? What does he assume?
text: His book is a primary source, which means it was written by someone who was there. Primary sources are powerful, but they are not neutral. Cabeza de Vaca wrote for the Spanish king. He described the people he lived with in careful detail. He wrote about what they ate, how they dressed, and where they traveled. In some passages, he treats them with real respect.

section: What does he notice? What does he assume?
text: But he also took many things for granted. He believed that the Spanish faith was true and that Spanish ways were the standard. He often measured others by that standard. When you read him, you can ask two questions. What does he notice? And what does he assume without saying so?

section: What does he notice? What does he assume?
text: Asking those questions turns a story into evidence. It can help you see the people he met, including the Karankawa, more clearly than he saw them himself.
💪 WHAT TO CARRY FORWARD

Cabeza de Vaca walked across Texas and found no gold, but he brought back something Spain valued just as much: a story. A story had turned into a rumor, and a rumor was about to send an army across the plains.

section: A rumor can send an army across a continent.
text: After **Estevanico** and his companions returned, Spaniards could not stop talking about the north. Was there a second Mexico out there, with cities full of gold? One huge **expedition** set out to find out. It crossed some of the strangest country any European had ever seen, including the Texas Panhandle, and it came back with nothing. This lesson follows it.

📚 PART 1 · FROM RUMOR TO FACT
The Seven Cities

The **viceroy** of New Spain wanted to know if the stories were true. In 1539, he sent a **friar** named **Fray Marcos de Niza** north, with Estevanico as a guide. Estevanico went ahead of the group and reached a town of the Zuni people, called **Cíbola**. The Zuni killed him there. Fray Marcos de Niza did not go in. He said that he saw the town from a hill far away, and that it looked bigger than Mexico City.
🌐 FOREIGN LANGUAGE VOCABULARY
**Cíbola** (SEE-boh-lah). The Spanish name for the Zuni towns in what is now New Mexico, where the "Seven Cities" were said to be.
**Fray Marcos de Niza** (fry MAR-kohs deh NEE-sah). A friar sent north in 1539 to check the stories about rich cities. "Fray" means "brother" and is used for friars.
**Estevanico** (es-teh-vah-NEE-koh). An enslaved man from Morocco who survived the Narváez expedition and later guided the friar Marcos de Niza north.

Many Spaniards already believed an old European story about seven rich cities somewhere across the sea. Now a friar seemed to have found them. A rumor turned into a "fact" in a few months, even though no Spaniard had walked into the town and looked inside.

Why did so many people believe it? Spain had just taken Mexico, and the riches there had been real. Men who had seen one golden city were ready to believe that another one lay farther north. A hopeful story spreads faster than a careful one. Each person who repeated the story made the city a little bigger.
📚 PART 2 · THE MARCH
Coronado sets out

In 1540, a young governor named **Coronado** led the largest expedition yet. It included several hundred Spanish soldiers, many Native **allies** and servants from Mexico, and herds of horses, cattle, and sheep. They marched north for months to Cíbola. They found a Zuni town built of stone and mud brick. There was no gold. Coronado's men fought their way in and found food, not treasure.

The size of this army shows how much Spain hoped to find. Feeding hundreds of people and thousands of animals on a long march was a huge job. The herds slowed the army and ate the grass along the way. Coronado had spent his own money on the trip, so he had much to lose if it failed.
The Zuni did not give up their town easily. They fought back, and Coronado was hurt when stones struck him. The Zuni people still live in that part of New Mexico today.

Later, when Coronado's men saw Cíbola up close, they were furious with the friar. He had made a small Zuni town sound like a golden city. Whether he lied or only saw what he hoped to see is something historians still debate.

The expedition spent the winter along the **Rio Grande**, where fighting broke out with the Pueblo people. By spring, the men were tired and angry. Then a man the Spaniards called "the Turk" told them about a rich land called **Quivira**, far to the east. He said its ruler ate from plates of gold.
🌐 FOREIGN LANGUAGE VOCABULARY
**Coronado** (kor-oh-NAH-doh). Francisco Vázquez de Coronado, the Spanish governor who led the expedition north in 1540.
**Quivira** (kee-VEE-rah). A land of farming towns in what is now Kansas. The expedition was told it was full of gold.
**Rio Grande** (REE-oh GRAHN-day). The great river that flows between Texas and Mexico to the Gulf of Mexico.

The Pueblo people had good reason to fight. The Spaniards needed food and warm clothing for the winter, and they took what they needed from the villages. When the people resisted, Spanish soldiers fought back hard. The story shows how an army that arrives with big hopes and no plan for supplies can quickly become a danger to the people nearby.
📚 PART 3 · THE LLANO ESTACADO
An ocean of grass

To reach Quivira, Coronado marched east onto the Great Plains. He crossed a high, flat grassland that the Spaniards called the Llano Estacado. Today we call it the Staked Plains. It lies in the Texas Panhandle. One Spanish soldier wrote that traveling across it was like being at sea. There were no trees, no hills, and no landmarks. A man could ride all day and see the same horizon in every direction.
The Spaniards feared getting lost. **Scouts** piled up **bison** dung and bones to mark a trail they could follow back. In many places there was little wood and little water.

Even measuring distance was a problem. Some of the Spaniards counted their steps to keep track of how far they had gone. A terrible hailstorm struck the army on the plains, smashing equipment and frightening the horses.

Here they met people who lived on the plains. The Spaniards called them **Querechos**. These **nomads** lived in tents made of tanned bison hides, and they followed the herds from place to place. They used dogs to carry their loads, because this was before the horse came to the plains. People today often link the Querechos to the **Apache**, who will become very important in the story of Texas.
🌐 FOREIGN LANGUAGE VOCABULARY
**Apache** (uh-PATCH-ee). A group of related peoples who lived on the plains and in the Southwest.

The dogs pulled a simple sled called a travois, made from poles. It was a clever way to move a camp without horses. When the horse reached the plains many years later, everything about this way of life would change.
🌐 FOREIGN LANGUAGE VOCABULARY
**Querechos** (keh-REH-chohs). The name the Spaniards gave to bison hunters they met on the plains.

This way of life shows how much people could do without a single horse. A bison gave meat, hides, bone, and sinew. Families worked together to follow the herds, and a whole camp could be packed and moved in a short time. The Spaniards were amazed at how easily the Querechos lived in a land where the army had trouble finding the next meal.
📚 PART 4 · QUIVIRA
The end of the road

At last, Coronado reached Quivira, in what is now Kansas. The people there lived in round houses made of grass, and they farmed corn. There was no gold. The Spaniards believed the Turk had lied to them, and he was put to death. In 1542, Coronado turned back. The long march had found no riches and no second Mexico.

Think about how hard the trip home must have been. The army had been on the road for two years. Men were sick, horses were worn out, and most of the cattle and sheep had been eaten. Coronado himself was hurt in a fall from his horse and was never quite the same. He returned to Mexico with little to show for it, and his reputation suffered.
People today link Quivira to the ancestors of the Wichita people. They farmed, hunted, and lived in settled towns, but they had nothing like the gold the Spaniards had been promised.

But the expedition did change what Spain knew. It had crossed a huge grassland, met people who lived by hunting bison, and seen farming towns far from Mexico. None of it matched the dream. And the dream itself had begun as a rumor that grew a little bigger each time somebody told it.
💪 WHAT TO CARRY FORWARD
Coronado came looking for a city of gold and found grass, wind, and people who lived on the bison. Spain still wanted a second Mexico, and another army was searching in the east at the same time.

section: How could a few hundred men topple an empire of millions?
text: In 1519, a Spanish officer named **Cortés** landed on the coast of Mexico with about five hundred soldiers. Two years later, one of the most powerful **empires** in North America was gone. The answer to how it happened is not what most people expect. The Spaniards did not win by themselves.

📚 PART 1 · THE MEXICA EMPIRE

section: A city of canals and causeways
text: A city of canals and causeways

section: A city of canals and causeways
text: In 1519, central Mexico was ruled by the Mexica. Their capital, Tenochtitlán, sat on an island in a lake. Wide roads called causeways connected it to the shore, and canals ran through the streets. Perhaps 200,000 people lived there, which made it as big as the largest cities in Europe.

section: A city of canals and causeways
text: Farmers grew food on small man-made islands in the lake. Huge markets sold everything from cloth to gold to turkeys. When Spanish soldiers first saw the city, one of them later said it looked like something out of a storybook.

section: A city of canals and causeways
text: 🌐 FOREIGN LANGUAGE VOCABULARY

section: A city of canals and causeways
text: **Mexica** (meh-SHEE-kah). The people who ruled the empire in central Mexico. They are often called the Aztecs.

section: A city of canals and causeways
text: **Moctezuma** (mohk-teh-SOO-mah). The ruler of the Mexica when Cortés arrived.

section: A city of canals and causeways
text: **Tenochtitlán** (teh-nohch-teet-LAHN). The capital city of the Mexica empire, built on an island in a lake. Today Mexico City stands on the same spot.

section: A city of canals and causeways
text: These floating gardens were built from mud and plants piled up in the shallow water. They produced a great deal of food and helped feed the city. A visitor from Spain, where most cities were smaller and more crowded, had never seen anything like it. This was no village waiting to be taken. It was a rich and busy capital, with its own laws, its own army, and its own officials.

section: A city of canals and causeways
text: The Mexica ruled by force. They conquered neighboring peoples and made them pay tribute. Cloth, corn, feathers, and gold flowed into Tenochtitlán from millions of people. The ruler, **Moctezuma**, sat at the top of this system. But many conquered peoples hated paying. They were waiting for someone who could help them break free.

section: A city of canals and causeways
text: The Mexica religion also included human sacrifice. The Spaniards were horrified by it. So were many of the peoples the Mexica had conquered, because **captives** from those peoples were often the victims. That is one reason so many were ready to join a **rebellion**.
📚 PART 2 · CORTÉS LANDS, 1519
Finding allies

Cortés sailed from Cuba in early 1519 with about five hundred soldiers and a few horses. They landed on the Gulf coast of Mexico. A young woman named **Malintzin** joined him there. She spoke the language of the Mexica and the language of the Maya, and she helped him understand and talk with the people he met.

Cortés was not even supposed to be there. The governor of Cuba had canceled his permission to lead the **expedition**, but Cortés sailed anyway. On the coast, he founded a town called **Veracruz** and had his men name him their leader. He also had his ships sunk so that nobody could turn back. Cortés had decided that he would win or he would not survive.
🌐 FOREIGN LANGUAGE VOCABULARY
**Veracruz** (veh-rah-KROOS). The main Mexican port on the Gulf of Mexico.

Think about how risky this was. Cortés had about five hundred men in a land of millions of people, far from any help. If the Spanish king or the governor of Cuba punished him for disobeying, he could lose everything. His only hope was to win so big that nobody could argue with him. That kind of gamble can end in ruin, and it nearly did.

As Cortés marched inland, he learned how many peoples resented the Mexica. In **Tlaxcala**, warriors fought the Spaniards at first. Then their leaders made a choice. They decided that the Mexica were a greater enemy than the strangers, and they became **allies**. Thousands of warriors from Tlaxcala and other peoples joined the march to the capital. This group of partners was a **coalition**.
🌐 FOREIGN LANGUAGE VOCABULARY
**Cortés** (kor-TEZ). Hernán Cortés, the Spanish officer who led the conquest of Mexico.
**Malintzin** (mah-LEEN-tseen). A young woman who joined Cortés on the coast and translated for him.
**Tlaxcala** (tlahs-KAH-lah). A region and people in central Mexico who were enemies of the Mexica.

Why would the leaders of Tlaxcala join the strangers who had just fought them? The answer is that they had their own reasons. For years the Mexica had pressed them hard, and they were hemmed in. They saw a chance to settle an old score. This was their war as much as it was Cortés's war. They did not give up their own goals when they joined him.
📚 PART 3 · THE CITY FALLS
Defeat, disease, and a siege

In November 1519, Cortés entered Tenochtitlán and was welcomed by Moctezuma. Within months, trouble broke out. Moctezuma died, and in June 1520 the Mexica drove the Spaniards out of the city. Many Spaniards died that night. For a while, it looked as though the conquest was over.

Then smallpox arrived. It came with the Spanish in 1520. The people of the Americas had never met this disease, and their bodies had no defense against it. It killed huge numbers of people, including leaders and warriors. Nobody planned this. The Spaniards did not understand disease, and they had not brought it on purpose. But it changed the war.

Cortés came back with his allies. They built boats for the lake and surrounded the city. For months, the coalition cut off the food and the fresh water. In August 1521, Tenochtitlán fell. The last Mexica ruler, **Cuauhtémoc**, was captured. The Spaniards began to build a new city on the same spot. It became Mexico City, the capital of Spanish rule in the Americas.
The **siege** lasted about seventy-five days. Disease swept through the city, and food ran out. By the end, many of the people inside were too weak to fight.
🌐 FOREIGN LANGUAGE VOCABULARY
**Cuauhtémoc** (kwow-TEH-mohk). The last Mexica ruler, who led the defense of the city.

The fall of the city was not a quick or easy victory. Fighting went on street by street and along the canals. The Spaniards and their allies tore down buildings as they went, to make room to fight. The defenders held on until the very end, and the people of the city suffered terribly. Those who won and those who lost both paid a heavy price.
📚 PART 4 · WHAT REALLY DECIDED IT

section: Not a few hundred, but a coalition
text: Not a few hundred, but a coalition

section: Not a few hundred, but a coalition
text: It is tempting to say the Spaniards won because they had steel swords and horses. Those helped, but they were not enough. A few hundred Spaniards could not have taken a city that large. They won because tens of thousands of allies fought beside them, because disease weakened the city, and because many peoples were glad to see the Mexica fall.

section: Not a few hundred, but a coalition
text: Some people tell this story as if the Spaniards were unstoppable. That is not what happened. They were nearly destroyed in 1520. They won in 1521 because the choices of many people, Spanish and Native, had lined up in their favor.

section: Not a few hundred, but a coalition
text: Things could have gone differently. If the leaders of Tlaxcala had made another choice, Cortés might have died on the road. Real people made hard choices, and those choices shaped the outcome.

section: Not a few hundred, but a coalition
text: We know much of this story from people who were there. **Díaz**, a Spanish soldier, wrote a long account of the conquest years later. As you read his words, ask what he saw with his own eyes and what he may have remembered differently after many years.

section: Not a few hundred, but a coalition
text: 🌐 FOREIGN LANGUAGE VOCABULARY

section: Not a few hundred, but a coalition
text: **Díaz** (DEE-ahs). Bernal Díaz del Castillo, a Spanish soldier who later wrote an eyewitness account of the conquest.
💪 WHAT TO CARRY FORWARD

The conquest of Mexico worked because a large, settled population already paid tribute to rulers, and Spain could take their place. Keep that in mind. The next question is what Spain actually won, and what happened when the same system reached a place that looked very different.

text: Moscoso Meets the Caddo: What Makes Texas Different from Mexico

section: Moscoso Meets the Caddo: What Makes Texas Different from Mexico
text: Age of Exploration
💡 GLOSSARY OF SUBJECT VOCABULARY
A few words in this lesson are worth a look before you read. They show up in bold, and you can hover over any of them for a reminder.
**agriculture** (AG-rih-kul-cher). Farming: growing crops and raising animals for food.
**bison** (BY-sun). The large, shaggy animal of the American plains, often called a buffalo.
**confederacy** (kun-FED-er-uh-see). A group of towns or peoples that join together under shared leaders for a common purpose.
**gradient** (GRAY-dee-ent). A steady change from one place to another.
**nomad** (NOH-mad). A person who moves from place to place instead of living in one town.
**region** (REE-jun). A large area with features that set it apart from the areas around it.
**route** (root). The path from one place to another.
**tribute** (TRIB-yoot). Payment in goods or labor that a conquered people must give to their rulers.
📖 TODAY'S FOCUS
Is there a second Mexico out there? One more army goes to find out.

While **Coronado** was crossing the plains in the west, another Spanish army was struggling through the east. After years of marching, it reached a part of Texas that looked like nothing the Spaniards had seen on the coast or the plains. This lesson compares three very different ways of life in Texas, and then steps back to look at the land itself. The land turns out to explain a great deal.

section: PART 1 THE ARMY REACHES EAST TEXAS
text: 📚 PART 1 · THE ARMY REACHES EAST TEXAS
A country of farms

Another Spanish army, led by **De Soto**, had spent three years marching through the southeastern United States. In 1542, De Soto died near the Mississippi River. An officer named **Moscoso** took command. The men now wanted only to go home. Moscoso led them west, hoping to find a land **route** to Mexico. A Portuguese soldier known as the Gentleman of **Elvas** wrote an account of the march.
By now, the army had lost many men to battles and sickness. The survivors had marched for years, and they were thin and tired. They needed food, and they needed a way out.
🌐 FOREIGN LANGUAGE VOCABULARY
**De Soto** (day SOH-toh). Hernando de Soto, a Spanish explorer who led an army through the southeastern United States.
**Elvas** (EL-vahsh). A town in Portugal. A Portuguese soldier on the expedition, known as the Gentleman of Elvas, wrote an account of it.
**Moscoso** (mohs-KOH-soh). Luis de Moscoso, the Spanish officer who took command after De Soto died.

In East Texas, they met the Caddo. The Spaniards walked into a country of farms. They found villages surrounded by fields of corn, beans, and squash. People lived in tall houses with grass roofs. After a long time with little food, the army found plenty.
🌐 FOREIGN LANGUAGE VOCABULARY
**Caddo** (KAD-oh). A group of peoples who lived in East Texas and farmed the land.

To see why this mattered, think about what the Spaniards had been eating. Their supplies had run out long before, and many of the men had been hungry for months. A village with stored corn was a rescue. At the same time, the Caddo had to decide how to treat an army of strangers. The Caddo had good reason to be careful.

section: PART 2 THE CADDO: A DIFFERENT TEXAS
text: 📚 PART 2 · THE CADDO: A DIFFERENT TEXAS
Settled, farming, and organized

The Caddo lived in one place and farmed the land. Their villages were permanent. They also joined their towns together under shared leaders, which we call a **confederacy**. There were three large Caddo confederacies. This was a society with farmers, leaders, trade routes, and ceremonies. It was very different from the coastal peoples who moved with the seasons, and from the **nomads** who followed the **bison** across the plains.

Each Caddo community had a leader called a **caddi**. The Caddo also built large earthen mounds for ceremonies and for the homes of important people. Their potters made beautiful bowls and jars, and their traders carried goods over long distances.
🌐 FOREIGN LANGUAGE VOCABULARY
**caddi** (KAD-ee). A Caddo leader. Each Caddo community had a caddi.

A mound was not just a pile of dirt. It took many people working together to build one, and that took planning, leaders, and shared beliefs. A society that could do this was well organized. It could feed many people, settle disputes, and hold ceremonies that brought distant towns together. Spaniards who expected to find simple villages were wrong.

Compare three ways of life in Texas. On the coast, people moved with the seasons and lived by fishing and gathering. On the plains, people followed the bison herds. In the east, people practiced **agriculture**. They stayed in one place and grew their food. Three peoples lived in one land, and each had found a different way to live in it.

Each of these ways of life made sense. The coastal families used the sea and the shore. The plains hunters used the herds. The Caddo used rich soil and steady rain. None of these peoples was backward or simple. Each had worked out a way to live well in the place where it stood, and each way took generations of skill.

section: PART 3 WHY SO DIFFERENT? THE LAND
text: 📚 PART 3 · WHY SO DIFFERENT? THE LAND

section: Four regions and a rainfall line
text: Four regions and a rainfall line

section: Four regions and a rainfall line
text: Texas is not one kind of place. Geographers divide it into four large regions. The Gulf Coastal Plains run along the coast and up into the east. The North Central Plains lie in the middle. The Great Plains cover the high, flat grasslands of the Panhandle and the west. The Mountains and Basins lie in the far west.

section: Four regions and a rainfall line
text: What ties the regions together is rain. In the far east, more than 50 inches of rain fall in a year. In the far west, fewer than 10 inches fall. Between the two, the rainfall drops steadily from east to west. This is a rainfall **gradient**. Rain decides which plants will grow, and what grows helps decide how people can live. That is a large part of why the Caddo farmed in the east, and why the bison herds roamed the drier plains.

section: Four regions and a rainfall line
text: Farmers need steady rain, or a river that can water their fields. West of the middle of the state, farming without that water is very hard. That helps explain why the villages of farmers lie in the east, and why the people of the dry plains followed animals instead of crops.

section: Four regions and a rainfall line
text: Look at how the line of rain shapes the whole map. Where rain is plentiful, forests grow and farms can thrive. Where it is moderate, grassland spreads and the bison do well. Where it is scarce, shrubs and desert take over, and fewer people can live. The land did not make anyone choose a particular life, but it set limits on the choices.
Check the map

Some maps and movies show Texas as one huge dry desert dotted with tall cactus. The big cactus with arms, called the saguaro, does not grow in Texas at all. Find a picture or map like that and ask what it leaves out. Which of the four regions does it show, and which does it hide? What would a student from East Texas say about it?
📚 PART 4 · THE VERDICT
No second Mexico

What did Spain want? It wanted a second Mexico. That meant a large settled population to put to work, a **tribute** system to take over, and wealth to carry home. The Caddo had a settled population, but their villages were far from Mexico, and there was no silver or gold. In the rest of Texas, the Spaniards found no cities and no tribute at all.

As the Spaniards went west from the Caddo towns, they found that the land grew drier. The Gentleman of Elvas wrote that the people there lived in small groups, hunted for their food, and had no corn. The army had little to eat and no good guides. Moscoso decided to turn back.

This was the verdict, and it came from the land as much as from the people. Spain's model needed a tribute system. East Texas had farmers but no gold. West of there, the land was too dry to feed a large population. A model built for one kind of place was failing in another.

After Moscoso turned back, his men built boats on the Mississippi and sailed to Mexico. Coronado had already gone home. Spain had its answer. There was no second Mexico in Texas. For about the next 140 years, Spain mostly turned away from this land. It would turn back in 1685, but only because someone else arrived first.
🌐 FOREIGN LANGUAGE VOCABULARY
**Coronado** (kor-oh-NAH-doh). Francisco Vázquez de Coronado, the Spanish governor who led the expedition across the plains.
💪 WHAT TO CARRY FORWARD

Texas is a land of different regions, and each one shaped a different kind of people. The coast, the plains, and the eastern woodlands could not support a Spanish tribute system, so Spain left. This is an important part of the story of why Spain left Texas alone for so long.

text: Shipwreck on the Island of Misfortune

text: Age of Exploration
💡 GLOSSARY OF SUBJECT VOCABULARY
A few words in this lesson are worth a look before you read. They show up in bold, and you can hover over any of them for a reminder.
**ecology** (ee-KAHL-uh-jee). How living things, including people, fit with the land and water around them.
**enslave** (en-SLAYV). To force a person to work for you without pay or freedom.
**expedition** (eks-pih-DISH-un). A long trip taken for a purpose, such as exploring or conquering.
**seasonal** (SEE-zun-ul). Changing with the seasons of the year.
**tribute** (TRIB-yoot). Payment in goods or labor that a conquered people must give to their rulers.
📖 TODAY'S FOCUS
Everything went wrong. Then the people the Spaniards came to rule kept them alive.

In 1528, a Spanish **expedition** set out to claim Florida and find riches. Within months, it fell apart. A few survivors washed ashore on a sandy island off the coast of Texas, with no ships, no food, and no help from Spain. This lesson tells what happened next, and why it matters for the question of who would own Texas.

📚 PART 1 · AN EXPEDITION FALLS APART

section: No gold, and no way home
text: No gold, and no way home

section: No gold, and no way home
text: The leader was a Spanish commander named Narváez. In 1528, he landed in Florida with about three hundred men. He had been told that gold waited inland. He marched into the country and found swamps, hunger, and fights with the people who lived there. There was no gold and no great city.

section: No gold, and no way home
text: **Cabeza de Vaca** served as treasurer, which meant that he kept track of money and goods for the king. He was not the leader, and he was not the man who made the big choices. Yet the choices he lived through shaped the rest of his life. A man who started out counting the king's gold ended up with no gold and almost nothing to wear.

section: No gold, and no way home
text: The Spaniards met strong resistance from the Apalachee people of northern Florida. Many men died from arrows and disease. The expedition had come to rule a land, and it could barely feed itself.

section: No gold, and no way home
text: After months, the men were sick and starving. They decided to build boats and sail along the Gulf coast to reach Spanish towns in Mexico. They had no shipbuilders and few tools, so they made what they needed from what they had. They melted their iron stirrups and spurs to make saws and axes. They sewed their shirts into sails. They made rope from palm fiber and horsehair, and they used horse hides to hold fresh water. They ate their horses as they worked.

section: No gold, and no way home
text: In the fall of 1528, five crowded boats set out. Storms, thirst, and hunger pulled them apart. Narváez himself was lost at sea. In November, two boats washed ashore on a sandy island off what is now the Texas coast. Among the survivors was Cabeza de Vaca, the expedition's treasurer. He named the island **the Island of Misfortune** (*Malhado*).

section: No gold, and no way home
text: 🌐 FOREIGN LANGUAGE VOCABULARY

section: No gold, and no way home
text: **Cabeza de Vaca** (kah-BEH-sah deh VAH-kah). Álvar Núñez Cabeza de Vaca, the treasurer of the expedition. He later wrote the story of what happened.

section: No gold, and no way home
text: **the Island of Misfortune (*Malhado*)** (mahl-AH-doh). The name Cabeza de Vaca gave to the island where his boat washed ashore.

section: No gold, and no way home
text: **Narváez** (nar-VAH-ess). Pánfilo de Narváez, the Spanish commander of the 1528 expedition to Florida.

section: No gold, and no way home
text: Imagine being on one of those boats. Thirst was a constant danger, and there was little fresh water to drink. The boats sat low in the water, and waves washed over the sides. Nobody on board had ever sailed this coast, and nobody could say how far it was to the nearest Spanish town.

section: PART 2 THE PEOPLE OF THE COAST
text: 📚 PART 2 · THE PEOPLE OF THE COAST

section: People who moved with the food
text: People who moved with the food

section: People who moved with the food
text: The island was not empty. People lived along this coast, and they are often called the **Karankawa**. The Spaniards did not use that name, and the groups they met had names of their own. These coastal people did not farm. They lived by the water, and they moved with the food.

section: People who moved with the food
text: 🌐 FOREIGN LANGUAGE VOCABULARY

section: People who moved with the food
text: **Karankawa** (kuh-RANG-kuh-wah). The name often used today for the coastal peoples of the Texas Gulf coast.

section: People who moved with the food
text: Here is how it worked. In the cooler months, families lived on islands and shores where they could catch fish and gather shellfish and roots. In warmer months, many moved inland to gather berries and the fruit of the prickly pear cactus, and to hunt. Their lives followed a calendar of food. This pattern is part of the **ecology** of the Gulf coast. Their way of life was **seasonal**, and it worked well for people who knew the coast.

section: People who moved with the food
text: These families traveled by canoe, carved from single tree trunks. They crossed the shallow bays and channels between the islands and the mainland, and they knew every inlet and shell bank. The Spaniards, with their heavy gear and clumsy boats, knew almost nothing about the coast. That difference mattered a great deal.

section: People who moved with the food
text: Knowing the coast was a form of wealth. A family that knew where the shellfish were thick in winter and where the berries ripened in summer would eat well. A family that did not would go hungry. The Spaniards had arrived in the worst possible state, with no skill in the one thing that mattered most on that shore.
📚 PART 3 · THE REVERSAL
First fed, then enslaved

Winter came hard. The Spaniards were weak, cold, and starving. They had no ships and no weapons that mattered. The people of the island gave them food and fire. Without that help, the Spaniards would have died within weeks.

Then things turned. A sickness spread among the island people, and some of them blamed the strangers. Most of the Spaniards died that winter. The few who lived were scattered among different groups. Cabeza de Vaca himself was **enslaved** for years. The men who had come to rule the land now lived at the mercy of the people they had meant to rule.

It helps to remember how little the Spaniards could offer in return. They had no goods to trade and no skills the island people needed. A group that is already short of food has to think hard before it shares with strangers. The surprise is not that the kindness ended. The surprise is that it began.

Of the men who landed on the island, only a handful lived through the winter. Cold, hunger, and sickness killed the rest. The coastal people were neither helpless hosts nor fierce enemies in this story. They were people making choices about food, fear, and family, just as the Spaniards were.

The words of Cabeza de Vaca help us here, because he wrote down what he lived through. He told of Spaniards so hungry that some did terrible things to stay alive. He also told of Native families who wept when the strangers suffered. His book shows both sides, and that is what makes it so useful to historians.
📚 PART 4 · WHAT THE SHIPWRECK SHOWS

section: A model with no system to take over
text: A model with no system to take over

section: A model with no system to take over
text: Think back to Mexico. There, Spain found a city of 200,000 people and a long list of towns that owed payment to the ruler. Here, there was nothing like that. There were no fields of corn to tax, no towns to govern, and no ruler to replace. There was no **tribute** to collect. The Spaniards could not command anyone. They needed the local people to survive, because those people knew the land.

section: A model with no system to take over
text: This is a hint about the whole story of Spain in Texas. The Spanish model needed a large, settled population. On the Texas coast, Spain found people who moved with the seasons and who owed nothing to anyone.

section: A model with no system to take over
text: The shipwreck also shows how much luck shaped these events. A storm decided where the boats came ashore. A sickness decided how the island people treated the strangers. A few small turns, and the story would have ended in silence.

section: A model with no system to take over
text: It is also a reminder that this story survives only because a few men lived. If they had not been fed, nobody would ever have heard of the island or of what happened there. Cabeza de Vaca wrote it all down, and his story continues as he walks across Texas.
💪 WHAT TO CARRY FORWARD

A shipwreck turned the Spanish model upside down. The people who expected to give orders had to take them, and the people they came to rule decided whether they lived or died. Keep that reversal in mind.
