💡 GLOSSARY OF SUBJECT VOCABULARY
A few words in this lesson are worth a look before you read. They show up in bold, and you can hover over any of them for a reminder.
**empire** (EM-pyr). A large area of land and many peoples ruled by one government.
**expedition** (eks-pih-DISH-un). A long trip taken for a purpose, such as exploring or conquering.
**navigation** (nav-ih-GAY-shun). The skill of finding your way, especially across the sea.
**Ottoman Empire** (AHT-uh-mun EM-pyr). A powerful empire, based in what is now Turkey, that controlled many trade routes between Europe and Asia.
**rival** (RY-vul). A person or country that competes against another.
**route** (root). The path from one place to another.
**spice** (spys). A plant product, such as pepper or cinnamon, used to flavor food. Spices were once worth a fortune in Europe.
**treasury** (TREZH-er-ee). The money of a government, and the office that takes care of it.
📖 TODAY'S FOCUS
What would you do if you found a whole world nobody in your country knew was there?

In the 1400s, Europeans did not know that two huge continents sat between them and Asia. They were looking for a faster way to reach the riches of the East. What they found instead changed the world, and it raised a problem that nobody had planned for. By the end of this lesson, you will see how three European **empires** began to work on that problem.

📚 PART 1 · WHY EUROPE WENT LOOKING

section: A long way to the money
text: A long way to the money

section: A long way to the money
text: In the 1400s, Europeans wanted goods from Asia. Silk, gold, and **spices** like pepper and cinnamon all came from far away. Merchants carried them across land and sea until they reached Europe. The trip was long, and every trader along the way took a share of the profit. By the time the goods arrived, they cost a lot.

section: A long way to the money
text: Spices were not just for flavor. Some were used as medicine, and all of them were light, easy to carry, and very valuable for their weight. A ship that carried a full load of pepper could make its owners rich. That is why so many people wanted a cheaper way to bring spices home.

section: A long way to the money
text: Then the **Ottoman Empire** grew strong. Its armies took the great city of Constantinople in 1453, and the Ottomans came to control many of the land **routes** to Asia. Europeans could still trade, but they paid more, and they had to deal with a powerful **rival**. Kings and merchants began to ask a simple question. Was there a way around?

section: A long way to the money
text: The Ottomans did not seal the door. They taxed the trade and made it harder to plan. A merchant who could not trust what goods would cost next year began to look for other options. Pressure like this does not force anyone to do one particular thing. But it makes people willing to try ideas they would have laughed at before.
Portugal shows the way

Portugal, a small country on the Atlantic coast, tried the sea. Its sailors built better ships and learned to find their way with the stars and new tools. This skill is called **navigation**. Step by step, Portuguese ships sailed farther down the coast of Africa. In 1498, a Portuguese captain named **Vasco da Gama** reached India by sailing all the way around Africa. Portugal had found a sea route to Asia, and it was not going to share it.
Every ship that came back from India loaded with spices made Portugal richer, and the rulers of Spain were watching closely. If Spain wanted a share, it would need a route of its own.
🌐 FOREIGN LANGUAGE VOCABULARY
**Vasco da Gama** (VAHS-koh dah GAH-mah). A Portuguese sea captain who sailed from Portugal to India in 1498.
📚 PART 2 · COLUMBUS, 1492
Spain tries a different road

Spain wanted a route of its own. An Italian sailor named Christopher Columbus had an idea. He would sail west across the Atlantic and reach Asia from the other side. Many experts thought the ocean was far too wide, and they were right. Columbus believed the distance was much shorter than it really is. Even so, Queen Isabella and King Ferdinand of Spain agreed to pay for his **expedition**. One of the men who helped find the money was a royal official named **Santángel**.
🌐 FOREIGN LANGUAGE VOCABULARY
**Santángel** (sahn-TAHN-hel). Luis de Santángel, a Spanish royal official who helped pay for Columbus's voyage.

You may have heard that Columbus was trying to prove the Earth is round. That is a myth. Educated Europeans already knew the Earth was round. The argument was about how big it was. Columbus guessed that Asia was close. The experts guessed that it was far away, and the experts were right.

In 1492, Columbus set out with three ships. After more than two months at sea, he reached an island in the Caribbean. He believed he had arrived at the edge of Asia, the lands Europeans called the Indies. So he called the people he met "Indians." The name stuck, even though he was wrong about where he was.

Columbus was also lucky. If the Americas had not been in his path, his ships would probably have run out of food and water in the middle of the ocean. One of the most important voyages in history could have ended with a few lost ships and a sad story told in Spanish harbors. Nothing about the outcome was certain.

Think about what Columbus needed to make his plan work. He needed money, ships, and a ruler willing to gamble. Isabella and Ferdinand had just finished a long war to drive the last Muslim kingdom out of Spain, and their **treasury** was thin. Still, the possible reward was huge. A rich new route to Asia could pay for a great deal.

After Columbus returned in 1493, he wrote a letter to Santángel describing what he had found. The letter was copied and printed, and the news spread across Europe. Soon every ruler wanted to know more.
Columbus made four voyages in all. He died in 1506 still believing that he had reached the edge of Asia. He never understood that he had found two continents that Europeans did not know about.

section: PART 3 THE PROBLEM NOBODY PLANNED FOR
text: 📚 PART 3 · THE PROBLEM NOBODY PLANNED FOR

section: The land was already full of people
text: The land was already full of people

section: The land was already full of people
text: Columbus had not found an empty world. Millions of people lived in the Americas, and they spoke hundreds of languages. Some lived in small bands that hunted and gathered their food. Others were farmers with villages and large fields of corn. Some ruled cities as big as the largest in Europe, as the story of Mexico will show.

section: The land was already full of people
text: Historians cannot agree on exactly how many people lived in the Americas in 1492. The estimates are very different, but nearly everyone agrees on one point. It was many millions.

section: The land was already full of people
text: This was a problem no European king had planned for. Spain, France, and England all wanted to claim land. But who owned it? And what should a European power do about the people who already lived there? Should it trade with them, fight them, put them to work, or push them away?
📚 PART 4 · THREE EMPIRES, THREE BEGINNINGS

section: Each power starts in a different place
text: Each power starts in a different place

section: Each power starts in a different place
text: Spain moved first, and it moved south. Its ships and soldiers settled the islands of the Caribbean and then pushed onto the mainland. That story is told in other lessons on Spain in the Americas. England sent an Italian sailor named John Cabot across the North Atlantic in 1497. He sailed for the English king and reached the coast of North America far to the north. France sent ships along the same coast. In 1534, **Cartier** sailed into the great St. Lawrence River, and France began to build a hold in the north.

section: PART 1 THE SPANISH ANSWER: CONQUER, CONVERT, INCLUDE

section: Take over, and put people to work
text: Take over, and put people to work

section: Take over, and put people to work
text: Spain's first answer was to conquer the people who already lived in a place. Spain then asked them to **convert** to Christianity and made them part of the Spanish system as workers. Spaniards believed they were bringing a good thing, their religion. They also wanted wealth. The people already living there would grow food, dig for silver and gold, and pay taxes. Spanish officials would sit at the top. A place ruled this way was called a **colony**.

section: Take over, and put people to work
text: Spain used a paper to say so out loud. It was called **the Requirement** (*Requerimiento*). Spanish officers read it to Native people, telling them to accept the Spanish king and the Church, or war would follow. Often it was read in Spanish to people who could not understand a word.

section: Take over, and put people to work
text: 🌐 FOREIGN LANGUAGE VOCABULARY

section: Take over, and put people to work
text: **the Requirement (*Requerimiento*)** (reh-keh-ree-mee-EN-toh). A Spanish paper from 1513 that was read aloud to Native peoples. It told them to accept the Spanish king and the Christian faith.

section: Take over, and put people to work
text: Notice what this model needed. Only a small number of Spaniards crossed the ocean. They did not plan to do the work themselves. They planned to rule over many people who would do it. The Spanish model worked best where a large population already lived and already knew how to farm and pay taxes to a ruler.

section: Take over, and put people to work
text: This is why Spaniards in Mexico often settled in towns near large Native populations. A Spanish landowner or official wanted workers close by. If he settled far from anyone, he would have nobody to put to work. Where the people were, the Spaniards went. Where the people were few, the Spanish model had little to hold on to.

section: Take over, and put people to work
text: For Spain, the model paid off. In the 1500s, huge amounts of silver from Spanish mines flowed back across the ocean, and it helped make Spain one of the richest and most powerful kingdoms in Europe. But Spaniards were always a small minority in their own colonies. The system depended on the labor of the people they ruled.

section: PART 2 THE FRENCH ANSWER: TRADE, ALLY, INTERMARRY
text: 📚 PART 2 · THE FRENCH ANSWER: TRADE, ALLY, INTERMARRY
Few settlers, many friends

France sent very few **settlers**. French traders built posts along the St. Lawrence River and traded with Native peoples for furs, especially beaver. Beaver fur was in high demand in Europe, where it was made into hats. France built a small town at Quebec in 1608, but it stayed small for a long time.

The French needed Native hunters and trappers to bring in the furs. So they did not try to rule them. They made **alliances** instead. Many French traders learned Native languages, and some **intermarried** with Native families. Their children grew up in both worlds. **Allies** also fought on the same side when trouble came.

French priests also traveled to Native villages to share their faith. They often lived there as guests, not as rulers. For a long time, New France had only a few thousand French settlers, while the English colonies grew to tens of thousands.

A trader also had to learn how to behave. In many Native communities, a guest who came with gifts and who listened was welcome, and a guest who came with demands was not. French traders who learned this did well. Those who did not tended to do poorly, because without friends there was nobody to bring them furs.

This model needed very few French people. What it needed most was friends. It worked best in a land of forests and rivers, where Native hunters knew the animals and the trails, and there were no big farming populations to tax.

section: PART 3 THE ENGLISH ANSWER: MOVE IN, KEEP APART, PUSH OUT
text: 📚 PART 3 · THE ENGLISH ANSWER: MOVE IN, KEEP APART, PUSH OUT
Whole communities cross the ocean

England tried something different. English settlers came in families, with men, women, and children, and they planned to stay. They built towns and farms that looked like the ones they had left. Jamestown in Virginia began in 1607. Plymouth in Massachusetts began in 1620.

English settlers wanted farmland more than they wanted Native workers or furs. They kept their own towns separate from Native villages. As their towns grew, they needed more land, and Native peoples were often **displaced**. There was trade and some friendship, but there was also a lot of conflict over who controlled the land.

English settlers also brought their ideas about government. They set up town meetings and elected assemblies, and they expected to run their own local affairs under the king. They believed that a settler who owned land had a say in how the colony was run.

Another reason the English model spread was simple. England had many people who wanted a fresh start. Some were poor farmers who had no land at home. Others wanted to worship in their own way. Ships carried thousands of them across the ocean over the years, and the more who came, the faster the colonies grew.
This model needed many settlers and a lot of open farmland. It worked best in a place with good soil and a climate like England's.

section: PART 4 AN ANSWER IS TIED TO A PLACE
text: 📚 PART 4 · AN ANSWER IS TIED TO A PLACE
No model is best everywhere

Look at the three models side by side. Each one was an answer to a problem, and each fit a certain kind of place. In central Mexico, millions of farmers already paid **tribute** to rulers, and the Spanish model could take that system over. In the northern forests, there were furs to trade and few farmers to tax, and the French model fit. On the eastern coast, there was good farmland and a growing number of English settlers, and the English model fit.

Another way to see the difference is to ask what each power wanted the land to give it. Spain wanted workers and silver. France wanted furs and allies who could supply them. England wanted ground to plow and room to grow. Because they wanted different things, each one was good at different kinds of places.

None of these answers was bound to win. Each one worked until it reached a place it did not fit. That is why the next question matters so much. Texas is not central Mexico. It is not the northern forest. It is not the English coast. So which model reaches Texas, and why that one?
Before you go on, write your guess in your notebook, along with one reason. Keep it, and check it again later. The question underneath it is a big one: who was going to own this place?
💪 WHAT TO CARRY FORWARD

You now have a set of three models to test. Spain conquers and rules. France trades and allies. England moves in and holds land apart. The Spanish model reached its greatest success in one of the largest cities in North America.

section: PART 1 1808: A KING WITHOUT A THRONE
text: 📚 PART 1 · 1808: A KING WITHOUT A THRONE
Napoleon takes Spain

In 1808, the French **emperor** Napoleon sent his army into Spain. He forced the Spanish king to give up the throne and put his own brother in the king's place. Many Spaniards refused to accept this. They rose up against the French, and local councils began to rule in the name of the king they considered legitimate.

Why did this matter so much? In the Spanish **empire**, the king was the link that held everything together. Every official, every court, and every church officer served in his name. When the king was gone, the whole chain of command was in doubt. Nobody had planned for this. Nobody had a rule for what to do when a foreign army took the king prisoner.

In New Spain, the question was how to respond. Should the **colony** obey the French king? Should it obey the Spanish councils? Or should it govern itself until the real king returned? The **viceroy** supported a plan for a council of local leaders. But Spaniards in Mexico City feared losing power, and in September 1808, they overthrew him in a **coup**. The **criollos** saw that their voices would not count, even in an emergency.
🌐 FOREIGN LANGUAGE VOCABULARY
**criollo** (kree-OH-yoh). A person of Spanish descent who was born in the Americas, not in Spain.

Think about how these choices looked to different people. A Spanish official in Mexico City wanted to keep things as they were, because he held his job from the old government. A landowner wanted a voice, because he felt he had earned one. A poor farmer wanted relief from **debts** and taxes. Each person asked who would help him, and each got a different answer.
📚 PART 2 · THE CRY OF DOLORES, 1810
A priest rings a bell

On September 16, 1810, a priest named **Hidalgo** rang the church bell in the town of Dolores and called his people to rise up. His speech is known as the **Cry of Dolores** (*Grito de Dolores*). Thousands of poor farmers and workers joined him. They captured towns and marched toward Mexico City.

Hidalgo was a parish priest, and he knew his people well. He had started projects in his town to help the poor earn a living. The crowd that followed him was made of many people who were poor and angry. They did not have training or good weapons. But they had numbers, and for a short time that was enough to frighten the Spanish government.

The movement was not tidy. Its members were angry at Spanish rule, at poverty, and at the unfair treatment of Native and mixed-race people. Hidalgo turned back before reaching Mexico City. In 1811, he was captured and executed. Others carried on the fight, but for years the **royalist** armies held the advantage.
🌐 FOREIGN LANGUAGE VOCABULARY
**Cry of Dolores (*Grito de Dolores*)** (GREE-toh deh doh-LOH-res). The speech Hidalgo gave on September 16, 1810, in the town of Dolores. It started the revolt.
**Hidalgo** (ee-DAHL-goh). Miguel Hidalgo, a priest who began the Mexican independence movement in 1810.

The fight was not only a fight against Spain. It was also a fight among Mexicans. Some joined Hidalgo at first, but turned away when his followers attacked their property. Others fought for the king, because they feared the poor more than they feared Spain. The war split families and towns, and it made peace harder to reach.
📚 PART 3 · TEXAS AT WAR, 1812 TO 1813

section: A bloody battle on the Medina
text: A bloody battle on the Medina

section: A bloody battle on the Medina
text: The fighting reached Texas in 1812. A Mexican rebel named Bernardo Gutiérrez joined with an American officer named Augustus Magee. Together they led a force of **volunteers**, many of them Americans from Louisiana, across the Sabine River. They took **Nacogdoches**, then **La Bahía**, then San Antonio. In 1813, they declared Texas independent as part of a **republic**.

section: A bloody battle on the Medina
text: 🌐 FOREIGN LANGUAGE VOCABULARY

section: A bloody battle on the Medina
text: **La Bahía** (lah bah-EE-ah). A Spanish fort and mission in South Texas. Today it is in the town of Goliad.

section: A bloody battle on the Medina
text: **Nacogdoches** (nak-uh-DOH-chiz). A town in East Texas, named for a Native people who lived nearby.

section: A bloody battle on the Medina
text: Notice that the army was called the Republican Army of the North. It was a mix of Mexican rebels and American volunteers. Gutiérrez wanted a free Mexico, and many of the Americans wanted adventure, land, or both. When Magee died, the army lost the leader who had held it together, and its members began to quarrel about what they were fighting for.

section: A bloody battle on the Medina
text: Spain sent a strong army under General **Arredondo**. On August 18, 1813, the two sides met near the **Medina** River south of San Antonio. The rebel army was crushed. Historians often call it the bloodiest battle ever fought on Texas soil. Arredondo's soldiers then marched into San Antonio and punished the people who had supported the **rebellion**.

section: A bloody battle on the Medina
text: Arredondo had trained his men well, and he had more soldiers and better supplies than the rebels. The royalists were disciplined, and the rebel army was divided. Even so, a Spanish victory was not certain until the fighting began. The rebels had won earlier battles, and they had taken the capital of the **province**.

section: A bloody battle on the Medina
text: The province was wrecked. Families fled to Louisiana. Ranches were **abandoned**, and the few **settlers** who stayed were poor and frightened. Texas entered the 1820s even weaker than before.

section: A bloody battle on the Medina
text: 🌐 FOREIGN LANGUAGE VOCABULARY

section: A bloody battle on the Medina
text: **Arredondo** (ah-reh-DOHN-doh). Joaquín de Arredondo, the Spanish general who crushed the rebels in Texas.

section: A bloody battle on the Medina
text: **Medina** (meh-DEE-nah). A river south of San Antonio. The battle fought there in 1813 was one of the bloodiest in Texas history.

section: A bloody battle on the Medina
text: The aftermath was cruel. Arredondo's men hunted down rebels, and many people were executed or **imprisoned**. Property was taken. Families who had supported the rebellion were punished, and some women were held and forced to work. A province that had so few people lost many of them in a single summer. Texas needed new settlers more than ever, and few wanted to come.
📚 PART 4 · 1821: INDEPENDENCE
Spain loses Mexico

The independence war lasted more than a decade. In 1820, a **revolt** in Spain forced the king to accept a **constitution**, and **conservative** leaders in New Spain worried about the new rules. **Iturbide**, an army officer who had fought the rebels, changed sides. He joined with a rebel leader and issued a plan that promised independence, the Catholic faith, and equal rights for Spaniards and Mexicans.

It is worth asking why Iturbide's plan worked when Hidalgo's did not. Iturbide offered something to nearly everyone. The Church kept its place, gained power, and Spaniards in Mexico were promised safety. Hidalgo had asked for much more change, much faster. Iturbide's plan was less a revolution than a deal, and many leaders were willing to sign it.

It worked. In September 1821, the armies entered Mexico City, and Mexico became independent. The new country **inherited** an enormous territory, a damaged economy, and a far northern province with three small towns and no real control. Texas had a new government and an old problem.
🌐 FOREIGN LANGUAGE VOCABULARY
**Iturbide** (ee-toor-BEE-deh). Agustín de Iturbide, a Spanish army officer who led the final push for Mexican independence.

Notice what the new country did not have. It had little experience running a country on its own, no strong national government, and no shared sense of who its leaders should be. A war had destroyed trust between many groups, and the army had become the most powerful body in the land. Mexico was free, but it was also unsettled, and that would shape every decision about Texas that followed.
💪 WHAT TO CARRY FORWARD

Napoleon's move in Spain set off a chain of events that ended three centuries of Spanish rule. It left Mexico free but poor, and it left Texas empty and scarred. The new nation had to decide what to do with its distant north.

What happens when the people who win a war cannot agree on how to run the country?

In 1821, Mexico became free of Spain. Winning **independence** was only the first job. The leaders still had to decide who would rule, what the rules would be, and who would obey them. This lesson follows a country that had no practice at any of that, from the hopeful start of 1821 to the fall of an **emperor** in 1823.

section: PART 1 A FREE COUNTRY WITHOUT A PLAN
text: 📚 PART 1 · A FREE COUNTRY WITHOUT A PLAN
A promise on paper

When Iturbide and the rebel leaders joined forces in 1821, they made a plan. Mexico would be independent, the Catholic Church would keep its place, and Spaniards and Mexicans would be treated as equals. The new country would be ruled by a king under written laws. The plan sounded fair to nearly everyone, and that is why it worked.
🌐 FOREIGN LANGUAGE VOCABULARY
**Iturbide** (ee-toor-BEE-deh). Agustín de Iturbide, a Spanish army officer who led the final push for Mexican independence.

The plan had a weak spot. It said that a Spanish prince would be invited to become king of Mexico. Spain had no interest in the offer, and the Spanish king refused to let any prince go. Mexico was left with a plan that called for a king and had no king to fill the job.

Think about how unusual the setting was. Mexico had been ruled by Spain for three hundred years. Hardly anyone alive had ever voted for a ruler or served in a national government. The people in **congress** were learning how to govern while they were doing it, and mistakes came quickly.

A temporary government took charge, and a congress met in Mexico City in early 1822 to write a **constitution**. The members of congress came from many **regions** and had many ideas. Some wanted a strong king. Some wanted a **republic**. Some wanted the army kept small. They argued for months, and the country waited.
A hero with no job

Iturbide was the most popular man in Mexico. He had won the war with Spain, and many soldiers and ordinary people loved him. But popularity is not the same as a plan for governing. Iturbide wanted a strong leader who could act quickly. Congress wanted to keep the power to make laws. The two sides began to distrust each other.

Meanwhile the country's money was running out. The war had damaged farms and mines, and the new government had few ways to collect taxes. It owed money to the army. Soldiers who are not paid grow restless, and restless soldiers look for someone to follow. In 1822, many of them looked to Iturbide.
📚 PART 2 · AN EMPEROR
The night of May 18

On the night of May 18, 1822, a sergeant in Mexico City led a crowd of soldiers through the streets shouting that Iturbide should be emperor. The crowd grew. Iturbide acted surprised, though many people at the time doubted that he was. The next day, congress met with the crowd outside and voted to make him emperor.

Iturbide took the throne as Agustín the First. In July, he was crowned in the great cathedral in a ceremony meant to look as grand as any in Europe. A Mexican emperor was an odd idea for a country that had just fought a war for freedom. But for a short time, it seemed to make the army and the crowds happy.

The new emperor soon found that he had the same problems as the old congress, and he no longer had anyone to blame. The **treasury** was empty. Congress still argued with him. In October, Iturbide shut the congress down by force and replaced it with a smaller group of men he picked himself. Now almost nobody could say that he governed by law.
The army turns

A young army officer named **Santa Anna** made the next move. He commanded the port of **Veracruz** and had once supported Iturbide. In December 1822, he turned against him and called for a republic. Santa Anna would soon become the most powerful and most troublesome man in Mexico, and this was his first big step.
🌐 FOREIGN LANGUAGE VOCABULARY
**Santa Anna** (SAN-tah AH-nah). Antonio López de Santa Anna, a Mexican army officer who became one of the most powerful men in Mexico.
**Veracruz** (veh-rah-KROOS). The main Mexican port on the Gulf of Mexico.

Other officers joined him. In February 1823, a group of generals signed a plan at **Casa Mata**. It called for a new congress and did not attack the emperor directly, but everyone understood what it meant. **Province** after province backed it. Iturbide's army, the only thing holding up his throne, was leaving him.
🌐 FOREIGN LANGUAGE VOCABULARY
**Casa Mata** (KAH-sah MAH-tah). A fort at Veracruz that gave its name to an army plan made in 1823.

Iturbide tried to save himself by calling congress back in early March. It was too late. On March 19, 1823, he gave up the throne in a letter to congress. In May, he sailed into **exile** in Europe. The **empire** had lasted about ten months, and nobody had planned for it to end this way.

section: PART 3 WHAT IT MEANT FOR TEXAS
text: 📚 PART 3 · WHAT IT MEANT FOR TEXAS
A grant approved twice

Stephen F. Austin was in the capital through all of this. Iturbide's government had just confirmed his grant, and now Iturbide was gone. Austin had to start again. The new leaders were a committee of three generals, and they looked at the grant carefully.

Notice the careful timing. Austin did not rush the new leaders. He presented his case, answered their questions, and waited for them to settle into their jobs. He knew that a government that had just taken power wanted to look orderly. A request that was calm and reasonable fit that need.

In April 1823, the new government agreed to honor Austin's grant. They did so because Austin had spent a year earning respect, because the plan to put **settlers** in Texas still made sense, and because several officials now knew him by name. A grant approved by one government, and then approved again by the one that replaced it, was much stronger than it had been before.

Austin's **colony** survived the fall of an empire because he had kept up good working relationships with the people who held power. He had also learned how thin the threads were that held a government together.

The Texas colony, meanwhile, kept on growing. Families cleared land, planted corn, and built cabins along the rivers. Most of them knew little about the fall of an emperor far away. Their daily lives depended on a government they had never seen, and on a man who was working hard to keep it friendly.
Lessons of a failed empire

Look at what the story shows. Mexico had won freedom from Spain, but it had no common idea of how to rule itself. The army was stronger than the congress. Popular leaders could gain and lose power in a few months. These weaknesses would trouble Mexico for decades.

Notice also that none of it was settled in advance. If Iturbide had listened to congress, or if the army had stayed loyal, Mexico might have had a steadier government. Because it did not, every later leader had to deal with a country where power was often decided by who commanded the soldiers.

Austin took away a simple lesson. Mexican governments changed often, and the people who held office mattered more than the paper they signed. He would have to prove this lesson again, in the capital and in Texas, many times over the years that followed.
💪 REMEMBER THIS QUESTION
Keep one question in mind: what holds a government together once the war that created it is over? In Mexico in 1823, the answer was not yet clear.

section: Was Texas the only part of Mexico that rose against its government?
text: When you read about the Texas Revolution, it can seem as if Texas stood alone. It did not. In the 1830s, one **province** after another rose against the government in Mexico City, because that government had thrown away the **federal** **constitution**. This lesson shows the whole map, and where Texas fits on it.

📚 PART 1 · A PRESIDENT CHANGES SIDES
Reform and reaction

In 1833, Mexico's new government began a program of **reforms**. The vice president, **Gómez Farías**, led the effort. The reforms cut back the privileges of the Church and the army, and they tried to open public life to new ideas. **Liberals** in Mexico cheered. Many others were alarmed.
🌐 FOREIGN LANGUAGE VOCABULARY
**Santa Anna** (SAN-tah AH-nah). Antonio López de Santa Anna, a Mexican army officer who became one of the most powerful men in Mexico.
**Zacatecas** (zah-kah-TEH-kahs). A silver-mining state in central Mexico with a strong state militia.
**Gómez Farías** (GOH-mes fah-REE-ahs). Valentín Gómez Farías, the Mexican vice president who led a program of reforms in 1833.

The Church, the army, and many wealthy landowners pushed back. They saw the reforms as an attack on the oldest institutions in the country. **Conservatives** wanted Mexico to move slowly and to keep its traditions. Protests spread, and the country divided into two camps that did not trust each other.

Think about why the reforms felt so threatening. The Church owned much land and ran schools and hospitals. The army had its own courts and privileges. Taking those away would change daily life for thousands of families. People who feel that their way of life is under attack will often follow any leader who promises to protect it.

Santa Anna had been elected as a friend of the liberals. But he was a man who followed power. In 1834, he saw that the conservatives were stronger, and he changed sides. He returned to the capital, dismissed the vice president, and sent the **congress** home. Many of the reforms were undone in a few months.
A strongman steps forward

Santa Anna fits a pattern that Mexico knew well in this period, the strongman (**caudillo**). A caudillo was a leader who ruled through the loyalty of his soldiers and followers rather than through laws and offices. Santa Anna called himself a defender of the nation. But he often acted as if he were the nation.
🌐 FOREIGN LANGUAGE VOCABULARY
**strongman (*caudillo*)** (kow-DEE-yoh). A military leader who rules by force and by the loyalty of his followers.

Notice what made a strongman possible. The government was weak, the **treasury** was empty, and the army was the only body that could keep order. When there is no common agreement on how to settle a dispute, the person with the most guns has the loudest voice. Mexico's early leaders had never settled that question.

Santa Anna was not simply a villain. He was brave, quick, and a skilled organizer of troops. He could also be generous when it suited him. But he lacked patience for laws that limited him, and he was willing to change his stated beliefs when his interests changed.
📚 PART 2 · THE FEDERAL SYSTEM FALLS
Centralists take charge

With Santa Anna's support, a new group of **centralists** took charge of the government. A centralist is someone who wants power held in the national capital. They believed that the states had too much freedom and that only a strong center could hold Mexico together. They had many friends in the army and the Church.

The centralists had reasons that sounded sensible to them. Mexico faced **rebellions**, an empty treasury, and the threat of **invasion** from abroad. They argued that a nation that could not act as one would not survive. Their mistake was to think that force could take the place of the consent of the provinces.

In 1835 and 1836, the centralists wrote a new constitution called the Seven Laws. It replaced the federal constitution of 1824. The states were turned into **departments** run from the capital, and their governors were chosen by the president. The power that the states had held for a dozen years was gone.

To many Mexicans, this was a betrayal of the compact that had made the country. The states had joined a federal **republic**. Now the republic was being swapped for something else without their consent. People in the provinces felt that the government in the capital had broken the agreement first.
The lesson of Zacatecas

The state of Zacatecas was one of the richest in Mexico, with silver mines and a strong state **militia**. When the new rules limited the size of state militias, Zacatecas refused to obey. Its leaders believed that they were defending the constitution, and they raised troops.

In May 1835, Santa Anna marched against them and won a quick victory. His soldiers then looted the city of Zacatecas. The message for other states was plain. Resistance would be crushed, and a federal system with armed states was no longer allowed.

Now Santa Anna had a victorious army and a free hand. The next trouble spot was to the north. In Texas, **settlers** who had been pressing for local rights were now outraged, and Santa Anna's government sent soldiers to the coast and the border. The path from Zacatecas to Texas was a direct one.
📚 PART 3 · A MAP OF REVOLTS
One province after another

Zacatecas was only the beginning. In 1835, Texas rose. In 1836, California declared itself a free state within Mexico. In 1837, rebels in New Mexico killed their governor and took over the capital before the army arrived. In 1839, **Yucatán** rebelled, and in 1840, three northern states joined in the short-lived Republic of the **Rio Grande**.
🌐 FOREIGN LANGUAGE VOCABULARY
**Rio Grande** (REE-oh GRAHN-day). The great river that flows between Texas and Mexico to the Gulf of Mexico.
**Yucatán** (yoo-kah-TAHN). A province on the Yucatán peninsula in southeastern Mexico.

Look at this list as a whole. These revolts did not share a leader or a plan. They happened in different places for different reasons. But they had something in common. Each province had been promised a federal republic, and each had been given a government that took its power away. The new system did not fit the old promise.

Texas was not unique, and its people did not yet believe that it was. Most Texans who took up arms in 1835 said that they were defending the constitution of 1824, as the people of Zacatecas had. They saw themselves as part of a much larger quarrel over how Mexico should be governed.
Which ones got away?

Most of these revolts failed. The army put down the rebellion in New Mexico. The Republic of the Rio Grande fell in less than a year. California's revolt ended in a deal with the government. In each case, the rebels were either defeated or won back their place in Mexico.

Notice a difference between the cases. California, New Mexico, and the Rio Grande states rose to win back a federal system. Yucatán and Texas, in the end, chose to leave. A fight to restore a constitution is very different from a fight to separate. Texas would travel from the first kind of fight to the second.

Only two provinces actually broke away. Yucatán declared **independence** for a time, but it rejoined Mexico in 1848. Texas broke away and did not come back. Out of all the revolts, it was the only one that stayed gone.

Why did Texas succeed where the others failed? Part of the answer is distance, since Texas was far from the center of Mexican power. Part is the colonists' ties to the United States, which sent **volunteers** and money. And part is the luck of one afternoon in April 1836, when a small army won an unlikely battle. None of it was certain in 1835.
💪 REMEMBER THIS QUESTION
Keep one question in mind: if so many provinces rose at once, why did only one stay free? The answer begins with geography, and with chance.

📖 TODAY'S FOCUS
A war over who would be king of Spain changed how Spain ruled half the world.

In 1700, the king of Spain died without a child to take his place. That sparked a war across Europe, and when it ended, a new royal family sat on the Spanish throne. The new family had new ideas about how to rule. They wanted a stronger government, more tax money, and tighter control of the **colonies**. Those changes are called the **Bourbon** **Reforms**, and they reshaped New Spain.

📚 PART 1 · A NEW ROYAL FAMILY
A war about a crown

For almost two hundred years, Spain had been ruled by one **dynasty**, the Hapsburgs. In 1700, the last Hapsburg king died with no child. Two families claimed the throne. One was the French Bourbon family, and the other was an Austrian branch of the Hapsburgs. Europe fought over the answer in the War of the Spanish Succession, which lasted from 1701 to 1714.
🌐 FOREIGN LANGUAGE VOCABULARY
**Bourbon** (BOOR-bun). A French royal family. A Bourbon prince became king of Spain in 1700.

The war ended with a peace **treaty** signed at **Utrecht** in 1713. A Bourbon, Philip V, became king of Spain. In return, Spain gave up its lands in Italy and the Netherlands. It was left with Spain itself and a huge **empire** in the Americas. That empire was now the most valuable thing the new dynasty had.
🌐 FOREIGN LANGUAGE VOCABULARY
**Utrecht** (YOO-trekt). A city in the Netherlands, where the peace treaty of 1713 was signed.

Notice how a fight about a family changed an empire. Nobody in the Americas had any say in who sat on the throne. Yet the winner would decide how they were taxed, who governed them, and what their children could hope to become. A quarrel in faraway Europe shaped what the people of San Antonio could expect from their government.
📚 PART 2 · WHAT THE REFORMS WERE
More control, more money

The Bourbon kings were influenced by the **Enlightenment**. They believed that a king should rule by reason and that a government should be well organized, efficient, and strong. They looked at the Spanish empire and saw a system that was slow, weak, and full of people who kept too much of the money. They set out to change it with a series of reforms.

The Enlightenment gave these kings a way to speak about what they wanted. If reason said the government should be efficient, then anything that slowed the government was a problem. Old customs, local privileges, and Church lands could all be called a waste. The kings did not see themselves as unkind. They believed they were making the empire work better. But a plan that looks reasonable in Madrid can feel harsh in a village far away.

The reforms had four main goals. The first was to **centralize** power in the hands of the king and his officials. The second was to collect more taxes. The third was to build a professional army and a better colonial government. The fourth was to limit the power of the Church. In 1767, the king expelled the Jesuits from the Spanish empire. The Jesuits had run many schools and **missions** in the Americas.

Each goal sounds sensible on its own, but together they changed who held power. Before, many decisions were made slowly, by local people who knew the place. After, more decisions were made by officials who answered to the king. A town could no longer count on friends in the local council to stand up for it. That was a big change for people who had been used to a good deal of independence.

The new officials were often sent from Spain. In New Spain, a new type of governor called an intendant was introduced in the 1780s to supervise a **province** and collect taxes. The changes worked, at least in money. Silver production and tax income rose sharply.

A professional army was also costly. The **Crown** had to pay soldiers, buy weapons, and build forts. It raised taxes to cover these costs, and the people who paid the taxes had little say in how the money was used. People notice when a government asks for more and gives them less of a voice in return.
📚 PART 3 · RESENTMENT
Left out of power

But the reforms made many people angry. The most important group was the **person of Spanish descent born in the Americas** (*criollo*). Before the reforms, criollos had held many local offices. Under the Bourbons, most of the highest posts went to officials born in Spain. A criollo who had grown up in the Americas, whose family had lived there for generations, could find himself passed over for a job by a newcomer.

Taxes were another source of anger. Merchants and landowners paid more than they ever had. The Church was angry about its lost privileges. Each group had a different complaint, and none of them was sure it could trust the Crown.
🌐 FOREIGN LANGUAGE VOCABULARY
**person of Spanish descent born in the Americas (*criollo*)** (kree-OH-yoh). A person of Spanish descent who was born in the Americas, not in Spain.

It helps to remember that these were not poor people. Many criollos owned land, ran businesses, or held positions in the Church. They were educated and proud. What hurt was not hunger but insult. They felt that a person born across the ocean was valued more than they were, though their families had built the colony. Being treated as lesser in your own home is hard to forgive.
📚 PART 4 · ON THE FRONTIER
A smaller, cheaper defense

On the northern **frontier**, the reforms meant doing more with less. The inspection by **Rubí** in the 1760s was part of them. In 1776, the king created a new government for the northern provinces, to make defense more efficient. Texas was part of it.
🌐 FOREIGN LANGUAGE VOCABULARY
**Rubí** (roo-BEE). The Marqués de Rubí, a Spanish officer who inspected the northern frontier from 1766 to 1768.

For Texas, doing more with less meant fewer soldiers, fewer forts, and fewer priests. Officials in the 1700s wrote long reports asking how to save money. Their answer was usually to pull back and to defend only what mattered most. That made sense on a budget sheet. It also meant that the people left in the province had to protect themselves.

In 1793, the missions around San Antonio were closed as missions, and their lands were given to **settlers** and the Church. This was the end of the plan to turn mission Indians into Spanish farmers. By then, Spanish Texas was smaller and weaker than it had been in 1750. East Texas had been **abandoned**, and the **Comanche** **raided** the settlements.
🌐 FOREIGN LANGUAGE VOCABULARY
**Comanche** (kuh-MAN-chee). A people who became the strongest power on the southern plains in the 1700s.

A mission that closed did not simply vanish. The buildings stayed, and many of the people who had lived in them stayed too. Their land was divided among families, and some mission residents became part of the growing Spanish-speaking town. In this way the old mission system faded into the ordinary life of San Antonio. The old walls of the missions are still there to see.
So the reforms strengthened the empire in one way and weakened it in another. The Crown took in more money, but it lost the loyalty of many of the people it ruled. That would matter very soon.
💪 WHAT TO CARRY FORWARD

The Bourbon Reforms were an attempt to make a huge empire work like a well-run machine. They raised money, but they also pushed away the people born in the Americas, who had the most to lose. When a crisis came, those people would not be on the Crown's side.

section: What did Spain actually win when it took Mexico?
text: When **Cortés** took **Tenochtitlán**, Spain won something much bigger than one city. It took over a working system for collecting wealth from millions of people. This lesson looks at how that system worked, how the Spanish **Crown** tried to govern it, and what made it succeed in central Mexico. It also looks at a problem hidden inside its success.

section: PART 1 NOT A CITY BUT A SYSTEM
text: 📚 PART 1 · NOT A CITY BUT A SYSTEM
What Spain really captured

The **Mexica** had a system. Millions of farmers grew crops, and officials kept records of who owed what to whom. Each year, towns sent **tribute** to the capital in goods and in labor. Cortés and the Spaniards did not have to invent any of this. They took over much of the old system and put themselves at the top. In that sense, the real prize was not the city of Tenochtitlán. It was the people, and the work they already knew how to do.
🌐 FOREIGN LANGUAGE VOCABULARY
**Cortés** (kor-TEZ). Hernán Cortés, the Spanish officer who led the conquest of Mexico.
**Tenochtitlán** (teh-nohch-teet-LAHN). The capital city of the Mexica empire. Mexico City stands on the same spot today.
**Mexica** (meh-SHEE-kah). The people who ruled the empire in central Mexico. They are often called the Aztecs.

The Spaniards also ruled through Native leaders. Local leaders who agreed to cooperate often kept some of their position and collected the tribute for their new rulers. This saved Spain the trouble of governing thousands of towns directly. Over time, the capital of the Mexica became the capital of New Spain, and Mexico City grew on top of the old city.

This was a clever way to rule, and it also shows how small the Spanish group was. There were only a few thousand Spaniards in all of New Spain in the early years, set among millions of Native people. A government that small could not run everything itself. It needed local leaders who knew the people, the languages, and the land.
📚 PART 2 · THE ENCOMIENDA
Labor as a reward

To make the system work, Spain used the **grant** of Native labor (*encomienda*). The Crown gave a Spaniard the right to collect tribute and labor from a group of Native families in a certain area. That Spaniard was called an **encomendero**. In return, he promised to protect those families and to teach them the Christian faith. He did not receive the land itself. He received the right to the work.
🌐 FOREIGN LANGUAGE VOCABULARY
**encomendero** (en-koh-men-DEH-roh). A Spaniard who held an encomienda.
**grant of Native labor (*encomienda*)** (en-koh-mee-EN-dah). A Spanish system in which the Crown gave a Spaniard the right to collect tribute and labor from a group of Native families.

In practice, many holders treated the workers harshly. Workers faced long hours in the fields and mines, and diseases like **smallpox** killed huge numbers of them. The Crown worried about this, partly for moral reasons and partly because it did not want its colonists to grow too powerful. In 1512, even before the conquest of Mexico, Spain issued the Laws of **Burgos**. They set rules for how workers should be housed, fed, and taught. But the laws did not end the system. They accepted it.
🌐 FOREIGN LANGUAGE VOCABULARY
**Burgos** (BOOR-gohs). A city in Spain. The Laws of Burgos (1512) were the first set of Spanish laws about how colonists should treat Native people.

Not everyone in the Spanish world agreed with the system. A **friar** named **Las Casas**, who had once held an encomienda himself, spoke out against its cruelty. He argued before the king that Native people had rights and should be treated as free subjects. His writing was widely read, and it helped push the Crown to pass new laws.
🌐 FOREIGN LANGUAGE VOCABULARY
**Las Casas** (lahs KAH-sahs). Bartolomé de las Casas, a Spanish friar who spoke out against the mistreatment of Native people.

The debate over how to treat Native people was not a side issue. Spanish priests and officials argued about it, and the king listened. That fact surprises many students. But arguing about a rule is different from changing a system. The laws changed on paper, and the people who gained from the system pushed back hard.

In 1542, new laws tried to stop encomiendas from being passed down from father to son. Colonists protested loudly, and the Crown softened the rules. Over the next century, the encomienda faded. Other forms of forced labor took its place, but the pattern stayed the same. Spaniards ruled, and Native workers did the work.

Why did colonists fight so hard to keep the system? Because the encomienda was their pay. A soldier who had risked his life in the conquest expected a reward, and a grant of workers was the reward he wanted. Take it away, and many of them would have wondered why they had come.
📚 PART 3 · GOVERNING NEW SPAIN
A viceroy and a church

Spain was thousands of miles away, so it needed someone to speak for the king. In 1535, the Crown created the **Viceroyalty** of New Spain. A viceroy ruled it from Mexico City. The viceroy collected taxes, appointed officials, and answered to the king.

The Church was just as important. Groups of **missionaries** arrived in Mexico in the 1520s. They built churches, set up schools, and worked to teach Native people the Christian faith. Government and Church worked side by side, and both depended on a large population living in settled towns.

The system also reached north. In 1546, Spaniards found rich silver at a place called **Zacatecas**. Mines need many workers, so people and supplies moved north to the new mines. Notice the pattern. Spain moved toward people it could put to work and wealth it could carry home.
🌐 FOREIGN LANGUAGE VOCABULARY
**Zacatecas** (zah-kah-TEH-kahs). A silver-mining state in central Mexico with a strong state militia.

The Crown also wanted its share. It took one fifth of all the silver that came out of the mines. This tax was called the royal fifth. Silver mined in Mexico was shipped across the ocean to Spain, and it paid for Spain's wars and its fleets.

Think about what that means for a king. Silver from Mexico paid his soldiers and his sailors, and it let him fight wars in Europe. A place that sent silver home was worth defending and worth the cost of governing. A place that sent nothing was not. This simple idea explains many Spanish choices, including the ones about Texas.

section: PART 4 A PROBLEM HIDDEN IN THE SUCCESS
text: 📚 PART 4 · A PROBLEM HIDDEN IN THE SUCCESS

section: What if there is no system to take over?
text: What if there is no system to take over?

section: What if there is no system to take over?
text: The Spanish model needed three things: a large settled population, a tribute system to take over, and wealth worth collecting. Central Mexico had all three. But what would happen if Spain reached a place that had none of them?

section: What if there is no system to take over?
text: The pattern is easy to state. Spain went where there were many people, a tribute system, and wealth. It did not go where those things were missing. That is why central Mexico filled with towns and churches, while other parts of the **empire** stayed almost empty for a very long time.

section: What if there is no system to take over?
text: In 1519, the same year Cortés landed in Mexico, a Spanish sailor named **Piñeda** sailed along the Gulf of Mexico coast and drew the first known map of it. His map included the coast of what is now Texas. He found no great cities and no farmers paying tribute. There was nothing for an encomendero to collect and no ruler to replace.

section: What if there is no system to take over?
text: 🌐 FOREIGN LANGUAGE VOCABULARY

section: What if there is no system to take over?
text: **Piñeda** (peen-YEH-dah). Alonso Álvarez de Piñeda, a Spanish sailor who mapped the Gulf of Mexico coast in 1519.

section: What if there is no system to take over?
text: The same problem shows up at other far edges of the Spanish empire, such as the dry lands of northern Mexico. A model built to take over an existing system struggles where no such system exists. Keep that question in mind as the story moves toward Texas.
💪 WHAT TO CARRY FORWARD

Spain's success in Mexico was real, and it came from a particular combination of people, tribute, and wealth. That success made the model look strong. But a model is only as strong as the place it fits. The next question is what happens when Spaniards arrive on a coast where that combination is missing.

💡 GLOSSARY OF SUBJECT VOCABULARY
A few words in this lesson are worth a look before you read. They show up in bold, and you can hover over any of them for a reminder.
**code** (kohd). A written set of rules or laws.
**colony** (KAH-luh-nee). A place settled and controlled by people from a faraway country.
**cover** (KUV-er). A place where a soldier can hide from enemy fire, such as a wall, a ditch, or a river bank.
**declaration** (dek-luh-RAY-shun). A formal public statement.
**grievance** (GREE-vens). A complaint about being treated unfairly.
**independence** (in-dih-PEN-dens). Freedom from the control of another country.
**jury** (JOOR-ee). A group of citizens who listen to a court case and decide who is right.
**militia** (muh-LISH-uh). A group of ordinary citizens who train to fight when their community needs them.
**petition** (peh-TISH-un). A formal request, often made to a government.
**raid** (rayd). A sudden attack made to take goods, animals, or captives.
**settler** (SET-ler). A person who moves to a new place to live there for good.
**verdict** (VUR-dikt). The decision of a jury or judge at the end of a trial.
📖 TODAY'S FOCUS
How do you govern a colony when the law that applies to you does not fit your way of life?

Austin's **colony** was part of Mexico, but nobody in the colony had grown up under Mexican law. Austin had to keep order, settle quarrels, and protect the **settlers** with very little help from the government far away. This lesson follows how he did it, and how a Mexican court system ended up with American habits inside it.

📚 PART 1 · ONE MAN, MANY JOBS

section: Power in one pair of hands
text: Power in one pair of hands

section: Power in one pair of hands
text: In the early years, Austin held more power than any single official would hold today. He was the empresario who brought in the families. He was the judge who settled disputes. He was also the commander of the colony's militia, a force of ordinary settlers who trained to defend their homes.

section: Power in one pair of hands
text: 🌐 FOREIGN LANGUAGE VOCABULARY

section: Power in one pair of hands
text: **colony agent (*empresario*)** (em-preh-SAH-ree-oh). A person who got a contract from the government to bring settlers to Texas.

section: Power in one pair of hands
text: That much power in one man would worry anyone. But it fit the circumstances. The colony was far from the state capital, and the Mexican government had few officials in Texas. Someone had to settle quarrels over land and cattle, catch thieves, and deal with **raids**. Austin was there, and he had the trust of both the settlers and the government.

section: Power in one pair of hands
text: Austin used the power with care. He wrote letters explaining his decisions. He listened to people who disagreed with him, and he tried to keep the settlers' goodwill. He knew that a colony run by force would not last, and he knew that the government in Mexico could take away his contract if he caused a scandal.

section: Power in one pair of hands
text: Austin also had to think about money. The colony had no regular taxes in its first years, and he often paid expenses out of his own pocket. Roads, courts, and a militia that was ready to march all cost something. Settlers gave labor and small fees. It was a thin and frugal government, but it kept order.
The code of 1824

In 1824, Austin wrote a set of rules for the colony. Today we call them his civil and criminal **code**. They **covered** crimes such as theft and murder, and they explained how courts should work, how land should be recorded, and what punishments should follow. The rules drew on Spanish law, on the laws of the United States, and on common sense.

A written code did several things. It told settlers what to expect. It reminded everyone that the colony was ruled by law and not just by Austin's wishes. And it showed Mexican officials that the colony was well run. When the officials accepted the code, it gave the colony a standing under Mexican law.
📚 PART 2 · MEXICAN FORMS, AMERICAN HABITS
Alcaldes and councils

Mexican law gave towns two main kinds of leaders. A mayor and judge (**alcalde**) heard cases and kept order. A town council (**ayuntamiento**) ran local business. Austin's colony set up alcaldes in each district. The settlers accepted this system, because it gave local people real authority over their own affairs.
🌐 FOREIGN LANGUAGE VOCABULARY
**town council (*ayuntamiento*)** (ah-yoon-tah-mee-EN-toh). The governing council of a Spanish or Mexican town.
**mayor and judge (*alcalde*)** (ahl-KAHL-day). A local official in Spanish and Mexican towns who acted as both mayor and judge.

**San Felipe** de Austin, on the **Brazos** River, became the center of the colony. It had stores, an inn, and a printing press where a newspaper was published. Settlers came here to record their land, to attend court, and to hear the news. It was the first real town of the American colony.
🌐 FOREIGN LANGUAGE VOCABULARY
**San Felipe** (sahn feh-LEE-peh). San Felipe de Austin, the main town of Austin's colony, on the Brazos River.
**Brazos** (BRAH-zus). A major river in Texas that flows to the Gulf of Mexico.
The problem of the jury

Here Mexican law and American habit did not fit. Americans expected a jury of ordinary citizens to decide guilt in a trial. Mexican law of the time did not provide for juries. A judge decided the case alone. To settlers from the United States, this felt like the loss of a basic right.

The settlers found a workaround. The alcaldes would call together a group of local men to hear the evidence and give their opinion. The group acted like a jury, although the law did not call it one. Then the official court, which was the body that made the legal decision, accepted the group's **verdict** and made it official.

Think about what a jury meant to these settlers. In the United States, jury trial was a protection honored for generations. A farmer who might be accused of a crime or sued over his land wanted his neighbors to decide, not one official. The jury was less a rule than a feeling of safety.

This solution kept both sides content for a time. The colony could say that its courts followed Mexican law. The settlers could say that they had their juries. It worked because Austin and the local officials cooperated and did not push the law to its limits. But it depended on goodwill, and goodwill could change.

section: A complaint that would not go away
text: A complaint that would not go away

section: A complaint that would not go away
text: When Mexico's government grew stricter, juries became a problem. The informal system had no firm place in the law. If an official chose to enforce the rules as they were written, trials by jury could stop. Settlers began to see this as a threat to their rights.

section: A complaint that would not go away
text: The complaint grew louder over time. Settlers listed trial by jury in their **petitions** to the government in 1832 and 1833. In 1836, when Texans wrote their **Declaration** of **Independence**, they listed the lack of jury trials among their **grievances** against Mexico. A small fix in a courtroom in the 1820s became a major cause in the 1830s.

section: A complaint that would not go away
text: Notice how long the complaint lived. A habit that started in 1824 was still on the list in 1836. The settlers did not forget what they had been used to, and they remembered when it was taken away. The small rights that people use every day are often the ones they defend most fiercely.

section: PART 3 A PATTERN FOR THE YEARS AHEAD
text: 📚 PART 3 · A PATTERN FOR THE YEARS AHEAD

section: Keep the form, change the practice
text: Keep the form, change the practice

section: Keep the form, change the practice
text: The colony's courts show a pattern that appears again and again. The settlers did not rebel against Mexican law. They kept its names and forms. Inside those forms, they placed American habits. They used Mexican words, Mexican offices, and Mexican procedures, and they filled them with the practices that they knew.

section: Keep the form, change the practice
text: This approach was clever, and it carried a risk. As long as the Mexican government left the colony alone, it could work smoothly. But sooner or later the government would look closely at what was actually happening. When it did, the gap between the form and the practice could look like disobedience.

section: Keep the form, change the practice
text: Think about how each side saw the same courtroom. A settler saw a fair trial with a jury. A Mexican official might see a law bent out of shape. Both could be sincere. The disagreement was about what the law meant, and that kind of disagreement is hard to settle without trust.

section: Keep the form, change the practice
text: Austin understood this. He worked to keep communication open and to show that the colony respected Mexican authority. Yet even the most careful leader cannot stop a government from changing, or a colony from drifting apart from the government that rules it.
💪 REMEMBER THIS QUESTION
Keep one question in mind: what happens when two peoples use the same words for different things? In San Felipe, a court was a court, but a jury meant something very different to each side.

A few words in this lesson are worth a look before you read. They show up in bold, and you can hover over any of them for a reminder.
**boundary** (BOWN-duh-ree). A line that separates one country, state, or territory from another.
**colony** (KAH-luh-nee). A place settled and controlled by people from a faraway country.
**debt** (det). Money that is owed to someone else.

Who were the people who built Austin's colony, and where did they come from?

Austin's first **settlers** did not come from Mexico or from Spain. They came from the American South, and they brought their farms, their tools, and their habits with them. This lesson looks at who they were, what Mexico asked of them, and how the shape of the land decided where they settled.

📚 PART 1 · WHO CAME, AND WHY
The Old Three Hundred

Austin's first colony was meant for three hundred families. The settlers who signed up early became known as the Old Three Hundred. Most of them received the papers for their land in 1824. They did not all arrive at once. Families came by boat along the coast and by wagon from Louisiana, and they built their first homes in the winter of 1821 and 1822.

Nearly all of them came from the American South. They were from Tennessee, Alabama, Mississippi, and Louisiana, a **region** that people at the time called the Old Southwest. These were farm families who knew how to clear land, plant cotton and corn, and live on a **frontier**. To them, Texas looked like more of the same land, only cheaper.

Think about how big a step this was. These families left friends, churches, and family graves in the United States. They crossed a border into a country with a different language and a different government. They did so because they believed the gain was worth the risk, and that belief was strong enough to carry them through hard years.

Money was a main reason. After the panic of 1819, many families in the United States were in **debt** and had little hope of buying good land. In Texas, they could receive a large tract for a small fee. A farmer could dream of owning more land than his father ever had.

Some settlers brought **enslaved** people with them. By the middle of the 1820s, roughly one in four people in the colony was enslaved. Slavery was part of the world these settlers came from, and cotton farming made it more valuable. Mexican law was uneasy about slavery, but the colony kept it in place, and that choice would cause trouble later.
What Mexico asked

Mexico set clear terms. A family that farmed could receive about 177 acres. A family that wanted to raise cattle could receive a **league** of land, which is about 4,428 acres. A family that did both could receive both tracts. The land cost almost nothing. A small fee paid for the surveying and the paperwork.

In return, settlers had to promise to obey Mexican law. Each settler took an **oath** of loyalty to Mexico, and the law said that settlers had to be Catholic. In practice, there were almost no priests in the colony, and few settlers were asked to prove much about their faith. The requirement was more a matter of form than of daily life.

Mexico did not pay Austin a salary for his work as **empresario**. His reward came from land and from fees paid by the settlers. This gave him a strong reason to keep the colony growing. It also gave the settlers a reason to watch how he used his power.
🌐 FOREIGN LANGUAGE VOCABULARY
**colony agent (*empresario*)** (em-preh-SAH-ree-oh). A person who got a contract from the government to bring settlers to Texas.

Notice the pattern in these terms. Mexico was not asking settlers to become Mexican in daily life. It asked them to follow a few rules and to keep the peace. The government wanted a barrier on the frontier more than it wanted neighbors who thought just like it did.

section: PART 2 THE SHAPE OF THE LAND
text: 📚 PART 2 · THE SHAPE OF THE LAND
Between the rivers

Look at where the colony sat. It stretched between the **Brazos** and the **Colorado**, from the Gulf coast northwest into the rolling prairie. Rivers were the highways of the time. Boats could carry cotton to the coast, and settlers could build farms along the banks where the soil was rich. Austin's capital, **San Felipe**, sat on the Brazos.
🌐 FOREIGN LANGUAGE VOCABULARY
**San Felipe** (sahn feh-LEE-peh). San Felipe de Austin, the main town of Austin's colony, on the Brazos River.
**Colorado** (kol-uh-RAD-oh). A river in Texas that flows to the Gulf of Mexico. It is not the Colorado River of the western mountains.
**Brazos** (BRAH-zus). A major river in Texas that flows to the Gulf of Mexico.

The northern edge of the colony followed an old Spanish road, the King's Highway. This was not an accident. The road crossed the rivers at the places where they could be **forded**, which means that they were shallow enough for wagons to cross. A **boundary** that lay where people already traveled was easy to find and easy to defend.

Rainfall mattered even more than the rivers. Near the town of Bryan, at the northern edge of the colony, about 41 inches of rain fall in a year. That is enough for cotton and corn without special help. The coast gets even more. Settlers who stayed between the rivers found the weather and the soil that they knew from home.
West of the Colorado

Go west of the Colorado, and the country changes quickly. Each mile brings less rain. The grass grows shorter, trees become scarce, and farming without extra water gets harder. By the time a traveler reaches the center of the state, the land is better for cattle and sheep than for cotton.

Ranching country is a different world. Cattle need open grass and water more than they need rain at planting time. Spanish ranchers had worked this country for a century. Later settlers would learn from them, and a new kind of Texas would grow up west of the cotton farms.

That is why Austin's colony took the shape it did. It sat where the rain and the rivers favored the kind of farming the settlers already knew. Farther west, they would have had to learn a different way of life. Settlers tend to stop where the land looks familiar, and the first colony stopped where it felt like home.
Hard work, slow growth

Settling was hard. The first families faced hunger, mosquitoes, floods, and sickness. Some left. Those who stayed cleared land with axes and oxen, planted corn first so that they would have food, and waited for the cotton to come in. A colony of cabins and cornfields takes years to turn into a community.

Austin kept a close eye on every family. He wrote to settlers, advised them where to build, and settled quarrels over land. He wanted a colony that would last, and he knew that a few unhappy families could damage its name in the capital. His careful work is part of why the colony grew steadily while other schemes failed.

In its crops, its labor, and its customs, the colony was the western edge of the American South, set down inside Mexico. The Mexican government had hoped for loyal farmers who would hold a dangerous frontier. It had received a piece of the Old Southwest instead.
💪 REMEMBER THIS QUESTION
Keep one question in mind: when a government invites strangers to settle, what does it really get? Mexico expected farmers. It got a whole way of life.

section: What happens to a patient peacemaker who loses his patience once?
text: In 1833, Stephen F. Austin carried the colonists' **petitions** to Mexico City. He got part of what he asked for. Then he wrote one hasty letter, and it cost him more than a year of his life. This lesson follows Austin's second trip to the capital and what it did to the most patient man in Texas.

📚 PART 1 · THE SECOND TRIP SOUTH
Carrying the petition

Austin left Texas in the spring of 1833 with the petitions from the convention in his bags. He was the right man for the job. He spoke Spanish well, he knew the officials, and he had spent ten years proving that the colonists could be trusted. When he reached Mexico City in July, he began the same patient work that had succeeded before.

He lived modestly in the city and tried to meet as many officials as he could. He also wrote letters home to keep the colonists informed. Many **settlers** did not understand how slowly the Mexican government worked. Austin's letters tried to explain that patience was the price of success.

Mexico was in a stormy mood. General **Santa Anna** had been elected president, but he did not like the daily business of governing. He often went home to his estate and left the work to the vice president, **Gómez Farías**, who was busy with **reforms**. Austin had to chase the man in power through a government that kept changing hands.
🌐 FOREIGN LANGUAGE VOCABULARY
**Gómez Farías** (GOH-mes fah-REE-ahs). Valentín Gómez Farías, the Mexican vice president who led a program of reforms in 1833.
**Santa Anna** (SAN-tah AH-nah). Antonio López de Santa Anna, a Mexican army officer who became one of the most powerful men in Mexico.

Austin presented the colonists' requests one by one. He asked for the **repeal** of the Law of April 6, 1830. He asked for relief from the **tariffs**. And he asked that Texas be made a state of its own, apart from **Coahuila**. Santa Anna listened, and Austin left some meetings feeling hopeful.
🌐 FOREIGN LANGUAGE VOCABULARY
**Coahuila** (koh-ah-WEE-lah). A state in northern Mexico that was joined to Texas in 1824.
A partial win

Part of the effort worked. The government agreed to repeal the part of the Law of April 6 that had shut the door to settlers from the United States. Families could once again come to Texas. For the colonists, this was a real victory, and it showed that Austin's patience could still move Mexican officials.

But the main request failed. Mexico City would not **grant** separate **statehood**. Santa Anna and his advisers said that Texas was still too young and too thinly settled. They urged Austin to wait. They also hinted that things might change once the country grew calmer.

Think about Austin's position. He had been in the capital for months, and his **colony** was waiting for news. He had won one important point and lost the biggest one. Many people would have come home, reported on what had been won, and tried again later. Austin was tired, worried, and far from home. He decided to push once more.

section: PART 2 A LETTER SENT TOO SOON
text: 📚 PART 2 · A LETTER SENT TOO SOON
The letter of October 2

On October 2, 1833, Austin wrote a letter to the town council of San Antonio. He told them that Texas had waited long enough. He urged the council to organize a state government on its own, without waiting for permission from Mexico City. He wrote in anger and in haste, worried that more delay would leave Texas with no protection at all.

It was a very different letter from the careful papers that Austin usually wrote. For ten years he had warned his neighbors against rash steps. Now, in one evening, he had suggested one himself. Austin later called the letter a mistake, and historians have called it his most unwise act.

The letter did not stay private. The San Antonio council sent it on to the state government, and from there it reached Mexico City. To Mexican officials, a request to organize a state government without permission looked like a plan to break the law. The one man they thought they could trust had put his name to something that frightened them.
Arrest and prison

Austin started for home in December, thinking that his work was done. In January 1834, at **Saltillo**, he was arrested. The soldiers sent him back to Mexico City under guard. He had not been charged with anything yet, but his freedom was gone.
🌐 FOREIGN LANGUAGE VOCABULARY
**Saltillo** (sahl-TEE-yoh). A city in Coahuila that served as the capital of the state of Coahuila y Tejas.

In the capital, Austin was held in a cold stone cell in an old prison. For a time, he was not allowed to write to anyone, and he did not know how long he would be kept. He had gone to Mexico City to carry a request for his neighbors. Now he was a prisoner of the government he had served for a decade.

Slowly, conditions improved. He was moved to better rooms, and he was allowed books and visitors. By December 1834, he was released on **bond**. A bond is a promise, backed by money, that a person will return for his trial. But he could not leave the city, because the government had not yet decided what to do with him.
📚 PART 3 · THE PEACEMAKER COMES HOME
Waiting for amnesty

For months more, Austin waited in Mexico City for the government to settle his case. In July 1835, a general pardon, called an amnesty, was announced, and he was free to go. He sailed home by way of New Orleans and reached Texas in September 1835. He had been away for more than two years.

The long wait took its toll. Austin was in poor health after the cold prison and the years of strain. He was also worried about his colony. The settlers who had once looked to him for every decision had been forced to make decisions alone. He was eager to see how much of his work had survived.

The Texas he found was not the one he had left. Soldiers had been sent to the coast. Neighbors were arguing about whether to submit or to resist. The old friends who had trusted him to bring back peace now wanted to know what he had learned. His answer would shape what Texas did next.
A changed man

Austin had gone south as a loyal Mexican citizen. He came home convinced that the government in Mexico City could not be trusted to keep its word. He had been jailed without trial for acts that, in his own mind, were attempts to help. He believed that the time for patient requests was over.

This was a huge change. Austin had spent ten years defending Mexico and urging calm. Now he told his neighbors that Texas must prepare to defend itself. When a man who has always chosen peace says that it is time to act, many listeners pay attention.

Look at what Austin's story shows. A conciliator is a person who works to bring people together and avoid a fight. Austin was the best conciliator Texas ever had. When even he decided that conciliation had failed, there was little hope left that the quarrel could be settled by talk.

His change did not make war certain. Choices still had to be made, by many people on both sides. But after September 1835, the colonists no longer had a leader whose main aim was to avoid a fight. The country was moving toward a crisis, and its calmest voice had gone quiet.
💪 REMEMBER THIS QUESTION
Keep one question in mind: what does it mean when the most patient person in a community decides that patience has run out?

📖 TODAY'S FOCUS
Why did the same kind of soldiers win one battle and lose the next?

In October 1835, a small group of **Texians** won a fight at **Concepción** by shooting from a riverbank. In March 1836, a much larger group of Texians, including some of the same men, was destroyed on an open prairie near **Goliad**. This lesson compares the two fights and shows how the ground, the weapons, and one hard decision made the difference.
