📚 PART 1 · A COMMANDER WHO WAITED
Fannin at Goliad

After the fall of the **Alamo**, about four hundred Texians sat in the old fort at **La Bahía**, near Goliad. Their commander was Colonel James Fannin. He was brave and well educated, and he had fought at Concepción. But he was uncertain about what to do next, and that uncertainty would cost him dearly.
🌐 FOREIGN LANGUAGE VOCABULARY
**Concepción** (kon-sep-see-OHN). A Spanish mission on the San Antonio River, south of the town of San Antonio.
**Goliad** (GOH-lee-ad). A town on the San Antonio River with a Spanish fort and mission.
**Coleto** (koh-LEH-toh). A creek near Goliad where Fannin and his men were caught in open country.
**La Bahía** (lah bah-EE-ah). A Spanish fort and mission in South Texas. Today it is in the town of Goliad.
**Alamo** (AL-uh-moh). A former mission in San Antonio that was used as a fort in 1835 and 1836.

On March 11, Sam Houston ordered Fannin to leave Goliad and fall back to Victoria. The Mexican army was close, and Houston wanted to gather every soldier he had. Fannin agreed, but he did not go. He waited for **scouts**, for wagons, and for another detachment. Each day made the **retreat** more dangerous.

Fannin had reasons to hesitate. Goliad had a strong fort with thick walls, and a commander who leaves a strong place for open country takes a risk. He also had sick soldiers, heavy wagons, and supplies to protect. A leader who is asked to give up a strong position needs great confidence, and Fannin had doubts about Houston's orders.

Think about the problem of a commander who cannot decide. Fannin did not ignore Houston's order. He doubted it, he delayed it, and he looked for reasons to wait. By the time he finally left on March 19, the Mexican general **Urrea** had moved fast and was only a few miles away.
🌐 FOREIGN LANGUAGE VOCABULARY
**Urrea** (oo-RAY-ah). José de Urrea, the Mexican general who defeated the Texian forces in southern Texas in 1836.

The retreat began badly. The Texians took along **cannon** and heavy wagons. A cart broke, and the oxen pulling it gave out. They had marched only a few miles before they stopped to rest in open prairie, near a creek called Coleto. They had no cover, and they had little water.
Surrounded on the prairie

Urrea's **cavalry** appeared on the horizon before the Texians could resume their march. Mounted soldiers with **lances** rode in a ring around the column. Mexican infantry followed behind. Fannin formed his men into a hollow square, with cannon at the corners and riflemen facing outward on every side.

The Texians fought well. They drove back several attacks, and their **rifles** killed many Mexican soldiers. But they had nowhere to go. Fannin was wounded. The men could see that the army around them was growing as reinforcements arrived. By night, the Texians had lost nine men and had dozens of wounded.

Think about the night that followed. The wounded cried out for water. The Texians piled up what they could, including carts and dead horses, to make a rough barrier. They hoped to hold out until help arrived. But nobody was coming, and every man in the square knew it by the time the sun rose.

The next morning, March 20, Urrea brought up cannon. The Texians were out of water, and their wounded were suffering. Fannin decided to **surrender**. He believed that his men would be treated as prisoners of war. They were marched back to the fort at Goliad and locked inside.

A week later, on March 27, a Palm Sunday, the prisoners were marched out of the fort in small groups and shot. **Santa Anna** had ordered the execution. More than three hundred men died. A few escaped, and a few were spared. The news spread across Texas, and "Remember Goliad" joined "Remember the Alamo" as a battle cry.
🌐 FOREIGN LANGUAGE VOCABULARY
**Santa Anna** (SAN-tah AH-nah). Antonio López de Santa Anna, a Mexican army officer who became one of the most powerful men in Mexico.

section: PART 2 THE SAME SOLDIERS, DIFFERENT GROUND
text: 📚 PART 2 · THE SAME SOLDIERS, DIFFERENT GROUND

section: Concepción and Coleto side by side
text: Concepción and Coleto side by side

section: Concepción and Coleto side by side
text: Look at the two fights side by side. At Concepción, ninety Texians won against a much larger force. At Coleto Creek, about three hundred Texians lost to an army of similar skill. Fannin himself had been at both. The soldiers were much the same. The difference was the ground.

section: Concepción and Coleto side by side
text: At Concepción, the Texians fought from a deep riverbank. They could load their rifles in safety and fire at soldiers crossing open ground. At Coleto, the Texians stood on a flat prairie with no ditch and no trees. Mexican cavalry could circle them, and Mexican cannon could bombard them without any shelter in return.

section: Concepción and Coleto side by side
text: That is the lesson of these two fights. Soldiers who fight from cover have a great advantage. Soldiers who fight in the open lose it. It is not enough for an army to be brave. It must also choose its ground, and Fannin's army had let the ground choose for it.
Rifle, musket, and lance

The weapons help explain why. The Texian soldiers carried a long rifle, sometimes called a Kentucky rifle. A skilled shooter could hit a target past two hundred yards. But the rifle took a long time to load, about a minute for each shot, and it had no blade on the end for close fighting.

The Mexican infantry carried a **musket**. It was less accurate and could not shoot as far, but it could be loaded much faster. It also carried a **bayonet**, which made the soldier dangerous in close combat. A line of Mexican infantry that reached the Texians could do terrible harm.

Mexican cavalry carried a lance, and its riders were famous for skill on horseback. A man on a horse with a long spear could ride down a soldier who was stopping to reload. In open country, the combination of cavalry and infantry was hard to beat.

Put these facts together. A rifleman behind a wall or a riverbank could shoot many times from a safe place and drive off an enemy. A rifleman in the open was slow, easy to surround, and easy to reach with a lance or bayonet. The weapon was only as good as the place where it was used.
A rule to remember

The Texians won when they fought from cover, and they lost when they did not. That rule held at Concepción, at San Antonio, and at Coleto Creek. It was not a law of nature. But it was close to one, and the smartest Texian leaders understood it.

This rule also helps explain the Alamo. The walls of the old **mission** kept a far larger army at bay for almost two weeks. Fighting from cover was not a guarantee of victory, but it gave a small band of men a real chance. Fighting in the open gave them almost none.

Notice that this rule is about choices. Fannin chose to stay too long, and he chose to rest on open ground. Each of those choices made his army easier to defeat. A different decision on March 11 might have brought his four hundred men safely to Houston's army, and the story of the war could have gone differently.
💪 REMEMBER THIS QUESTION
Keep one question in mind: what does it cost a commander to wait? At Goliad, the answer was measured in lives.

section: PART 1 A MISSION FOR THE APACHE
text: 📚 PART 1 · A MISSION FOR THE APACHE
San Sabá, 1757

The **Lipan** Apache were under pressure from the Comanche, and some of them asked Spain for a mission. Spanish officials liked the idea. A mission would help keep the Lipan as **allies**. There were also **rumors** of silver in the hills nearby, and Spain hoped to find mines there.
🌐 FOREIGN LANGUAGE VOCABULARY
**Lipan** (LIP-un). A group of Apache who moved south into Texas.
**Comanche** (kuh-MAN-chee). A people who became the strongest power on the southern plains in the 1700s.
**Apache** (uh-PATCH-ee). A group of related peoples who lived on the plains and in the Southwest.

The idea looked good from Mexico City. A mission would make the Lipan into Spanish subjects, farmers, and allies. It would also put a Spanish presence on the edge of the plains, where the Comanche ruled. Officials hoped it would open the way to more missions and, perhaps, to mines. They spent a great deal of money on the plan. They had not asked what the Comanche would think.

In 1757, Spain built a mission on the **San Sabá** River, and a fort a few miles away. Colonel **Ortiz Parrilla** commanded the soldiers. But the plan had a flaw. The Lipan came and went, and almost none of them settled at the mission. They wanted protection from the Comanche, not a new way of life. And their enemies were watching.
🌐 FOREIGN LANGUAGE VOCABULARY
**Ortiz Parrilla** (or-TEEZ pah-REE-yah). Diego Ortiz Parrilla, the Spanish colonel who commanded the fort at San Sabá.
**San Sabá** (sahn sah-BAH). A river in Central Texas. Spain built a mission and fort there in 1757.

Think about what the soldiers and priests saw in the first months. Few Lipan came, and those who did came and went. The priests had few people to teach, and the soldiers had a fort to guard and no clear enemy in sight. Everyone knew the Comanche were somewhere to the north. Nobody knew when they would come.
📚 PART 2 · THE ATTACK, 1758
A force of two thousand

In March 1758, a large force gathered around the mission. It was led by the Comanche and included allies from several other peoples, among them the **Taovayas**. The Spaniards counted about two thousand warriors. Many carried guns, and some of the guns were French.

The attackers burned the mission and killed eight people, including two priests. The survivors ran to the fort and held out inside. The mission was never rebuilt. It was the only Spanish mission in Texas destroyed in this way.

A priest named **Molina** survived the attack and wrote an account of it. Because of him, we know what the attackers looked like and what they did. His account is one of the main sources for this story. Like any witness, he wrote from his own view, and he had good reason to fear the people who attacked him.
🌐 FOREIGN LANGUAGE VOCABULARY
**Molina** (moh-LEE-nah). Fray Miguel de Molina, a Spanish priest who survived the attack on the San Sabá mission and wrote an account of it.

Why did they strike? The Lipan were their enemies, and Spain had just built a mission for them. To the Comanche and their allies, the mission was a base for their enemies and a threat. They did not need to fight Spain in general. They could remove a small outpost of it.
🌐 FOREIGN LANGUAGE VOCABULARY
**Taovayas** (tah-oh-VAH-yahs). A Wichita people who lived in fortified villages on the Red River and fought with the Comanche.
📚 PART 3 · THE FAILED PUNISHMENT, 1759

section: A Spanish army on the Red River
text: A Spanish army on the Red River

section: A Spanish army on the Red River
text: Spain wanted to punish the attackers. In 1759, Colonel Ortiz Parrilla led about five hundred men north to the Red River, including soldiers, Apache allies, and others. They found a Taovayas village protected by a log wall and a ditch. A flag flew over it that Spaniards believed was French.

section: A Spanish army on the Red River
text: The battle lasted about four hours. The defenders were well armed and well placed, and the Spaniards could not break through. Spanish soldiers began to panic. They chose to **retreat**, and they left their **cannons** behind. It was one of the worst defeats Spain ever suffered on the Texas **frontier**.

section: A Spanish army on the Red River
text: The result shocked Spain. A Spanish army had been beaten by Native peoples defending a village with a wall, a ditch, and good weapons. News of the defeat spread, and other peoples on the frontier took note. Spain's power on the plains had always depended on a belief that its soldiers could not be beaten. That belief was broken.

section: A Spanish army on the Red River
text: The lesson was clear. Spanish soldiers had no good way to catch mounted warriors on open ground. And Spain could not afford to try again.

section: A Spanish army on the Red River
text: Part of the problem was the size of Texas. A Spanish army could march a few hundred miles into the plains, but it could not keep marching. Horses tired, food ran low, and the long road home was open to attack. The Comanche, who lived on the plains, had no such problem. They could retreat, circle back, and strike again, on their own ground and on their own terms.
📚 PART 4 · SPAIN DRAWS A LINE
Rubí's report

Spain sent an officer named **Rubí** to inspect the whole northern frontier. From 1766 to 1768, he traveled to every fort. He found them poorly placed, poorly supplied, and spread too thin. His report recommended that Spain pull back. It should hold a shorter line of strong forts, and it should give up places it could not defend.
🌐 FOREIGN LANGUAGE VOCABULARY
**Rubí** (roo-BEE). The Marqués de Rubí, a Spanish officer who inspected the northern frontier from 1766 to 1768.

The inspector was not looking for a fight. He was looking for facts. He measured distances, counted soldiers, and asked what each fort was really worth. Many of the forts he saw protected little and cost a lot. His job was to give the king a clear picture, even if the picture was not pleasing.

In 1772, the **Crown** issued new **regulations** that put much of his plan into effect. A year later, Spain ordered East Texas **abandoned**. **Settlers** in the East Texas missions and towns were told to leave and move to San Antonio. The Crown gave up a part of Texas that it had first claimed to protect from the French.

This was a hard choice for Spain. East Texas had been claimed first, and the missions there were older than San Antonio. Families who had lived there for decades were told to pack up and go. Many did not want to leave. Some later returned, and their return led to the founding of the town of **Nacogdoches**. Even so, the order showed that Spain was now thinking about what it could keep, not what it could claim.
🌐 FOREIGN LANGUAGE VOCABULARY
**Nacogdoches** (nak-uh-DOH-chiz). A town in East Texas, named for a Native people who lived nearby.

Geography helps explain the decision. West and north of San Antonio, the land rises and the rainfall drops. Open, drier country lies beyond. Missions that depended on farms and ditches could not live there, and neither could Spanish settlers. The edge of Spanish power roughly followed the edge of the country where farming was possible.

Look at a rainfall map next to a map of Spanish Texas. The settlements, missions, and forts follow the wetter lands of the south and east. They stop where the rain stops. Spain did not draw this line on purpose. It was a line that the climate, the Comanche, and Spain's own limits drew together. Spain could cross the line with an army, but it could not stay.
💪 WHAT TO CARRY FORWARD

San Sabá was a mission built for one people and destroyed by another. The attack and the failed punishment showed Spain that it could not rule the plains by force. So the Crown drew a line and stayed behind it. The line was not drawn on a map by chance. It followed the land.

📚 PART 1 · A CANNON AT GONZALES
Come and take it

In 1831, the Mexican government had given the town of Gonzales a small cannon to defend itself against **raids**. Four years later, relations with Mexico were tense. The commander of the soldiers in Texas wanted the cannon back. He feared that the colonists might use it against Mexican troops, and he sent a lieutenant named **Castañeda** with about a hundred soldiers to collect it.
🌐 FOREIGN LANGUAGE VOCABULARY
**Gonzales** (gon-ZAL-es). A town in Texas where the first shots of the Texas Revolution were fired.
**Concepción** (kon-sep-see-OHN). A Spanish mission on the San Antonio River, south of the town of San Antonio.
**Castañeda** (kahs-tah-NYAY-dah). Francisco de Castañeda, the Mexican officer sent to take back the cannon at Gonzales.

The people of Gonzales said no. They buried the cannon in a field, then dug it up and mounted it on wheels. They painted a white banner with a picture of the cannon and four words, "Come and Take It." When the Mexican soldiers arrived at the river, the Texians were waiting on the far bank.

Volunteers from nearby towns hurried to join them. By October 2, about 150 Texians were gathered. At dawn, they fired the cannon and charged. There was a short **skirmish**. A single Mexican soldier was killed, and the Mexican troops pulled back. Very few shots were fired, but the shooting had started.

Think about how small the spark was. Nobody in Gonzales wanted a war over a cannon. But the cannon had become a symbol. To the colonists, giving it up meant giving up the right to defend themselves. To the Mexican officer, letting them keep it meant letting a **colony** set the rules. Neither side could easily back down.
An army of the people

News of Gonzales spread quickly. Volunteers streamed to the town, and they chose Stephen F. Austin to lead them. Austin had just returned from prison in Mexico City, and he did not want war. But he accepted the job, because he believed that his neighbors needed a leader they trusted.

The Texians marched on the Mexican **garrison** at **Goliad** and took the fort at **La Bahía** without much fight. Then they turned toward San Antonio, where General **Cos** had gathered Mexican troops. The Texian army was an odd force. It had farmers, merchants, lawyers, and boys, and its supplies were poor. But the men knew how to shoot.
🌐 FOREIGN LANGUAGE VOCABULARY
**La Bahía** (lah bah-EE-ah). A Spanish fort and mission in South Texas. Today it is in the town of Goliad.
**Goliad** (GOH-lee-ad). A town on the San Antonio River with a Spanish fort and mission.
**Cos** (KOHS). Martín Perfecto de Cos, the Mexican general who commanded the troops in San Antonio.
📚 PART 2 · THE FIGHT AT CONCEPCIÓN
A fight from the riverbank

On the night of October 27, about ninety Texians under Jim Bowie and James Fannin camped near the old Concepción **mission**, south of San Antonio. They chose a spot beside the river, where a deep, steep cutbank gave them cover. Soldiers behind a cutbank could load and fire without being easy targets.

At dawn on October 28, General Cos sent hundreds of soldiers against them, with a cannon. Fog covered the field at first. When it lifted, the Mexican soldiers advanced across open ground in plain view. The Texians fired from behind the riverbank, one careful shot after another. They drove back charge after charge.

By the end of the fight, the Mexican army had lost dozens of men, and the Texians had lost one. The result astonished everyone. Ninety men with **rifles** had beaten a force many times larger. Word of the victory raised the hopes of Texians across the colonies.

Notice why the Texians won. The Mexican army was brave and well trained, but it fought in the open. The Texians had good rifles and good cover. A soldier behind cover can aim carefully, and a soldier in the open must keep moving and cannot fire back easily. This idea about cover will matter again in later battles.
📚 PART 3 · CAPTURING SAN ANTONIO
Ben Milam leads the way

The Texian army settled outside San Antonio for a **siege** through November. The weather turned cold, supplies ran low, and many volunteers went home. Austin left to serve as a representative to the United States, and Edward Burleson took command. In early December, the officers voted to give up and **retreat**.

Then Ben Milam stepped forward. He was an old frontiersman and a veteran of earlier fights in Mexico. On the morning of December 5, he called for volunteers to follow him into the town. About three hundred men agreed. They attacked before dawn and began to fight house by house through the streets.

For four days, the Texians dug through walls, climbed onto roofs, and drove Mexican soldiers back toward the old **Alamo** and the main plaza. Milam was killed by a sniper on December 7. Others took his place. On December 9, General Cos asked for terms. The Mexican soldiers **surrendered** and agreed to leave Texas.
🌐 FOREIGN LANGUAGE VOCABULARY
**Alamo** (AL-uh-moh). A former mission in San Antonio that was used as a fort in 1835 and 1836.

Look at the choices that led to this moment. Austin could have refused to lead. Milam could have gone home with the rest. The Texians could have waited for the Mexican army to starve them out. Each choice went the other way, and by the end of the year the colonists held the main town of the **province**.

By the middle of December, there were no Mexican soldiers left in Texas. Texians held San Antonio and the Alamo with it. It seemed that the war was over, and that the colonists had won. They had no way of knowing that the largest army was still on its way.
What were they fighting for?

In November, while the army besieged San Antonio, delegates met at **San Felipe** in a meeting called the **Consultation**. They had to decide what the war was about. Many wanted **independence**. But most did not. The Consultation declared that Texians were fighting to defend the Mexican Constitution of 1824, which **Santa Anna** had thrown out.
🌐 FOREIGN LANGUAGE VOCABULARY
**Santa Anna** (SAN-tah AH-nah). Antonio López de Santa Anna, a Mexican army officer who became one of the most powerful men in Mexico.
**San Felipe** (sahn feh-LEE-peh). San Felipe de Austin, the main town of Austin's colony, on the Brazos River.

That choice had a purpose. By fighting for the old constitution, Texians could claim to be loyal Mexicans who defended the law. They could also hope that **liberal** Mexicans in other states would join them. A fight for the constitution could draw **allies**, but a fight for independence would draw only enemies.

The Consultation set up a **provisional** government, with Henry Smith as governor and Sam Houston as commander of the regular army. It was a temporary government meant to last until a better one could be built. But the leaders quarreled with each other almost at once, and the volunteers answered to different chiefs.

The plan for a campaign shows the confusion. Some leaders wanted to attack the city of **Matamoros**, at the mouth of the **Rio Grande**, and join Mexican **federalists**. That plan made sense only if the war was about restoring the constitution. Nobody would plan such a trip if the war had already become a war of separation.
🌐 FOREIGN LANGUAGE VOCABULARY
**Rio Grande** (REE-oh GRAHN-day). The great river that flows between Texas and Mexico to the Gulf of Mexico.
**Matamoros** (mah-tah-MOH-rohs). A Mexican city near the mouth of the Rio Grande.

That is the question that the next months would answer. In December 1835, Texians still said that they were fighting for Mexico's constitution. By March, they would be fighting for something very different, and the men at the Alamo may not have known which war they were in.
💪 REMEMBER THIS QUESTION
Keep one question in mind: when does a fight to restore a law turn into a fight to leave the country? The answer was not clear to the people living through it.

text: Moses Austin got his **grant** in January 1821. By June, he was dead. His son Stephen had to decide whether to carry on a plan he had not made. This lesson follows how Stephen F. Austin took up that **obligation**, why so many Americans were ready to move to Texas, and why the whole arrangement was full of irony.

📚 PART 1 · MOSES AUSTIN'S GRANT, 1821
A father's last effort

Moses Austin had traveled hard to reach San Antonio, and he traveled hard to get home. He fell sick on the road, and by the time he reached Missouri he was weak. He died in June 1821 without ever having brought a single family to Texas.

The trip home was long, and Moses was already worn out. He had made the journey in winter, and he was sick on the road. By the time he reached his family, he was too weak to recover. Whether he knew how large his plan would become, nobody can say.
He left one last wish. He wanted his son Stephen to finish the work. It was a lot to ask. The grant was not a sure thing, and the promise would be hard to keep.

This is a moment where one person's choice mattered a great deal. Moses had been given permission by Spain, but a permit is only paper. Nobody else had the contract, the plan, or the connections. If Stephen said no, the grant would probably have faded away, and the first American colony might not have been founded when it was. History turned on a young man's answer.

Think about what Stephen's choice also meant for the families who would come. Thousands of lives would be shaped by a decision made by one man in New Orleans in the summer of 1821. He did not know that. He only knew that a promise had been left in his hands.

section: PART 2 STEPHEN TAKES UP THE WORK
text: 📚 PART 2 · STEPHEN TAKES UP THE WORK

section: A young man with other plans
text: A young man with other plans

section: A young man with other plans
text: Stephen F. Austin was twenty-seven. He had grown up in Missouri and been educated in Connecticut and Kentucky. He had served in the Missouri legislature and had worked as a judge. When his father died, he was in New Orleans, studying law. He had not planned to become a colonizer.

section: A young man with other plans
text: He was not a rough frontiersman. He was careful and serious, and he liked to read and write letters. People who met him often noticed how patient he was. He wanted a life in the cities of the United States, and Texas meant swamps, heat, and years of hard work far from home. The job ahead needed a person who could deal with officials, settle arguments, and keep a promise over many years.

section: A young man with other plans
text: But he **inherited** the obligation. He traveled to San Antonio and met the new governor. The authorities agreed to honor his father's grant. Austin explored the land between the **Brazos** and **Colorado** rivers, chose a place for his colony, and began recruiting settlers.

section: A young man with other plans
text: 🌐 FOREIGN LANGUAGE VOCABULARY

section: A young man with other plans
text: **Brazos** (BRAH-zus). A major river in Texas that flows to the Gulf of Mexico.

section: A young man with other plans
text: **Colorado** (kol-uh-RAD-oh). A river in Texas that flows to the Gulf of Mexico. It is not the Colorado River of the western mountains.

section: A young man with other plans
text: The timing was awkward. The grant had come from Spain, but Spain no longer ruled Mexico by the end of that summer. Stephen would have to ask the new government to honor an agreement made by the old one. Nobody could be sure the new rulers would agree. The plan could have ended before it started.

section: A young man with other plans
text: Think about what it means to take on a duty you did not choose. Stephen could have said that the grant was his father's, not his. He could have walked away, and nobody would have blamed him. Instead, he treated the promise as his own. The old word for that kind of steady character is responsibility, and it is one of the virtues that shaped this story.

section: A young man with other plans
text: Responsibility does not mean that a person enjoys the job. It means that a person keeps going when it would be easier to stop. That kind of steadiness is what turned a paper grant into a working colony. A colony needs more than land. It needs a leader, laws, neighbors, and trust, and all of those had to be built.
📚 PART 3 · WHY AMERICANS?

section: Cheap land and a fresh start
text: Cheap land and a fresh start

section: Cheap land and a fresh start
text: Many Americans were ready to move. The panic of 1819 had left a great number of them in **debt**. Land in the United States now had to be paid for in cash, and it cost more than many families could afford. In Texas, land was nearly free.

section: Cheap land and a fresh start
text: Compare the offers. In the United States, a family might pay a high price in cash for land. In Texas, the price was small, and a family could pay over time. That difference was strong enough to make people leave their homes. Families packed wagons, crossed rivers, and started over in a country where the laws, language, and religion were not their own.

section: Cheap land and a fresh start
text: Cotton was another reason. The soil of the lower Brazos and Colorado valleys was good for it, and cotton prices were high. Many of the settlers were from the Old Southwest, where cotton farming was growing. Some were slaveholders, and others hoped to become planters. Slavery was part of this story from the beginning.

section: Cheap land and a fresh start
text: Slavery shaped the colony from the start, and it caused arguments that would grow. Some settlers brought **enslaved** people with them, and others hoped to buy them later. Mexico's leaders were uneasy about slavery, and their laws on the subject changed several times in these years. The colony would have to find a way to live with those laws. The question would come back again and again.
📚 PART 4 · THE IRONY

section: A Mexican frontier with an English model
text: A Mexican frontier with an English model

section: A Mexican frontier with an English model
text: Think about what this arrangement meant. Mexico wanted a **buffer** against outsiders, and it invited settlers from the country it feared most. The settlers would live under Mexican laws, but they would bring American habits. The **colony agent** (*empresario*) system let Mexico use the English model, but with Spanish legal forms.

section: A Mexican frontier with an English model
text: There is also a point about timing. Spain had spent three hundred years failing to fill Texas. The English model, when it came, began to fill the river valleys in a few years. The place had not changed. The difference was the model, and the kind of people who came with it. That is the answer to the long puzzle of the three towns.

section: A Mexican frontier with an English model
text: This is the hinge of the whole story. Everything before it was a prologue about a **province** that Spain could never fill. What comes after is the story of a colony. The community that would become Texas began not with the land itself, but with the people Austin brought to it.

section: A Mexican frontier with an English model
text: 🌐 FOREIGN LANGUAGE VOCABULARY

section: A Mexican frontier with an English model
text: **colony agent (*empresario*)** (em-preh-SAH-ree-oh). A person who got a contract from the government to bring settlers to Texas.

section: A Mexican frontier with an English model
text: Keep one question in mind as you finish. Why would a government that feared Americans invite them in? Part of the answer is fear of something worse, and part is hope. Both feelings were real, and both pushed Mexico toward a choice that would change the map.
💪 WHAT TO CARRY FORWARD

The empresario system was Mexico's answer to the problem Spain never solved. It would fill the land with people. It would also fill it with people whose ideas about government and land came from somewhere else. That is the tension at the center of what follows.

section: Could Texas survive on its own?
text: By the early 1840s, Texas had been independent for five years. It had won its war, but it still had no peace with Mexico, no money, and no way to defend its border. This lesson follows a string of bold and costly adventures, and the foreign powers who began to take an interest in the **Republic**.

📚 PART 1 · LAMAR'S BIG IDEA
The Santa Fe Expedition

President Lamar had big plans. In 1841, he sent about three hundred men, with wagons of goods, on a long journey across the plains to Santa Fe, in New Mexico. Texas claimed that its western border reached the **Rio Grande**, and Lamar hoped that the people of Santa Fe would welcome Texan rule and trade.
🌐 FOREIGN LANGUAGE VOCABULARY
**Mier** (mee-AIR). A Mexican town on the Rio Grande where a Texan force was captured in 1842.
**Rio Grande** (REE-oh GRAHN-day). The great river that flows between Texas and Mexico to the Gulf of Mexico.

It was a bad plan from the start. The party was not sure of the way. They wandered for weeks across dry plains, ran short of food and water, and met hostile bands of Native warriors. By the time they reached New Mexico, they were worn out and spread thin.

The New Mexican governor, **Armijo**, had been warned. His soldiers captured the Texans without a fight. The prisoners were marched hundreds of miles south to Mexico City, and many were held in prison for months. Lamar's dream of a Texas that reached to Santa Fe had cost the Republic many of its best men.
🌐 FOREIGN LANGUAGE VOCABULARY
**Armijo** (ar-MEE-hoh). Manuel Armijo, the governor of New Mexico who captured the Texan Santa Fe Expedition.

Think about what this showed. Texas was a young and small country, and it had tried something that only a great power could do. A failure like this made the Republic look weak to its neighbors. It also showed that Texas leaders did not always plan carefully before they acted.
Raids on San Antonio

Mexico never accepted the loss of Texas, and in 1842 it showed that it was still a threat. In March, a small Mexican force under General **Vásquez** rode into San Antonio. The town was nearly empty, because most people had fled, and the Mexican troops soon left again. But the point was made.
🌐 FOREIGN LANGUAGE VOCABULARY
**Vásquez** (VAHS-kes). Rafael Vásquez, a Mexican general who led a raid on San Antonio in 1842.

Think about how a **raid** felt to a family in San Antonio. Word came that soldiers were on the road, and people left their homes with whatever they could carry. A small force with no plan to stay could still empty a town. The Republic had no way to guard every road, and everyone knew it.

In September, a larger force under General **Woll** captured San Antonio again and held it for a time. A group of Texans rode to help, and Woll's troops killed many of them in a fight known as the Dawson **Massacre**. Woll **retreated** south, taking prisoners with him.
🌐 FOREIGN LANGUAGE VOCABULARY
**Woll** (VOHL). Adrián Woll, a Mexican general who captured San Antonio in September 1842.

Texans were furious. The new president, Sam Houston, was in his second term, and many of his people demanded a revenge. But Houston knew that the Republic had little money and no real army. He moved cautiously, which made him unpopular again. Many men decided to go to war without him.
📚 PART 2 · THE MIER EXPEDITION
Across the Rio Grande

In the late fall of 1842, a force of about three hundred Texan **volunteers** marched to the Rio Grande. They meant to punish Mexico for the raids. Their orders were to protect the border, but many of the men had other ideas. They crossed the river anyway, and attacked the Mexican town of Mier on December 26.

The Texans fought well in the streets and killed many Mexican soldiers. But the Mexican force was much larger. After a day of fighting, the Texan leaders decided to give up, thinking that they would be treated as prisoners of war. They were marched south into Mexico.

Along the way, the prisoners made a daring break for freedom. They overpowered their guards and escaped into the mountains. But the country was dry and hard, and they had no food. Within days, most were recaptured, starving and weak. **Santa Anna**, who had returned to power in Mexico, was furious.
🌐 FOREIGN LANGUAGE VOCABULARY
**Santa Anna** (SAN-tah AH-nah). Antonio López de Santa Anna, a Mexican army officer who became one of the most powerful men in Mexico.
The black bean lottery

Santa Anna ordered that the recaptured men be punished. He wanted every tenth man shot. To decide who would die, the guards used a lottery. They put one bean in a jar for each prisoner. Seventeen of the beans were black, and the rest were white. Each prisoner, one by one, had to reach in and draw a bean.

The men who drew white beans lived. The men who drew black beans were shot. A prisoner named William Preston Stapp later wrote about it, and his story is one of the most chilling accounts of the war. He described how calmly many of the men took their beans, and how they met their end.

The black bean lottery shocked Texas. It stirred up new anger against Mexico. At the same time, it showed how costly it was to go to war without a plan. Seventeen men died because of a risky campaign, and the surviving prisoners spent months in Mexican prisons.
📚 PART 3 · OTHER POWERS TAKE NOTICE
Britain and France

While Texas struggled, powerful countries across the ocean began to pay attention. Britain and France both recognized Texas as an independent nation. They saw several benefits. Texas could supply cotton for their mills, and it could be a buyer for their goods. It could also be a barrier to the growth of the United States.

Think about Britain's interest from a map. Texas had a long coast on the Gulf of Mexico, wide plains for cotton, and a growing number of **settlers**. A friendly Texas could give British ships a base in a **region** that the United States considered its own backyard. Distant powers had good reasons to care.

Britain had another goal as well. It had ended slavery in its own **empire**, and many British leaders hoped to see it ended elsewhere. Some of them thought that an independent Texas, tied to Britain by trade, might one day be persuaded to move away from slavery. Texans listened politely, and some hoped for British help against Mexico.

Houston understood the game. He let it be known that Texas was talking with Britain and France. He did not want to leave the Republic in the hands of a foreign power. But he hoped that the news would make leaders in Washington worry, and make them more willing to offer annexation. It was a clever use of a weak hand.
Why Washington worried

The British interest alarmed Americans a great deal. A cotton-growing, slaveholding republic under British influence, right on the border of the United States, seemed dangerous. Some feared that Britain would build ports and forts there. Others feared that it would use its influence to end slavery in Texas.

This alarm was greater in Washington than in Mexico City. Mexico wanted Texas back and was not afraid of British help. But American leaders worried about their own border, their own trade, and their own future. They began to think that **annexing** Texas might be safer than leaving it alone.

By 1844, Texas sat in a very odd position. It was independent, but it could not pay its **debts**. It had friends and enemies on every side. The choice between staying independent and joining the United States was becoming the central question in the Republic, and the United States was starting to ask it too.
💪 REMEMBER THIS QUESTION
Keep one question in mind: why would several countries care so much about a small, poor republic? Texas had land, cotton, and a border that mattered to everyone.

A few words in this lesson are worth a look before you read. They show up in bold, and you can hover over any of them for a reminder.
**alliance** (uh-LY-ens). A partnership between countries that agree to help each other.
**ally** (AL-eye). A person or group that joins with another to work toward the same goal.
**colony** (KAH-luh-nee). A place settled and controlled by people from a faraway country.
**empire** (EM-pyr). A large area of land and many peoples ruled by one government.
**expedition** (eks-pih-DISH-un). A long trip taken for a purpose, such as exploring or conquering.

**mutiny** (MYOO-tuh-nee). A revolt by soldiers or sailors against their own leaders.
**region** (REE-jun). A large area with features that set it apart from the areas around it.
**rival** (RY-vul). A person or country that competes against another.
📖 TODAY'S FOCUS
A map error, a lost fleet, and a colony that lasted less than four years.

France built its American **empire** on furs and friendship. In the 1680s, a French explorer set out to carry that empire to the Gulf of Mexico. He never reached the place he was aiming for. Instead he landed on the coast of Texas, and his mistake changed the history of the whole **region**.

text: From the St. Lawrence to the Gulf

section: From the St. Lawrence to the Gulf
text: By now you know how France did things. French traders paid Native peoples for furs, made **alliances**, and kept their settlements small. The heart of New France was the St. Lawrence River and the Great Lakes. La Salle was an explorer who pushed that system farther west and south. In 1682, he paddled down the Mississippi River to the Gulf of Mexico. He claimed the whole river valley for King Louis XIV and named it Louisiana, in honor of the king.

section: From the St. Lawrence to the Gulf
text: Nearly all of the wealth of New France came from the fur trade. The French did not try to turn Native peoples into workers or to take over their land. Because they needed skilled trappers, they worked to keep good relations. This worked in the north, where Native hunters knew the forests and rivers, and where a French trader could sail home each year with a boat full of furs.

section: From the St. Lawrence to the Gulf
text: Then La Salle went back to France with a bold plan. He would plant a **colony** at the mouth of the Mississippi. From there, France could trade with Native peoples up the river. It could also threaten the silver mines of Spain, France's old **rival**. The king agreed to help.

section: From the St. Lawrence to the Gulf
text: 🌐 FOREIGN LANGUAGE VOCABULARY

section: From the St. Lawrence to the Gulf
text: **La Salle** (lah SAHL). Robert Cavelier, Sieur de La Salle, a French explorer.

section: From the St. Lawrence to the Gulf
text: La Salle was a driven and difficult man. He had a talent for big plans, and he could inspire men to follow him. He could also be harsh, proud, and slow to listen. Many of the people who sailed with him did not like him. These traits matter, because a leader's character can decide whether a hard journey succeeds or fails.
📚 PART 2 · A COSTLY MISTAKE
Lost at sea

In 1684, La Salle sailed from France with four ships and about three hundred people. There were soldiers, workers, families, and priests. Trouble started early. La Salle argued with the captain of the navy ship, and sickness spread through the crowded decks. Worse, nobody could find the river.

In those days, sailors could not measure **longitude**. It tells how far east or west a ship has traveled. Without it, the crew had to guess, and they guessed wrong. They sailed right past the mouth of the Mississippi by hundreds of miles. In February 1685, the ships entered **Matagorda** Bay on the coast of Texas.

A ship's captain could tell how far north or south he was by looking at the sun and stars. East and west was much harder. Clocks of the day lost time at sea, so the best a sailor could do was guess from his speed and direction. A small mistake grew bigger every day. That is how a fleet aiming for one river ended up hundreds of miles away.

When La Salle first saw the coast, he suspected that his ships had gone too far west. Still, he hoped that one of the rivers flowing into the bay was a branch of the Mississippi. He spent weeks exploring the shore and the bay looking for it. Meanwhile his supplies shrank and his men grew restless.

La Salle chose to stay. He built a small fort near the bay and called it Fort St. Louis. Ships were lost one by one. Spanish pirates captured one on the way across. Another ran aground. A third, called La Belle, sank in 1686. More than three hundred years later, in 1995, archaeologists found La Belle in the mud at the bottom of the bay.
🌐 FOREIGN LANGUAGE VOCABULARY
**Matagorda** (mat-uh-GOR-duh). A large bay on the Texas coast, where La Salle landed in 1685.

Think about the choice La Salle faced. He could have given up and sailed away, but he had spent the king's money and staked his name on this plan. Going home with nothing would have meant shame. Pride and hope may have pushed him to stay, and the colony paid the price.
📚 PART 3 · FORT ST. LOUIS
A fort without friends

The French model needed friends, but La Salle had none on this coast. Early on, French colonists took canoes from the **Karankawa**, and the two groups began to fight. The colonists also had little food and no farms. Snakes, sickness, and hunger killed many of them. Within two years, only a few dozen were left.
🌐 FOREIGN LANGUAGE VOCABULARY
**Karankawa** (kuh-RANG-kuh-wah). The name often used today for the coastal peoples of the Texas Gulf coast.

The French model of friendship had little chance here. La Salle's party had arrived as strangers with weapons, not as traders with goods. For the Karankawa, the French were people who took canoes and stayed where they were not wanted. They had no reason to treat them as **allies**.

There were no furs to trade, no allies to trade with, and no French town within hundreds of miles. La Salle decided to walk overland to find the Mississippi and bring help from Canada. In March 1687, somewhere in East Texas, a group of his own men murdered him in a **mutiny**. His colony never learned what had happened to him.

The few crops the colonists planted did poorly. La Salle made several trips along the coast and inland to look for the Mississippi and for help. Each trip cost him men, to sickness, accident, and fighting.

Life at the fort was miserable. The ground was hard, the water was bad in places, and the men had not planned for a long stay. Some of the colonists died of disease. Others wandered off and were never seen again. Without fresh supplies from France, the little settlement slowly fell apart.

section: PART 4 THE END OF THE COLONY
text: 📚 PART 4 · THE END OF THE COLONY
What was left

Back at the fort, the survivors were mostly women and children. In the winter of 1688 to 1689, the Karankawa attacked. They killed most of the people who remained and took some of the children. The French colony in Texas was over in less than four years.

A few men escaped. **Joutel** was one of them. He had left with a small party that followed La Salle north. They found French outposts on the Mississippi and in Canada, and eventually he reached France. He wrote a journal of the **expedition**, and it is one of our best sources for what happened.
🌐 FOREIGN LANGUAGE VOCABULARY
**Joutel** (zhoo-TEL). Henri Joutel, a French soldier who survived La Salle's expedition and wrote a journal about it.

The colony failed because the French model needed what this place did not have. It needed Native friends, fur to trade, and a French town nearby. La Salle had none of the three. But the failure did not end the story. Spanish officials in Mexico heard about Fort St. Louis. They saw a French colony on a coast Spain had never settled. They realized they could lose Texas, and that made them act.
💪 WHAT TO CARRY FORWARD

One bad guess about longitude put a French colony in Texas, and the French model fell apart there. But the colony sent a warning to Spain. For more than a hundred years, Spain had ignored Texas. After Fort St. Louis, it could not afford to.

📖 TODAY'S FOCUS
What happens when a country chooses war instead of peace on its own frontier?

The **Republic** of Texas elected two very different presidents. Sam Houston wanted peace with Native peoples. Mirabeau Lamar wanted them gone. This lesson follows Lamar's choice, a brutal fight at a council in San Antonio, and a **Comanche** **raid** that reached the sea.

section: PART 1 TWO THEORIES OF THE FRONTIER
text: 📚 PART 1 · TWO THEORIES OF THE FRONTIER
Houston and Lamar

The Republic of Texas had to decide what to do about the Native peoples who lived on its land. Houston believed in peace. He had lived among the Cherokee as a young man, and he thought that **treaties** and trade would cost less than war. Texas could not afford an army, and he did not want to fight one.
🌐 FOREIGN LANGUAGE VOCABULARY
**Comanche** (kuh-MAN-chee). A people who became the strongest power on the southern plains in the 1700s.

Mirabeau Lamar had a very different view. He was a poet and a soldier who had fought at **San Jacinto**. He became president in December 1838, and he said openly that Native peoples should be driven out of Texas. Under Lamar, the government built forts, raised soldiers, and began a policy of expulsion.
🌐 FOREIGN LANGUAGE VOCABULARY
**San Jacinto** (san hah-SIN-toh). A river and a battlefield on the coastal plain of Texas, near the modern city of Houston.

Think about the two ideas. Houston's policy was cheap, and it kept the border quieter, but it did not satisfy **settlers** who wanted the land. Lamar's policy was expensive, and it brought raids and revenge, but it promised room for more farms. Each leader believed that his way would protect the Republic.

In short, the frontier was the real war of the Republic. Mexico threatened but rarely invaded. The Comanche and other peoples were close by every day. How Texans treated them would decide whether farms could spread west, and whether families could sleep in peace.
The Cherokee War

Lamar began with the Cherokee in East Texas. He declared that their treaty with Houston was void, since the **Senate** had never approved it. He argued that they had no right to the land, and he sent soldiers to make them leave. The Cherokee asked to stay. Their chief, Bowles, tried to avoid a fight.

In July 1839, Texan troops met the Cherokee near the Neches River. The Cherokee were outnumbered. In two days of fighting, many were killed, and Chief Bowles, who was in his eighties, was shot and killed on the field. The survivors fled north across the Red River. East Texas was open to settlement.

The Cherokee War was brief, and it lasted only a few days. But it showed the policy that Lamar would follow. He was willing to break old agreements and to use force when he thought it would help. The Native peoples of Texas were watching, and what they saw was not reassuring.
📚 PART 2 · THE COUNCIL HOUSE FIGHT

section: A parley that ended in blood
text: A parley that ended in blood

section: A parley that ended in blood
text: In the winter of 1840, a group of Comanche leaders sent word that they wanted to talk. In March, about sixty-five Comanche, including twelve chiefs, rode into San Antonio. They came to a **parley** at the Council House, a stone building in the town. They brought one **captive**, a young girl named Matilda Lockhart.

section: A parley that ended in blood
text: Matilda was in terrible condition. She had been held for months, and she had been badly treated. She told Texan officials that there were other captives held by the Comanche. The Texans had told the Comanche to bring all of their captives. Now it seemed that the Comanche had brought only one.

section: A parley that ended in blood
text: The Texan officials decided to hold the chiefs as **hostages** until the other captives were returned. They told the chiefs, and soldiers entered the room. The Comanche refused to be held. A fight broke out, and it spread into the streets. When it ended, thirty-five Comanche and seven Texans were dead.

section: A parley that ended in blood
text: A woman named Mary Maverick watched the fight from her house. Her account is one of the best records of what happened. She described the shouting, the shots, and the terror in the streets. She also described how the settlers were shaken by what had taken place in their own town.

section: A parley that ended in blood
text: The Comanche saw the event as a betrayal. They had come under a flag of peace, and many of their leaders had been killed. Whatever the Texans believed about the captives, the Comanche believed that their word had been broken. They would not forget it.
📚 PART 3 · THE GREAT RAID
Victoria and Linnville

In August 1840, a large force of Comanche warriors rode south, led by a war chief named Buffalo Hump. They moved far below the settled frontier, through country that the Texans thought was safe. They struck the town of Victoria, drove off horses, and killed settlers.

Then they rode to the coast. At Linnville, a port on the Gulf, the townspeople had barely time to flee by boat into the water. The warriors looted the warehouses, burned the buildings, and took goods that they had never seen before. For a few days, the Comanche stood on the shore of the Gulf of Mexico.

On the way home, they were met at Plum Creek by a force of Texans and **Tonkawa** **scouts**. The Comanche were slowed down by captured horses and by loot. The Texans attacked, and many of the raiders were killed. But the main body escaped, and the raid went down as one of the boldest in the history of the frontier.
🌐 FOREIGN LANGUAGE VOCABULARY
**Tonkawa** (TONG-kuh-wah). A Native people of central Texas who were enemies of the Comanche and allies of the Texans.

section: Why the Comanche were so hard to beat
text: Why the Comanche were so hard to beat

section: Why the Comanche were so hard to beat
text: The Comanche were the greatest horsemen on the plains. A rider could hang along the side of a galloping horse and shoot from beneath its neck. He could ride for days with little food. A warrior carried a short bow, and he could fire arrow after arrow while his horse was in motion.

section: Why the Comanche were so hard to beat
text: Compare this to the weapon of a Texan soldier. A rifleman had to stop, pour in powder, ram down a ball, and prime the gun before he could fire again. A warrior with a bow could shoot perhaps twenty arrows in the time that it took to reload one shot. In open country, that was a terrible advantage.

section: Why the Comanche were so hard to beat
text: Behind the skill was a way of life. Comanche children learned to ride when they were small. The tribe followed the **bison**, and every family depended on horses. A people so used to the saddle could not be caught by foot soldiers. Texans needed some new way of fighting if they were ever to win.
A captive who stayed

One story from these years shows how deep the conflict went. In 1836, Comanche warriors attacked Fort Parker, a settlers' stockade. They took a nine-year-old girl, Cynthia Ann Parker. She was adopted into the Comanche people, learned their language, and grew up as one of them.

Cynthia Ann married a Comanche chief and had children, including a son, **Quanah**, who became a great leader. In 1860, Texas Rangers under Sul Ross found her camp and took her back. By then, she had lived with the Comanche for twenty-four years. She had no wish to return, and she never settled easily among the Texans.
🌐 FOREIGN LANGUAGE VOCABULARY
**Quanah** (KWAH-nah). Quanah Parker, the son of Cynthia Ann Parker, who became a great Comanche war chief.

Her story reminds us that the frontier was not simple. Families were broken and joined across the line. The same events brought grief to settlers and to the Comanche. To understand the war, you have to see how it looked from both sides.
💪 REMEMBER THIS QUESTION
Keep one question in mind: what does it cost a country to choose war on its own frontier? The Republic could not pay, and the Comanche could not be beaten with the tools it had.

section: A new nation, an empty province, and a very risky idea.
text: When Mexico became independent, it **inherited** Spain's claim to Texas. It also inherited Spain's problem. The **province** was almost empty, dangerous, and far from the capital. This lesson explains how Mexico came to a decision that surprised many people. It decided to invite **settlers** from the United States.

📚 PART 1 · WHAT MEXICO INHERITED
Empty land and empty pockets

In 1821, Mexico's government looked at its northern **frontier** and saw trouble. Texas had only a few thousand settlers. The war had wrecked towns and ranches, and the government had very little money to rebuild them. The **Comanche** **raided** deep into northern Mexico, far beyond Texas, and Mexican soldiers could not stop them.
🌐 FOREIGN LANGUAGE VOCABULARY
**Comanche** (kuh-MAN-chee). A people who became the strongest power on the southern plains in the 1700s.

The numbers tell the story. In 1821, a few thousand people lived in a province that was larger than France. Most lived in San Antonio and a few other places, and the rest of the land was held by Native peoples or by no one. A government that could not protect its own towns could not protect a country-sized frontier.

There was also a danger on the other side. The United States had bought Louisiana in 1803, and its settlers were moving west. American adventurers had already crossed into Texas more than once. Mexican leaders worried that if they did nothing, Americans would simply take the land.

The new government had its own troubles. It had to build a nation out of a war, and its leaders did not even agree on what kind of government to have. They worried about money, about the army, and about **rivals** at home. A far northern province with a few thousand people was not at the top of the list. But it was not a problem that could be ignored for long.

The United States and Spain had argued over Texas for years. In 1819, a **treaty** set the border between them at the Sabine River on the east, but some Americans still said that Texas belonged to the United States. Mexican leaders knew about this. They knew that a border on a map did not stop people who wanted land.
📚 PART 2 · THE BUFFER IDEA

section: People who will defend their own land
text: People who will defend their own land

section: People who will defend their own land
text: The solution was an old one with a new twist. If the province needed people, perhaps it could invite them. Settlers who owned land in Texas would have a reason to defend it against raiders. They would also make a buffer against the dangers of both the Comanche and other foreigners.

section: People who will defend their own land
text: Spain had used the same idea when it brought the Canary Islanders to San Antonio in 1731. The new twist was who the settlers would be. This time they would come from another country, and they would come in much larger numbers.

section: People who will defend their own land
text: It was a risky plan. The new settlers might not be loyal. But the officials who made it believed the risk of doing nothing was larger. They also believed that settlers from the United States, who knew how to farm and fight on a frontier, were the best choice. The laws required them to follow Mexican law and to become Catholics.

section: People who will defend their own land
text: Officials also hoped that settlers would trade with Mexico, pay taxes, and make the land produce. A frontier with farms and ranches would feed soldiers, supply towns, and bring in money. A frontier with nothing would only cost money. In their minds, a risky plan was better than a sure failure.

section: People who will defend their own land
text: Not every Mexican leader liked the plan. Some feared that people from the United States would never become loyal Mexicans. They pointed to the language, the religion, and the habits that the settlers would bring. Supporters answered that the settlers would be bound by **oath** and by law. The argument went on for years, and it did not go away.
📚 PART 3 · MOSES AUSTIN'S PETITION
A request in San Antonio

The invitation began even before **independence**. Moses Austin was a Connecticut-born businessman who had moved to Spanish Missouri to mine lead. A financial panic in 1819 ruined him. He decided to make a new start in Texas. In December 1820, he traveled to San Antonio with a **petition** to settle three hundred families.

Austin's reasons were plain. He needed money, and he thought Texas could give it to him. He had already seen how a settlement could grow on the frontier in Missouri. He believed that good land and a few hundred families could do the same in Texas. It was a business plan, but it was also a plan to rebuild his life.

The governor at first told him to leave. But Austin met an old acquaintance, the Baron de **Bastrop**, who spoke for him. In January 1821, the Spanish authorities approved his request. The plan was now official. The man who had started it would not live to carry it out.
🌐 FOREIGN LANGUAGE VOCABULARY
**Bastrop** (BAS-trup). The Baron de Bastrop, a Dutch-born official in San Antonio who helped Moses Austin.

Bastrop mattered. He knew the officials and he spoke for Austin. His help turned a refusal into a yes. A different governor, or a different friend, might have meant a different story. Small things like this can change everything that comes after.
📚 PART 4 · THREE LAWS
The rules for settlers

After independence, Mexico wrote its own laws. The first was the Imperial Colonization Law of January 1823. It offered land to families who would settle. Next came the General Colonization Law of August 1824, which left the details to the Mexican states. Texas was joined with its neighbor, and the state of **Coahuila y Tejas** passed its own law in 1825.
🌐 FOREIGN LANGUAGE VOCABULARY
**Coahuila y Tejas** (koh-ah-WEE-lah ee TAY-hahs). The Mexican state that included both Coahuila and Texas after 1824.

Look at how the laws changed. The 1823 law came from an **emperor**, **Iturbide**, who soon fell from power. The 1824 law came from the new **republic**. The 1825 law came from the state government. Each time, the government changed, but the idea stayed the same. That shows how much Mexico's leaders wanted settlers, even when they could not agree on much else.
🌐 FOREIGN LANGUAGE VOCABULARY
**Iturbide** (ee-toor-BEE-deh). Agustín de Iturbide, a Spanish army officer who led the final push for Mexican independence.

The 1825 law set up the **colony agent** (*empresario*) system. A government contract allowed an empresario to bring in families, usually a few hundred, within a set number of years. In return, the empresario received land. Farmers could receive a plot of about 177 acres. Ranchers could receive a **league**, which is about 4,428 acres. Settlers had to swear loyalty to Mexico and accept the Catholic faith.

The terms were generous. Land was nearly free, and Mexico saw this as the price of a safe frontier. What Mexico did not yet know was how many people would accept the offer, and what they would bring with them.
🌐 FOREIGN LANGUAGE VOCABULARY
**colony agent (*empresario*)** (em-preh-SAH-ree-oh). A person who got a contract from the government to bring settlers to Texas.

There were conditions. A settler had to farm the land, build a home, and take an oath. The **colony** agent had to bring in the number of families promised, or the contract could be canceled. Some limits were put on settling near the border or the coast. These rules showed that Mexico wanted settlers, but it also wanted to stay in control.
💪 WHAT TO CARRY FORWARD

Mexico did not choose to invite Americans because it loved the idea. It chose them because it had too few people, too little money, and too many dangers. A plan born of weakness would have large and surprising results.

text: Why would Texans want a state of their own inside Mexico?

section: Why would Texans want a state of their own inside Mexico?
text: In 1824, Mexico adopted a **constitution** that gave real power to its states. That sounded wonderful to Texas **settlers**, who liked local control. But Texas was not made a state of its own. It was joined to a neighbor, and the trouble that followed lasted more than a decade.

section: PART 1 A NEW KIND OF GOVERNMENT
text: 📚 PART 1 · A NEW KIND OF GOVERNMENT
Power for the states

After the **empire** fell, Mexico had to choose a new kind of government. In October 1824, a new **congress** finished a constitution that made Mexico a **republic**. It had a president, a congress, and courts. It also did something important. It divided power between the national government and the states.
🌐 FOREIGN LANGUAGE VOCABULARY
**Coahuila** (koh-ah-WEE-lah). A state in northern Mexico that was joined to Texas in 1824.

This idea is called federalism, and a country built on it is called **federal**. In a federal system, each state has its own government and makes many of its own laws, while the national government handles things like defense and money. The United States works this way. In Mexico, the constitution of 1824 made it the law of the land.

Mexico's lawmakers borrowed from two places. They looked at the Constitution of the United States, which **Arizpe** and others had studied closely. They also looked at the Spanish constitution of 1812, which had been written during the war against Napoleon and had given local governments a larger role. The result mixed ideas from both.
🌐 FOREIGN LANGUAGE VOCABULARY
**Arizpe** (ah-REES-peh). Miguel Ramos Arizpe, a priest and lawmaker from northern Mexico who helped shape the idea of a federal republic.

The new constitution was not a copy of either model. It said that the Catholic Church would be the only religion of the nation. It created nineteen states and several territories. And it left a lot of room for the states to decide matters for themselves, which is exactly what many local leaders wanted.
Why this mattered to Texas

Texas settlers liked the idea of local government. Most of them had grown up in states of their own, with their own legislatures and courts. A federal republic seemed to promise that decisions about their daily lives would be made close to home. Many believed that Mexico now had a government much like the one they had left.

Think about the settlers' memories. Many had watched lawmakers in their home states argue in open halls and pass laws that touched their farms and their stores. They believed that a government works best when it is close enough for ordinary people to reach. A lawmaker who lives down the road is easier to talk to than a minister in a far city.

That hope shaped how they saw their future. Austin and others spoke warmly about the constitution of 1824. They took an **oath** to defend it. Later, when the constitution was in danger, they would fight to protect it, because it was the legal foundation of their right to govern their own affairs.
📚 PART 2 · TEXAS TIED TO COAHUILA
One state, two peoples

But Texas did not get a state of its own. The constitution did not say how many people a state needed, and Texas had too few. In 1824, a state law joined Texas to its neighbor to the southwest. The new state was called **Coahuila y Tejas**. The name was long, and so were the miles.
🌐 FOREIGN LANGUAGE VOCABULARY
**Coahuila y Tejas** (koh-ah-WEE-lah ee TAY-hahs). The Mexican state that included both Coahuila and Texas after 1824.

Coahuila had far more people than Texas. In the state legislature, Texans were always outvoted. The capital was at **Saltillo**, hundreds of miles from the **colonies** on the **Brazos**, across hard country. A lawmaker from Texas might spend weeks on the road just to take his seat.
🌐 FOREIGN LANGUAGE VOCABULARY
**Saltillo** (sahl-TEE-yoh). A city in Coahuila that served as the capital of the state of Coahuila y Tejas.
**Brazos** (BRAH-zus). A major river in Texas that flows to the Gulf of Mexico.

The state courts were far away too. A settler with a land dispute might need to send for papers or travel for weeks to get an answer. Laws were written in Spanish by people who had never seen a Texas farm. Texans began to feel that decisions about them were being made by people who did not know them.

Think about the different interests. Coahuila was mostly dry ranching and mining country. Texas was filling with cotton farmers and growing towns. The two parts of the state wanted different roads, different land laws, and different kinds of help. Even honest lawmakers in Saltillo had trouble serving both.
The first petitions

Almost at once, Texans began asking for a state of their own. A request for statehood within Mexico was not **rebellion**. It was a way of asking Mexico to carry out its own constitution. Texans made the request politely, and they made it again and again.

The Mexican government always found a reason to wait. Texas was too small, officials said, or the time was wrong, or the country had other worries. Each delay made the petitioners more impatient. Over the next decade the request never stopped, and each refusal made it harder to believe that the system could be changed from within.

Notice what the settlers were asking. They were not asking to leave Mexico. They were asking to be treated as a full part of it. A people who ask to be included are in a very different position from a people who ask to leave. That difference would matter a great deal in 1835.

section: PART 3 A FEDERAL SYSTEM WITH WEAK SPOTS
text: 📚 PART 3 · A FEDERAL SYSTEM WITH WEAK SPOTS
Strong on paper

The constitution of 1824 gave Mexico a good framework, but it depended on habits that the country had not yet built. Federal systems work when people trust the rules, when states obey the national government, and when leaders accept the results of elections. These habits grow slowly, and Mexico had been free for only three years.

Compare Mexico's problem with the problem of the United States. The American states had been colonies with their own assemblies for more than a century before they joined together. Mexico's **provinces** had been ruled from the capital by Spain's viceroys for three hundred years. The states had little practice at governing themselves, and the capital had little practice at sharing power.

Several things were missing. The **treasury** was weak, the army was powerful, and many leaders cared more about their own **region** than the whole country. A constitution is only as strong as the people who are willing to follow it. Its weaknesses were already visible in the first years.

Texas stood in an unusual position. The settlers were among the strongest supporters of the federal system, because they liked its promise of local control. If that system failed, they stood to lose more than most. This is one reason that the story of Texas and the story of Mexico are so closely tied.

What the settlers wanted was simple: a legislature near home, courts they could reach, and laws that fit their lives. The constitution of 1824 seemed to offer these things. For a decade, many Texans believed that their hopes could be met inside Mexico. Their belief rested on a document, and a document needs people willing to defend it.
💪 REMEMBER THIS QUESTION
Keep one question in mind: what is a constitution worth if the people in power will not follow it? The settlers' hopes rested on that answer.

section: Three buildings were supposed to make a colony. What went wrong?
text: Spain had a plan for the northern **frontier**. It was a set of three institutions, each with its own job. A priest, a soldier, and a **settler** would work together to turn a wild frontier into a Spanish **province**. This lesson looks at how that plan was supposed to work, and how it worked in Texas.

📚 PART 1 · THE PLAN
Three institutions, one goal

Spain built its frontier with three tools. The first was the mission. Priests would **congregate** Native people into a community, teach them the Christian faith, and train them in farming and trades. The second was the fort (*presidio*). Soldiers lived there and protected both the mission and the road. The third was the town (*pueblo*). This was a civilian town where Spanish settlers would live and eventually take over.
🌐 FOREIGN LANGUAGE VOCABULARY
**fort (*presidio*)** (preh-SEE-dee-oh). A Spanish fort where soldiers lived and guarded the frontier.
**town (*pueblo*)** (PWEB-loh). A Spanish word for a town. On the frontier, a pueblo was a town of civilian settlers.

The plan had an end date. After about ten years, the mission was supposed to hand its land and its people over to the Church and the local government. The Native people would be Spanish subjects. The priests would move on to a new frontier and start again.

This was a real idea with a real logic. Spain had seen it work before, and it did not need a large army to carry it out. A few priests, a small group of soldiers, and a handful of families could, on paper, turn a whole **region** into a Spanish province. That is why the plan appealed to officials who were always short of money. The question was whether the places Spain tried it on looked anything like the places where it had worked before.

The design came from earlier success in Mexico, where missions had grown up among peoples who already farmed. It was also cheap. A mission cost far less than an army. By turning Native people into farmers and taxpayers, the plan promised that a frontier could pay for itself.

section: PART 2 MISSION LIFE AT SAN ANTONIO
text: 📚 PART 2 · MISSION LIFE AT SAN ANTONIO
Work, worship, and water

At San Antonio, five missions eventually stood along the river. Each had a church, workshops, and fields. The mission day followed the church bells. People prayed, worked, ate, and slept to a schedule. They learned to weave, build, farm, and care for cattle. Many were taught Spanish.

A visitor to a mission would have seen a walled compound. Inside were a church, a storehouse for grain, living rooms, and workshops. Outside were orchards, fields, and pastures. Cattle and sheep grazed on the land around it. A mission could grow much of its own food, and extra corn and beef went to the presidio.

The mission also changed who people were. A person who joined was given a Christian name and a place in the mission's work schedule. Children were baptized and taught prayers. The priests believed they were doing good. Many Native families, on the other hand, were giving up their old ways of finding food and their old ties to relatives. It was a big trade, and not everyone who made it was glad.

Water was the key. Missions dug **acequias** from the river to carry water to the fields. Some of those ditches still run in San Antonio today. They are one of the lasting marks of Spanish settlement. This way of bringing water to crops is called **irrigation**.

But life at a mission was also hard. People who had lived freely were now expected to follow a strict routine. And disease was a constant danger. **Epidemics** of **smallpox** and measles swept through the crowded missions. Epidemics killed so many people that missions needed new arrivals just to stay the same size. Many Native people came to missions voluntarily, for food and for protection from their enemies, especially the **Apache** and later the **Comanche**.
🌐 FOREIGN LANGUAGE VOCABULARY
**irrigation ditch (*acequia*)** (ah-SEH-kee-ah). A ditch that carries water from a river to farm fields.
**Comanche** (kuh-MAN-chee). A people who became the strongest power on the southern plains in the 1700s.
**Apache** (uh-PATCH-ee). A group of related peoples who lived on the plains and in the Southwest.

People did not always stay. Some left to return to their old way of life, especially when food was short or when sickness struck. Priests sometimes sent soldiers to bring them back. That shows an important truth about the system. A mission worked only as long as people had a reason to stay, or no better place to go.
📚 PART 3 · WHERE IT HALF-WORKED

section: Some peoples joined, others did not
text: The system worked best with small groups who had lost land and food to enemies. In South Texas, many groups often called **Coahuiltecan** joined the missions. They were hunter-gatherers living in a harsh, dry land, and the missions offered them a more certain meal.

section: Some peoples joined, others did not
text: 🌐 FOREIGN LANGUAGE VOCABULARY

section: Some peoples joined, others did not
text: **Coahuiltecan** (koh-wheel-TEK-un). The name used for many small groups who lived by hunting and gathering in South Texas and northern Mexico.

section: Some peoples joined, others did not
text: The system worked less well with the **Caddo** of East Texas. They already had farms and towns and leaders. They did not need the missions, and they did not want to give up their own way of life. Many of them preferred to trade with the French. The East Texas missions struggled and, in time, closed.

section: Some peoples joined, others did not
text: 🌐 FOREIGN LANGUAGE VOCABULARY

section: Some peoples joined, others did not
text: **Caddo** (KAD-oh). A group of peoples who lived in East Texas and farmed the land.

section: Some peoples joined, others did not
text: And with the Comanche, the system failed completely. A mounted people who followed the **bison** could not be gathered into a mission. They had no reason to join, and a great deal of power to resist. Why the Comanche were so powerful is a story of its own.

section: Some peoples joined, others did not
text: Two more facts are worth noticing. Missions kept Native people near Spanish settlements, which made them a kind of shield against **raids**. And missions sometimes sheltered people who were fleeing war or enemies. A mission was never only a prison or only a refuge. It was a mixture, and different people experienced it differently.
📚 PART 4 · THE ONLY COLONISTS
Families from the Canary Islands

Spain had a hard time getting civilians to move to Texas. Almost nobody wanted to go. In 1731, the **Crown** paid for about fifteen families from the Canary Islands, off the coast of Africa, to cross the ocean and settle at San Antonio. They founded a town beside the presidio and mission. It was the only large group of civilian settlers Spain ever sent to Texas at its own expense.

Think about how those families must have felt. They left their homes on an island with green hills and rain, crossed the ocean, and then traveled across Mexico to a dry frontier far from anything they knew. They were promised land, special rights, and the chance to choose their own town leaders. They were also promised protection from raiders. The promises were easier to make than to keep.

That tells you how thin the Spanish effort really was. A system built on missions, soldiers, and a few dozen families could hold a few places. It could not fill a province. For that, Spain would have needed what it had in central Mexico: millions of people already living and working on the land.

A civilian town needed settlers who would stay. But few people wanted to move to a place with so little protection and so few rewards. Most of the people in Texas towns were soldiers' families, retired soldiers, and Native people who had left the missions. The plan for the town had always depended on a stream of settlers that never came.
💪 WHAT TO CARRY FORWARD

The mission, the presidio, and the pueblo were a clever plan. It worked where people already needed what it offered. Where they did not, it barely worked at all. It is fair to ask how much the plan actually produced, and the numbers are surprising.

📖 TODAY'S FOCUS
What do you do when the government that gave you permission no longer exists?

In 1821, Stephen F. Austin held a land **grant** from Spain. Then Spain lost Mexico, and the grant became a piece of paper from a government that was gone. This lesson follows Austin on a long trip to Mexico City, where he had to ask a brand new government to keep his father's promise.
