section: PART 1 A GRANT FROM A GOVERNMENT THAT WAS GONE
text: 📚 PART 1 · A GRANT FROM A GOVERNMENT THAT WAS GONE
Paper from the wrong government

In the summer of 1821, Stephen F. Austin rode into San Antonio with his father's grant in his hands. The Spanish governor welcomed him and agreed to honor it. Austin explored the land between the **Brazos** and **Colorado** rivers, chose a place for his colony, and went back to Louisiana to find **settlers**. By the end of that year, the first families were arriving.
🌐 FOREIGN LANGUAGE VOCABULARY
**Colorado** (kol-uh-RAD-oh). A river in Texas that flows to the Gulf of Mexico. It is not the Colorado River of the western mountains.
**Brazos** (BRAH-zus). A major river in Texas that flows to the Gulf of Mexico.

But the ground had shifted under him. In September 1821, Mexico won its **independence**, and Spain no longer ruled the land where Austin's settlers were building cabins. The grant had come from the king of Spain. A new country now owned Texas, and the new country had never agreed to anything. Austin's colony had no legal footing at all.

Austin could have waited and hoped that someone would notice him. He chose not to. If the new government did not **confirm** the grant, his settlers could lose their land, and he would lose the money he had spent. The only place to ask was the capital. In December 1821, he left for Mexico City, about a thousand miles away.
A long road

The trip took months. Austin crossed deserts and mountain passes, passed through towns where almost nobody had heard of Texas, and finally reached Mexico City on April 29, 1822. He did not speak Spanish well yet. He had no friends in the government. He carried a few letters of introduction and a great deal of patience.

The country itself was a hard place to cross. Roads were poor, and rivers flooded in the rainy season. Travelers had to watch for robbers on the lonely stretches. A trip that takes a day or two by car today took Austin about four months. Every mile of it reminded him how far Texas was from the people who would decide its future.

Think about how this looked from the capital. The leaders there had just won a war, and they were arguing about how to run a country. A request from an American to bring American families into Texas was a small matter next to those problems. Austin had to find a way to make his problem matter to people who already had many others.

section: PART 2 A YEAR IN A CITY IN TURMOIL
text: 📚 PART 2 · A YEAR IN A CITY IN TURMOIL
An emperor in the making

Austin arrived in the middle of a political crisis. The man who had led Mexico to independence was Agustín de **Iturbide**. Iturbide had many supporters in the army, but he did not get along with the **congress**. Mexico had no king, and nobody had agreed on what kind of government the country should have.
🌐 FOREIGN LANGUAGE VOCABULARY
**Iturbide** (ee-toor-BEE-deh). Agustín de Iturbide, a Spanish army officer who led the final push for Mexican independence.

On the night of May 18, 1822, soldiers and a crowd marched through the streets shouting for Iturbide to become **emperor**. The next day, congress voted to make him emperor while the crowd waited outside. Austin watched all of this from the city. In July, Iturbide was crowned in a ceremony that looked a lot like the courts of Europe.

Austin wrote letters about what he saw. He was surprised by how quickly power could shift and how much depended on friendships and favors. He could see that the new emperor's hold on the country was shaky. A leader who had won a war was learning that governing a country was a very different job.
Learning the game

Austin used his time well. He studied Spanish every day until he could read and write it with ease. He learned who held power in each office and who could be trusted. He paid calls on officials, waited in outer rooms, and came back again when he was told to return later. He had no other way to be heard.

Austin also met **Arizpe**, a priest and lawmaker from northern Mexico who had helped shape the idea of a **federal** **republic**. The two men talked about how the United States was governed. Austin translated the U.S. **Constitution** into Spanish for Arizpe. In return, Austin gained a friend who knew how Mexican lawmakers thought.
🌐 FOREIGN LANGUAGE VOCABULARY
**Arizpe** (ah-REES-peh). Miguel Ramos Arizpe, a priest and lawmaker from northern Mexico who helped shape the idea of a federal republic.

He also had to make himself useful. Officials wanted to know about the lands in the north, and Austin was one of the few people who had walked them. He answered questions, explained how a colony might help guard the **frontier**, and wrote out his requests with care. Slowly, officials who had ignored him began to listen.

Austin was far from home, and the colony he had started depended on whether his trip succeeded. His settlers waited without a clear answer, and some of them grew nervous. It took a lot of steadiness to stay in a strange city with no promise that the trip would work. Many people would have given up and gone home. Austin stayed.

section: PART 3 A LAW THAT FITTED HIS PLAN
text: 📚 PART 3 · A LAW THAT FITTED HIS PLAN
The Imperial Colonization Law

In early January 1823, Iturbide's government passed the Imperial Colonization Law. It was the first Mexican law to lay out how colonists could receive land in Texas. Austin had spent months talking with officials about what such a law should say, and many of its terms matched what he had asked for. The law offered land to families who would settle, and Austin's colony fit it well.

The law set aside land for each farmer and each rancher, and it rewarded the person who brought in the families. It also said that settlers had to obey Mexican law and practice the Catholic faith. These were the terms that Austin would use in his colony for years to come. He had not only won a favor. He had helped to shape the rules.

In February, the government confirmed Austin's grant under the new law. He had what he came for. His settlers would be allowed to stay, and he would be allowed to bring in more families. After nearly a year of waiting, a long trip, and many meetings, the colony stood on legal ground again.

There was one problem. The government that had confirmed Austin's grant was about to fall. Army officers were already turning against the emperor, and by March 1823 he would be forced to give up his throne. Austin's hard-won paper was signed by a ruler who would soon be gone. What happened next shaped the future of Texas.
What Austin learned

Austin came home with more than a signed paper. He had learned that Mexican governments could change quickly, and that the people he knew often mattered more than the rules written on paper. A friend in the right office was worth more than a clause in a law. He had also learned how little Mexico's leaders knew about Texas.

These were lessons that would shape the colony for years. Austin would keep careful ties with officials in the capital and in the state government. He would keep his people calm when news from the capital was bad. He would also make this long trip a second time, and it would go far worse.
💪 REMEMBER THIS QUESTION

Keep this question in mind: when a government falls, who keeps its promises? Austin found that the answer was whoever he could persuade, and that persuading people takes time, patience, and good friends.

💡 GLOSSARY OF SUBJECT VOCABULARY
A few words in this lesson are worth a look before you read. They show up in bold, and you can hover over any of them for a reminder.
**cannon** (KAN-un). A large gun on wheels that fires heavy metal balls.
**constitution** (kon-stih-TOO-shun). The basic written laws that set up a government and say what it can and cannot do.
**cover** (KUV-er). A place where a soldier can hide from enemy fire, such as a wall, a ditch, or a river bank.
**declaration** (dek-luh-RAY-shun). A formal public statement.
**enslave** (en-SLAYV). To force a person to work for you without pay or freedom.
**federal** (FED-er-ul). A system of government where power is shared between a national government and state governments.
**garrison** (GAIR-ih-sun). A group of soldiers stationed in a place to guard it.
**independence** (in-dih-PEN-dens). Freedom from the control of another country.
**mission** (MISH-un). A religious settlement where priests taught Native people the Christian faith.
**picket** (PIK-it). A guard post set out in front of an army to give early warning of danger.
**retreat** (rih-TREET). To pull back from a battle or a danger.
**settler** (SET-ler). A person who moves to a new place to live there for good.
**siege** (seej). When an army surrounds a place and tries to force it to give up.
**surrender** (suh-REN-der). To give up to an enemy.
**Texian** (TEK-see-un). A word used in the 1830s for a settler in Texas who came from the United States.
**volunteer** (vol-un-TEER). A person who joins an army by choice, not because of an order.
📖 TODAY'S FOCUS
Why did a few men stay in an old mission to face a huge army?

In the winter of 1836, about two hundred men gathered inside the walls of the **Alamo**, an old Spanish **mission** in San Antonio. A Mexican army of several thousand marched toward them. This lesson explains why the Alamo was held, who was inside, and why its defenders may not have known that Texas had declared **independence**.

📚 PART 1 · WHY HOLD THE ALAMO?
A fort at San Antonio

After the victory in December, most of the Texian army went home. A small garrison stayed in San Antonio, in the old mission chapel and walled yard that people called the Alamo. The place had thick walls, but they enclosed a very large space. It would take many men to defend it, and there were never enough.
🌐 FOREIGN LANGUAGE VOCABULARY
**Alamo** (AL-uh-moh). A former mission in San Antonio that was used as a fort in 1835 and 1836.
**Tejano** (teh-HAH-noh). A Texan of Mexican descent.
**Brazos** (BRAH-zus). A major river in Texas that flows to the Gulf of Mexico.

Think about the problem of defending the Alamo. Its walls enclosed about three acres, and the chapel and the long barracks were in poor repair. Fewer than two hundred men could not **cover** every wall at once. The defenders added **cannon** and patched the weak spots, but it was a poor place to stand against a big army.

In January, Sam Houston sent Jim Bowie to San Antonio with a task. He was to look over the Alamo and decide whether it could be held. If not, he was to pull out the cannon and blow up the walls. Bowie arrived, saw the place, and decided that it was worth saving.

On February 2, Bowie wrote to the governor, speaking for himself and Colonel Neill, the commander. He asked for men, money, and supplies. He wrote that they would rather die in these ditches than give up the post to the enemy. It was a strong sentence, and it showed how seriously the two men took the place.

Why was San Antonio so important? Many Texians thought of it as a **picket** guard, an outpost out in front of the army. A force there could slow an invading army and give the **settlers** farther east time to prepare. It was also a fort that Texians might use as a bargaining tool, since the Mexicans would want it back.
Leaders and volunteers

The garrison grew a little each week. Lieutenant Colonel William B. Travis came with a few dozen soldiers, and Davy Crockett arrived with **volunteers** from Tennessee. When Colonel Neill left to care for a sick family, Travis and Bowie agreed to share command. The two men were very different, and they did not always agree.

Not everyone inside was an American. A company of Tejanos, led by Juan **Seguín**, had joined the garrison. These Mexican-born Texans had fought for the **federal** **constitution**, and they lived in the area. For them, the Alamo was home. The defense of the Alamo was never a simple case of Americans against Mexicans.
🌐 FOREIGN LANGUAGE VOCABULARY
**Seguín** (seh-GEEN). Juan Seguín, a Tejano leader who raised a company of fighters for Texas.
📚 PART 2 · THE SIEGE
Thirteen days

On February 23, 1836, **Santa Anna** 's army arrived in San Antonio. The Texians had expected a longer wait. They hurried into the Alamo and raised a flag. Santa Anna ran up a red flag from the church tower in San Antonio. It meant that no mercy would be given. The siege began.
🌐 FOREIGN LANGUAGE VOCABULARY
**Santa Anna** (SAN-tah AH-nah). Antonio López de Santa Anna, a Mexican army officer who became one of the most powerful men in Mexico.

Santa Anna's army was large, but it was not all in San Antonio on the first day. More soldiers arrived over the following days. The army was also tired from a hard march through winter. Santa Anna had pushed his men fast to catch the Texians by surprise, and many of his soldiers were young recruits with little training.

On February 24, Travis wrote a letter to the people of Texas and all Americans in the world. He said that he was surrounded by a thousand or more Mexican soldiers, that he had been bombarded for twenty-four hours, and that he would never **surrender** or **retreat**. He asked for help. He signed it, "Victory or death."

That letter shows how Travis understood the siege. He was asking for men and he believed that help would come. Bowie fell seriously ill, and Travis commanded alone. Seguín was sent out of the fort with messages and slipped through the Mexican lines. The Texians waited, hoping that Colonel Fannin would arrive from **Goliad**.
🌐 FOREIGN LANGUAGE VOCABULARY
**Goliad** (GOH-lee-ad). A town on the San Antonio River with a Spanish fort and mission.

Fannin set out with his men and then turned back. A wagon broke, and he doubted whether he could reach the Alamo in time. On March 1, thirty-two volunteers from **Gonzales** slipped into the fort, and they were the last to arrive. After that, no more help came.
🌐 FOREIGN LANGUAGE VOCABULARY
**Gonzales** (gon-ZAL-es). A town in Texas where the first shots of the Texas Revolution were fired.

Think about the long days of the siege. Cannon fire fell on the walls daily. The defenders had little rest. Each morning they could see the army growing larger around them. They knew the odds. Yet they stayed, and their reasons were different. Some were fighting for Texas, some for their friends, and some for their own idea of honor.
The final assault

Early in the morning of March 6, Santa Anna ordered his soldiers to attack from all sides. The Texians fired as the Mexican columns came forward. The attackers reached the walls, climbed over, and opened the gates. By dawn it was over. Almost all of the defenders were dead, including Travis, Bowie, and Crockett.

Several women, children, and an **enslaved** man named Joe were allowed to leave. One woman, Susanna Dickinson, carried the news to the Texian army. Santa Anna wanted people to know what had happened, so that other Texians would be afraid. The effect was the opposite. The story did not frighten Texians into surrender. It made them angry.

section: PART 3 A DECLARATION THEY NEVER HEARD
text: 📚 PART 3 · A DECLARATION THEY NEVER HEARD
Independence at Washington-on-the-Brazos

During the siege, a convention was meeting in a rough building at the town of Washington-on-the-Brazos, about 150 miles away. On March 2, the delegates voted to declare independence from Mexico. Texas was no longer fighting for the Constitution of 1824. It was fighting to be a separate country.

Think about the delegates at Washington-on-the-Brazos. They worked in an unfinished building with no glass in the windows, in cold weather, while an army marched on their neighbors. They approved the **declaration** in a single day. They knew that it might cost them everything.

The Alamo's defenders almost certainly never learned of this. Messages took days to travel, and Mexican soldiers surrounded the fort. The men inside had come to defend a place, and perhaps a constitution. They died four days after independence was declared, without knowing that the war they were fighting had changed.

Because of this, historians are careful about what they say the defenders died for. We know they died for their friends, for the fort, and for the cause of Texas. We do not know what each man believed about independence. That uncertainty is part of what makes the story so human.

Out of the loss, a rallying cry arose. Within weeks, Texian soldiers were shouting, "Remember the Alamo!" It would help turn grief into resolve. The Alamo did not win the war. But it bought time, it cost the Mexican army many soldiers, and it showed Texians what the war was costing.
💪 REMEMBER THIS QUESTION
Keep one question in mind: how should we describe what people fought for when they did not know all that had changed around them?

section: Can a general win a war by running away?
text: After the **Alamo** and **Goliad**, the **Texian** cause seemed lost. **Santa Anna** had a large army and Texas had a small one. For six weeks, General Sam Houston **retreated** east, while thousands of **settlers** fled before him. Then, in a single afternoon, everything changed. This lesson follows that long retreat and the eighteen minutes that ended the war.

📚 PART 1 · THE LONG RETREAT
The Runaway Scrape

When news of the Alamo reached the Texian settlements, panic spread. Families loaded wagons, gathered children, and set out east toward the Louisiana border. Rain had turned the roads to mud, rivers were swollen, and many people walked. The flight was called the Runaway Scrape, and thousands took part.
🌐 FOREIGN LANGUAGE VOCABULARY
**Santa Anna** (SAN-tah AH-nah). Antonio López de Santa Anna, a Mexican army officer who became one of the most powerful men in Mexico.
**Goliad** (GOH-lee-ad). A town on the San Antonio River with a Spanish fort and mission.
**Alamo** (AL-uh-moh). A former mission in San Antonio that was used as a fort in 1835 and 1836.
**San Jacinto** (san hah-SIN-toh). A river and a battlefield on the coastal plain of Texas, near the modern city of Houston.

The Texian army was only a few hundred men when Houston took command in March. He pulled back from **Gonzales** and began to march east, with the Mexican army behind him. The government of the new **republic** also fled, first to Harrisburg and then to Galveston Island. Texas was losing its homes and its capital at once.
🌐 FOREIGN LANGUAGE VOCABULARY
**Gonzales** (gon-ZAL-es). A town in Texas where the first shots of the Texas Revolution were fired.

Think about what this looked like to the people who were running. They had heard that the Alamo had fallen and that Goliad had been a slaughter. They had no army that seemed able to protect them. Many of them cursed Houston for retreating when he should have been fighting.

Houston heard the complaints. Government officials urged him to stop and fight, and his own soldiers grew restless. Some officers talked of choosing a new general. Houston held on to his command and kept moving, because he believed that one battle lost would end Texas for good.
Houston's reasons

Houston had a plan, or at least he said so later. Texas had one army. If he risked it in an open fight against a larger force, as Fannin had done, and lost, there would be nothing left. He wanted to gather strength, train his men, and wait until Santa Anna made a mistake.

He also knew that Santa Anna had divided his army. The Mexican general had sent columns in several directions to chase settlers and the Texian government. Each column was weaker than the whole, and each moved farther from supplies. Time, Houston believed, was working against the army that was far from home.

At Groce's plantation on the **Brazos**, Houston stopped for almost two weeks. His men drilled, rested, and received two small **cannon**, a gift from the people of Cincinnati, Ohio, called the Twin Sisters. Reinforcements arrived. When he finally marched, his army numbered around nine hundred.
🌐 FOREIGN LANGUAGE VOCABULARY
**Brazos** (BRAH-zus). A major river in Texas that flows to the Gulf of Mexico.
📚 PART 2 · THE BATTLE
Santa Anna overreaches

Think about what the time at Groce's plantation did. Many of Houston's men had never drilled together. They learned to march, to load in order, and to hold their fire until they were told. That discipline would matter when they crossed the meadow at San Jacinto, because a ragged charge would have broken under the Mexican guns.

In mid-April, Santa Anna pushed ahead with a small, fast force, hoping to catch the Texian government and end the war at once. He burned the town of Harrisburg, found the government gone, and then learned that Houston's army was close by. He had outrun his supplies and most of his own army.

Houston turned toward him. On April 19, the Texians reached a spot where Buffalo **Bayou** meets the San Jacinto River. Santa Anna made camp on a low piece of ground with **marsh** behind him and the bayou on one side. It was a poor place to fight, though he did not seem to see it.

Reinforcements reached Santa Anna on the morning of April 21, which raised his force to about 1,300 men. Houston had a few hundred fewer. But that morning, a **scout** destroyed the only bridge across the bayou behind Santa Anna's camp. Now neither army could easily escape, and Houston knew where the fight would take place.
Eighteen minutes

The Mexican soldiers were resting in the afternoon sun when the Texians attacked at about half past four. They came across a long meadow, holding their fire until they were close. Then they poured volleys into the camp, and ran forward shouting, "Remember the Alamo! Remember Goliad!"

The Mexican army was caught off guard. Many soldiers had no time to form a line. Officers shouted orders that nobody heard. The soldiers who tried to run found the marsh behind them and the bayou beside them. There was no room for the **cavalry** to maneuver and no way for anyone to retreat.

Anger drove many of the Texian soldiers. Some had friends or relatives who had died at the Alamo and Goliad. They fought with a fury that was hard to control, and some of them kept on killing after the battle was won. Houston and other officers tried to stop it, with mixed success.

The main fight lasted about eighteen minutes. After that, the Texians pursued the survivors across the plain. Hundreds of Mexican soldiers were killed, and hundreds more were taken prisoner. The Texians lost fewer than a dozen men. It was one of the most lopsided victories in American history.

The next day, soldiers found a man hiding in the grass, dressed in a plain private's coat. When the prisoners saw him, some called him "El Presidente." It was Santa Anna. The president of Mexico was now a **captive**, and the war was almost over.
📚 PART 3 · WEIGHING THE ACCOUNTS
Why this ground?

Look at what the ground at San Jacinto did. Mexican cavalry, so dangerous at **Coleto** Creek, could not use its speed in a marsh. Mexican soldiers could not form the lines that made their **muskets** deadly. And no one could run away, because the bridge was gone. The place took away every advantage the Mexican army had.
🌐 FOREIGN LANGUAGE VOCABULARY
**Coleto** (koh-LEH-toh). A creek near Goliad where Fannin and his men were caught in open country.

Houston did not simply rely on luck. He picked the moment and the place, he held his men back until they were close, and he used the surprise of a late-day attack. But luck was also on his side. If Santa Anna had camped on higher ground, or if his other columns had been closer, the result could have been very different.
Houston and his critics

Historians still weigh Houston's own account of the campaign. In his official report, he describes a careful plan. He retreated to gain strength, then struck when the moment came. His supporters say that it was the only way to win, and that his patience saved Texas.

His critics see it differently. They say that he did not plan a battle at San Jacinto from the start, and that he nearly lost his army through delay. They argue that the retreat cost homes and lives, and that he was lucky that Santa Anna made mistakes. A report written by the victor will always try to make the victory look inevitable.

A careful reader will keep both views in mind. Houston showed real strengths: he kept his army together, he refused to be rushed, and he fought at the right time. He also took risks, and he benefited from enemy errors. Good history shows how a hard choice looked at the time, not just how it looked afterward.
💪 REMEMBER THIS QUESTION
Keep one question in mind: how much of a great victory comes from a leader's plan, and how much from the mistakes of the other side?

A few words in this lesson are worth a look before you read. They show up in bold, and you can hover over any of them for a reminder.
**bankrupt** (BANK-rupt). Unable to pay what you owe.
**caracole** (KAIR-uh-kohl). A cavalry move in which riders gallop up, fire a pistol, and wheel away to reload.
**cavalry** (KAV-ul-ree). Soldiers who fight on horseback.
**dragoon** (druh-GOON). A soldier who rides a horse to the battle but gets off to fight on foot.
**empire** (EM-pyr). A large area of land and many peoples ruled by one government.
**frontier** (frun-TEER). The edge of settled land, where a country meets wild or unclaimed country.
**patent** (PAT-ent). An official paper that gives an inventor the sole right to make and sell an invention.
**republic** (rih-PUB-lik). A country ruled by elected leaders instead of a king.
**revolver** (rih-VOL-ver). A pistol with a spinning cylinder that holds several bullets and can fire many shots without reloading.
**rifle** (RY-ful). A gun with grooves inside the barrel that make it much more accurate at long range.
**scout** (skowt). A person sent ahead to learn where the enemy is and what the land is like.
**settler** (SET-ler). A person who moves to a new place to live there for good.
**skirmish** (SKUR-ish). A small fight between small groups of soldiers.
**treaty** (TREE-tee). A written agreement between countries.
📖 TODAY'S FOCUS
How did a failed invention from New Jersey change the war on the Texas frontier?

In 1836, a young inventor named Samuel Colt **patented** a gun that could fire several shots without reloading. Almost nobody wanted it. His company went **bankrupt**. But a few Texas Rangers with these pistols changed the way the **frontier** was fought, and gave Colt a second chance. This lesson follows how it happened.

📚 PART 1 · A GUN NOBODY WANTED
Colt's invention

Samuel Colt was a young man from Connecticut with an idea. He designed a pistol with a rotating cylinder, so that the shooter could fire five or six times without stopping to reload. In 1836, he received a patent, and he started a company in Paterson, New Jersey, to make the new weapon.
🌐 FOREIGN LANGUAGE VOCABULARY
**Comanche** (kuh-MAN-chee). A people who became the strongest power on the southern plains in the 1700s.

The invention was clever, but Americans did not rush to buy it. Army officers thought that it was too delicate for a battlefield. Ordinary buyers found it expensive. Colt could not find enough customers, and his company went bankrupt in 1842. For a time, it looked as if the revolver would be forgotten.

Think about how often a good idea fails at first. The revolver worked. But the people who might have used it did not yet see the need, and the people who understood the need did not yet know about it. The idea needed the right problem to make its worth plain.
The Navy's pistols

The **Republic** of Texas did buy some of the pistols. In 1839, the Texas Navy ordered a large number of Colt revolvers for its sailors. The navy was in trouble, though. It had little money, and its ships were poorly supplied. By the early 1840s, the navy was mostly laid up in port.

That left a stock of unused revolvers in storage. The pistols were passed along to the Texas Rangers, a force of mounted riflemen who guarded the frontier. The Rangers were not soldiers by training. They were men who knew the country and could ride and shoot. And they had a problem that the revolver was made to solve.
📚 PART 2 · THE RANGERS

section: Jack Hays and the fight at Walker's Creek
text: Jack Hays and the fight at Walker's Creek

section: Jack Hays and the fight at Walker's Creek
text: The Texas Rangers began as small groups of armed men who watched the frontier for danger. Over time, some companies became permanent, and the best ones had leaders who learned the country and its enemies. One of these leaders was Captain Jack Hays, a slender young man who commanded a company based near San Antonio.

section: Jack Hays and the fight at Walker's Creek
text: In June 1844, Hays was riding with about fifteen Rangers when a much larger band of Comanche, perhaps seventy warriors, came upon them in the hills along the upper Guadalupe River. In the past, a party that small would have run or dismounted and formed a tight circle. Hays did neither. He ordered his men to charge.

section: Jack Hays and the fight at Walker's Creek
text: The Rangers fought from the saddle, firing their five-shot revolvers as they rode. Each man could fire several times before the Comanche could close the gap. The warriors, who had expected single-shot guns and a pause to reload, found themselves facing rapid fire. They broke and fled with heavy losses.

section: Jack Hays and the fight at Walker's Creek
text: Samuel Walker, one of the Rangers, wrote about the fight to Colt. The battle was fought near a stream that came to be called Walker's Creek. The story spread through Texas and then beyond. A company of fifteen men had beaten a force of seventy, with weapons that most people had written off.

section: Why this had never worked before
text: Why this had never worked before

section: Why this had never worked before
text: To see why this was so surprising, look at how cavalry fought in earlier centuries. Horsemen with pistols had tried a move called the **caracole**. They would gallop toward the enemy, fire a shot, and wheel away to reload. The idea sounds good, but it never worked well. A single shot was not worth giving up the force of a charge.

section: Why this had never worked before
text: Think about the problem from the Comanche side. A Comanche rider had already solved it with the bow. He could shoot while charging, and he could shoot many times. In the revolver, the Rangers had found a tool that matched what the best mounted warriors on the plains had done for generations.

section: Why this had never worked before
text: Armies tried other plans. **Dragoons** rode horses to a fight, then got off and fought on foot like infantry. That used the horse for travel but not for battle. Against a mounted enemy that could circle and strike, a soldier on foot was at a disadvantage. The old problem remained.

section: Why this had never worked before
text: The revolver changed the math. With five or six shots ready, a rider could fire, keep charging, and fire again. He no longer had to choose between speed and firepower. A man on a horse could now do what the Comanche had long done, and he could do it with a gun.

section: PART 3 FROM A CREEK BED TO AN EMPIRE
text: 📚 PART 3 · FROM A CREEK BED TO AN EMPIRE
The Walker Colt

Samuel Walker later met Colt and told him what the Rangers wanted. They needed a heavier, stronger pistol that could be carried in a saddle holster. Together, Walker and Colt designed a new model in 1847, which was called the Walker Colt. It was a large and powerful weapon.

The United States Army was fighting a war with Mexico, and it ordered a thousand of the new pistols. The order saved Colt's business. He opened a new factory in Connecticut, and the Colt company grew into one of the best-known gunmakers in the world. His **empire** began with a **skirmish** in a Texas creek bed.

Notice how this story connects a failed inventor, a poor navy, and a few brave riders. No one planned it. The revolver found its use because of a danger that Texas faced, and the danger found an answer because a few Rangers took a chance on a weapon that was out of favor.

section: Scouts, councils, and a new policy
text: Scouts, councils, and a new policy

section: Scouts, councils, and a new policy
text: The Rangers did not fight alone. **Tonkawa** **scouts** guided them through the country and warned them of danger. The Tonkawa were old enemies of the Comanche, and they were glad to join a force that fought them. A scout who knew every trail was worth as much as a **rifle**.

section: Scouts, councils, and a new policy
text: 🌐 FOREIGN LANGUAGE VOCABULARY

section: Scouts, councils, and a new policy
text: **Tonkawa** (TONG-kuh-wah). A Native people of central Texas who were enemies of the Comanche and allies of the Texans.

section: Scouts, councils, and a new policy
text: Meanwhile, Houston had returned to the presidency in 1841, and he reversed Lamar's policy. He sought peace with Native peoples, and in 1843 and 1844 he held councils with leaders of many groups at a place called **Tehuacana** Creek. The **Waco** and others sent delegates, and some agreed to **treaties**.

section: Scouts, councils, and a new policy
text: 🌐 FOREIGN LANGUAGE VOCABULARY

section: Scouts, councils, and a new policy
text: **Tehuacana** (tay-wah-KAH-nah). A creek in central Texas where councils with Native peoples were held in the 1840s.

section: Scouts, councils, and a new policy
text: **Waco** (WAY-koh). A Native people of the Wichita family who lived along the Brazos River.

section: Scouts, councils, and a new policy
text: Ranger life was hard. Men rode for days with little food, slept on the ground, and risked death in every fight. They were paid little, and most of them supplied their own horses and guns. Yet young men eagerly joined, because the Rangers had a reputation and a sense of purpose.

section: Scouts, councils, and a new policy
text: These councils did not end the fighting. Many Comanche refused to come, and **settlers** kept moving onto Native land. But the combination of talks, scouts, and mounted Rangers with revolvers began to change the balance. By the end of the 1840s, the settlers on the frontier were safer than they had been.
💪 REMEMBER THIS QUESTION
Keep one question in mind: why do good inventions sometimes wait for the right moment? The revolver waited for a frontier that needed it.

💡 GLOSSARY OF SUBJECT VOCABULARY
A few words in this lesson are worth a look before you read. They show up in bold, and you can hover over any of them for a reminder.
**abandon** (uh-BAN-dun). To leave a place or a project for good.
**colony** (KAH-luh-nee). A place settled and controlled by people from a faraway country.
**escarpment** (es-KARP-ment). A long, steep slope between higher ground and lower ground.
**expedition** (eks-pih-DISH-un). A long trip taken for a purpose, such as exploring or conquering.
**mission** (MISH-un). A religious settlement where priests taught Native people the Christian faith.
**raid** (rayd). A sudden attack made to take goods, animals, or captives.
**rival** (RY-vul). A person or country that competes against another.
**settler** (SET-ler). A person who moves to a new place to live there for good.
📖 TODAY'S FOCUS
Spain ignored Texas for 140 years. Then a French ship ran aground in the wrong bay.

When Spain heard about Fort St. Louis, officials in Mexico City were alarmed. A French **colony** on the Gulf coast could threaten Spain's silver mines. So Spain did something it had not done in almost a century and a half. It began to settle Texas. This lesson follows that rushed effort, from the first **missions** to the founding of San Antonio.

📚 PART 1 · PANIC IN MEXICO CITY
Hunting for the French

Spanish officials heard about the French colony in 1685. They sent ships to search the coast, and then they sent soldiers overland. A governor named **de León** led several **expeditions** north from Mexico. In 1689, he found what was left of Fort St. Louis. The buildings were burned and the ground was littered with bones. The French were gone, and the **rival** colony was dead.

Spain's silver mines in northern Mexico were its richest source of income. A French fort within reach of those mines was a serious danger. Spanish officials also feared that the French would join Native peoples against Spain. For more than a century, Texas had seemed like a useless backwater. Now it looked like a doorway into the heart of New Spain.

A king has to think about what could happen, not only what has happened. The French had not attacked Mexico. But a fort so near to Spanish lands could become a base for **raiders** and for trade with Native peoples. Spain did not know how many ships France might send next. Spanish leaders chose to treat the danger as real, and they spent money to deal with it.

But Spain was not reassured. If the French could land in Texas once, they could do it again. The Spanish government decided that the safest way to hold Texas was to settle it. A claim on paper was not enough.
🌐 FOREIGN LANGUAGE VOCABULARY
**de León** (deh leh-OHN). Alonso de León, a Spanish officer who led expeditions into Texas to find the French colony.
📚 PART 2 · THE FIRST MISSIONS
East Texas, 1690

The Spanish plan was to build missions among the **Caddo** of East Texas. In 1690, a priest named **Massanet** helped found the first one. The Caddo greeted the Spaniards by saying a word that sounded like " **Tejas**," which means "friends." The Spaniards began using it as the name of the land, and it became Texas.
🌐 FOREIGN LANGUAGE VOCABULARY
**Massanet** (mah-sah-NET). Damián Massanet, a Spanish priest who helped found the first East Texas mission.
**Tejas** (TAY-hahs). A Caddo word meaning "friends." The Spaniards used it, and it became the name Texas.
**Caddo** (KAD-oh). A group of peoples who lived in East Texas and farmed the land.

The mission did not last. Sickness spread through the Caddo villages, and many people died. Some blamed the priests. A drought hurt the crops. Soldiers were too few to help. By 1693, the Spaniards chose to **abandon** the missions, and they buried their bell and left. Texas was empty of Spaniards again.

Looking back, the first mission shows what the Spanish model needed. The priests had no way to force the Caddo to stay or to listen. The Caddo had farms, villages, and leaders, and the Spaniards depended on them for food. When the mission lost the trust of the Caddo, it had no power to hold on.

Notice that nobody planned this outcome. Spain did not set out to lose the missions, and the Caddo did not set out to push the priests away. Disease, drought, and distance did much of the work. A different year, with better rain and fewer deaths, might have made the missions last longer, and the story of Texas could have gone another way.
📚 PART 3 · THE FRENCH NEXT DOOR
Trade against religion

Spain was gone, but France was not. In 1714, a French trader named **St. Denis** set up a trading post at **Natchitoches**, on the Red River, just across the likely border. He traded cloth, tools, and guns to the Caddo. Then he traveled all the way to the **Rio Grande**, where Spanish officials arrested him. Later they used his knowledge to guide a new expedition back into East Texas.
🌐 FOREIGN LANGUAGE VOCABULARY
**Rio Grande** (REE-oh GRAHN-day). The great river that flows between Texas and Mexico to the Gulf of Mexico.

The story of St. Denis shows how different the two models were. He was a trader, not a conqueror, and he made friends easily. He also fell in love with the granddaughter of a Spanish commander, and the two later married. A Spanish soldier at a mission could hardly match that kind of welcome.
🌐 FOREIGN LANGUAGE VOCABULARY
**Natchitoches** (NAK-uh-tish). A French trading post on the Red River, founded in 1714. It is now a town in Louisiana.
**St. Denis** (san deh-NEE). Louis Juchereau de St. Denis, a French trader who worked in Louisiana and Texas.

St. Denis also shows how much one person's choices could matter. He crossed borders that were supposed to be closed, he learned the languages of the people he met, and he knew how to make a friend. A different trader might have been caught and forgotten. Because of him, Spanish officials learned how close the French were and how much they had to lose.

This was the French model working beside the Spanish model. The French offered trade. The Spaniards offered a new religion and a place to live under priests. Many Caddo people preferred the French goods, especially guns. In 1716, Spain founded new missions in East Texas, but they depended on supplies from far away, and the French trading post stayed busy.

This time Spain brought soldiers and more supplies, but the old problem remained. The East Texas missions were hundreds of miles from the nearest Spanish town of any size. Supplies came slowly over rough roads. Every cart that broke down or river that flooded meant hunger. Spain needed a closer, steadier base between the Rio Grande and the Caddo country.
📚 PART 4 · SAN ANTONIO, 1718
Building on the springs

Spain needed a base between the Rio Grande and East Texas. In 1718, it chose a place where a river and a series of springs came out of the ground. A mission was built there, and next to it a **fort** (*presidio*) to protect it. The settlement was called San Antonio de **Béxar**. It is the city of San Antonio today.
🌐 FOREIGN LANGUAGE VOCABULARY
**presidio** (preh-SEE-dee-oh). A Spanish fort where soldiers lived and guarded the frontier.
**Béxar** (BEH-har). The Spanish name for the settlement at San Antonio.

Why there? Water. West of that spot, a long **escarpment** rises across Texas. At its base, water flows out of the rock in springs. Springs mark a line across the country, and towns like San Antonio, San Marcos, and Austin sit along it. Spanish **settlers** needed water for crops, and the springs offered the best supply for hundreds of miles.

The springs gave more than water. A river valley with water, wood, and good soil could support crops and cattle. Open grassland nearby gave horses and cattle plenty to eat. The mission, the fort, and later the town all drew on the same water, and they shared it through ditches.

A base like this also needed people. Soldiers and their families came north from Mexico to make the place a real town. It was slow work. The settlers had to dig ditches, build houses, and plant fields before they could eat. Texas gave them water, but nothing else came easily.

San Antonio became the center of Spanish Texas. But notice what it was. It was a base built in a hurry, as a defense against a rival. Spain had not found anything in Texas worth the cost. It had come because of a French ship.
💪 WHAT TO CARRY FORWARD

Spain came to Texas because it was afraid, not because it saw riches. That helps explain why its effort stayed so thin. Settling a land to defend it is very different from settling a land to profit from it.

💡 GLOSSARY OF SUBJECT VOCABULARY
A few words in this lesson are worth a look before you read. They show up in bold, and you can hover over any of them for a reminder.
**bayou** (BY-oo). A slow, muddy stream in flat, wet country.
**colony** (KAH-luh-nee). A place settled and controlled by people from a faraway country.
**constitution** (kon-stih-TOO-shun). The basic written laws that set up a government and say what it can and cannot do.
**federal** (FED-er-ul). A system of government where power is shared between a national government and state governments.
**independence** (in-dih-PEN-dens). Freedom from the control of another country.
**jury** (JOOR-ee). A group of citizens who listen to a court case and decide who is right.
**petition** (peh-TISH-un). A formal request, often made to a government.
**reform** (rih-FORM). A change made to fix or improve a system.
**regulation** (reg-yoo-LAY-shun). An official rule.
**repeal** (rih-PEEL). To cancel a law.
**resolution** (rez-uh-LOO-shun). A formal statement of what a group has decided or wants.
**settler** (SET-ler). A person who moves to a new place to live there for good.
**statehood** (STAYT-hood). Being a full state with its own government inside a larger country.
**tariff** (TAIR-if). A tax on goods that are brought into a country.
📖 TODAY'S FOCUS
What do you do when a government decides that your success is a danger?

By the late 1820s, thousands of American **settlers** lived in Texas, and Mexico City began to worry. A general was sent to see the situation, and his report frightened the government into new laws. This lesson follows how those laws, and the quarrels that came after them, pushed Texas and Mexico apart.

section: PART 1 A GENERAL LOOKS AT TEXAS
text: 📚 PART 1 · A GENERAL LOOKS AT TEXAS
The inspection of 1828

In 1828, the Mexican government sent General **Mier** y Terán to inspect the border with the United States. He was a careful man, trained as a scientist and an engineer. He traveled through Texas for months, counting people, measuring land, and talking with settlers and with Native peoples. He wrote down what he saw.
🌐 FOREIGN LANGUAGE VOCABULARY
**Mier y Terán** (mee-AIR ee teh-RAHN). Manuel de Mier y Terán, a Mexican general and scientist who inspected Texas in 1828.
**Mier** (mee-AIR). A Mexican town on the Rio Grande where a Texan force was captured in 1842.

What he saw alarmed him. American settlers far outnumbered Mexicans in East Texas. They spoke English, followed American customs, and kept in close touch with the United States. Many of them knew little about Mexican law and cared less. Mier y Terán feared that Mexico might lose Texas without a shot being fired.

His own feelings were mixed. Mier y Terán admired the energy of the settlers and praised the richness of the land. He saw clearly that Texas could become wealthy, and that was part of the danger. A rich land full of people who looked north toward the United States was a prize that another country might someday want.

His report suggested several remedies. Mexico should put soldiers and forts in key places. It should bring in Mexican and European families to settle the land. It should encourage trade between Texas and the rest of Mexico instead of with the United States. In short, Mexico should act before the situation grew worse.

Think about how this looked from the capital. To officials in Mexico City, the settlers were guests who had been invited for a purpose. Now a respected general said that the guests outnumbered their hosts and might not leave. The report did not call for war, but it left leaders deeply uneasy.
The Law of April 6, 1830

In April 1830, President **Bustamante** 's government passed a law based on those fears. It said that no more settlers from the United States could come into Texas. It called for new forts and soldiers along the coast and the border. And it said that Mexico would collect its customs, which are taxes on goods brought into the country.
🌐 FOREIGN LANGUAGE VOCABULARY
**Bustamante** (boos-tah-MAHN-teh). Anastasio Bustamante, the Mexican president whose government passed the Law of April 6, 1830.

The law did not push out the settlers who already lived in Texas, and Austin worked to make sure that his **colony** 's contracts stayed in force. But the message was clear. Mexico City no longer trusted the colonists. Families who had planned to join relatives in Texas now found the road closed.

Settlers resented the law for several reasons. They felt that it treated them as suspects instead of neighbors. The soldiers sent to enforce it were often convicts or poorly paid men who caused trouble. And the **tariffs** hurt farmers who depended on imported tools and supplies. A government that seemed to be pulling away was creating the very distance it feared.
📚 PART 2 · TROUBLE AT ANAHUAC
A fort on the bay

One of the new forts stood at **Anahuac**, a small port on Galveston Bay. It had a customs house, and the officer in charge was Colonel Bradburn. Bradburn was strict about the rules. Settlers who shipped goods through the port had to pay taxes and follow **regulations** that they thought were unfair.
🌐 FOREIGN LANGUAGE VOCABULARY
**Anahuac** (AN-uh-wak). A small port on Galveston Bay where Mexico built a fort and a customs house.

Think about what a customs house meant for a settler. In earlier years, ships had come and gone with very little interference. Now each cargo had to be counted, taxed, and approved by an officer who spoke another language. Farmers who had learned to expect little from their government suddenly felt it at every dock.

Tempers rose in 1832. Bradburn arrested a young lawyer named William B. Travis and another settler, and he refused to let them go. Neighbors gathered and marched on the fort. For some weeks the two sides faced each other, and there was a real danger of a fight.

The settlers wrote a statement, called the Turtle **Bayou** **Resolutions**, to explain what they were doing. They did not say that they were rebelling against Mexico. They said that they supported General **Santa Anna**, who had risen against President Bustamante and claimed to be fighting for the **federal** **constitution** of 1824. They presented themselves as defenders of the real Mexico.
🌐 FOREIGN LANGUAGE VOCABULARY
**Santa Anna** (SAN-tah AH-nah). Antonio López de Santa Anna, a Mexican army officer who became one of the most powerful men in Mexico.

This was a clever and sincere move. A rebel against the government is a rebel. But a defender of the constitution has the law on his side. The settlers wanted to show that their quarrel was with one officer and one unfair law, and not with Mexico. Soon, Mexican army officers in Texas gave in, and Bradburn left.

section: PART 3 WHAT THE CONVENTIONS ASKED FOR
text: 📚 PART 3 · WHAT THE CONVENTIONS ASKED FOR
Two meetings at San Felipe

After Anahuac, Texans decided to speak with one voice. In October 1832, delegates from across the colonies met at **San Felipe** for a convention, and Austin helped lead it. Six months later, in April 1833, they met again. Delegates wrote **petitions** to the Mexican government and chose men to carry them south.
🌐 FOREIGN LANGUAGE VOCABULARY
**San Felipe** (sahn feh-LEE-peh). San Felipe de Austin, the main town of Austin's colony, on the Brazos River.

It helps to read what they actually asked. They did not ask for **independence**. They asked for **statehood** inside Mexico, so that Texas would no longer be tied to **Coahuila**. They asked Mexico to **repeal** the Law of April 6, so that families could come again. They asked for relief from the tariffs. And they asked for trial by **jury**.
🌐 FOREIGN LANGUAGE VOCABULARY
**Coahuila** (koh-ah-WEE-lah). A state in northern Mexico that was joined to Texas in 1824.

Each of these requests was a request to be treated as a full and equal part of Mexico. Texans did not claim anything that the constitution of 1824 did not seem to offer. Notice how reasonable the list is. A people planning to break away would not likely spend its time asking for mail service and court **reform**.

But Mexico City was not an easy audience. The government had many other problems, and it saw the Texans through the eyes of General Mier y Terán's report. The more Texans argued that they were loyal, the more some officials suspected that they were bargaining. Each side believed that the other was not fully honest, and trust was running out.
A gap that kept widening

By 1833, two stories were being told. In one, Texas was a loyal and patient part of Mexico that asked only for what the constitution promised. In the other, Texas was a growing foreign colony that would someday demand to leave. Both stories contained some truth, and both led to action.

Think about how each side read the same events. A Mexican officer saw armed crowds marching on a fort. A settler saw citizens defending a neighbor from an unlawful arrest. Neither view was foolish. The sadness of these years is that each side had good reasons to be afraid.

Austin, as always, chose patience. He packed the petitions and set out for Mexico City, determined to explain what Texans wanted and to remove the doubts. His journey would take him to the center of Mexican power, and it would not end the way that he hoped.
💪 REMEMBER THIS QUESTION
Keep one question in mind: how can two groups, each sure of its own good faith, drift into distrust? The years from 1828 to 1833 show how it can happen.

section: Why did a country that won its independence give it up?
text: For nine years, Texas was a nation of its own. Then, in 1845, it joined the United States. This lesson follows the failed **treaty**, the election that decided the question, the terms of annexation, and the one problem that was left unsolved: where the border of Texas lay.

📚 PART 1 · A TREATY THAT FAILED
Tyler and the Senate

By 1844, President John Tyler of the United States wanted to **annex** Texas. He believed that it would help his country, and it would help him win a second term. His secretary of state, John C. Calhoun, worked out an agreement with the **Republic**. On April 12, 1844, the two sides signed an annexation treaty.

A treaty with another country needs two thirds of the **Senate** to approve it. Tyler did not have the votes. Many senators from the North opposed adding a new slave state. Others feared a war with Mexico. And some thought that the whole matter was being rushed for political reasons.

Calhoun made things worse. In a letter to the British minister, he defended slavery, and the letter was published. Many Northerners were disgusted, and it turned a debate about land into a debate about slavery. It became harder for senators from the North to vote yes.

In June 1844, the Senate rejected the treaty by a wide margin. It looked as if annexation was dead. Texans, who had hoped to join the United States for years, were disappointed. Some began to think again about staying independent and making deals with Britain and France.
An election that settled it

But the matter was not over. The presidential election of 1844 was only a few months away, and annexation became one of its main issues. Henry Clay, the Whig candidate, tried to avoid the question. James K. Polk, the Democrat, said plainly that he wanted Texas to join the Union.

Polk won, and by a small margin. Many Americans, especially in the South and West, read his victory as a sign that the country wanted to grow. Tyler, who was about to leave office, took the result as a green light. He decided to try again, using a different method.

Think about how elections shape history. A small number of votes in a few states decided the next president. And the next president's views decided whether Texas would join the nation. No treaty, no battle, and no speech had been as powerful as that single election.
📚 PART 2 · THE JOINT RESOLUTION
A second way in

Tyler's new plan did not need a treaty. Instead, **Congress** would pass a joint **resolution**, which is a kind of law that needs only a majority in each house. Supporters could count on a majority more easily than on two thirds. In early 1845, both houses voted yes.

President Tyler signed the resolution on March 1, 1845, just days before leaving office. It offered Texas a place in the Union. But the offer was only an offer. Texas had to accept it. The people of the Republic would have to decide whether to give up their **independence**.

That decision was not simple. The government of Texas had also received an offer from Mexico, backed by Britain and France. Mexico would recognize Texas as independent, if Texas agreed not to join the United States. Some Texas leaders weighed the offer carefully. But most voters wanted to join the Union.
Texas says yes

In the summer of 1845, a convention met in Austin. On July 4, it voted to accept the American offer. In October, Texas voters approved the new **constitution** for a state. In December, President Polk signed the bill that made Texas the twenty-eighth state of the Union.

Notice how many hands it took. The United States Congress made an offer. The Republic's president, Anson Jones, called a convention, and the Texas Congress also had to vote. Then the voters had to approve the new constitution. A change that large needed many people to agree, and each of them had a chance to say no.

The terms were unusual. Texas kept its public lands, which it could use to pay its **debts**. It also kept its public debt, so the United States did not have to pay for it. And Texas kept the right to divide itself, later on, into as many as five states.

Slavery was part of the deal, too. The resolution said that in any states carved out of Texas north of a certain line, slavery would be banned. South of the line, slavery would be allowed. It was a compromise that reflected the deep split in the country over slavery.

Look at what Texas gained and what it gave up. It gave up its flag, its president, and its place as a separate nation. It gained safety, a market for its cotton, and the strength of a larger country. For many Texans, it was a good trade. For Mexico, it was a threat.

section: PART 3 A BORDER WITHOUT A LINE
text: 📚 PART 3 · A BORDER WITHOUT A LINE
Nueces or Rio Grande?

The resolution left one question open. Where did Texas end? Texas claimed that its southern border was the **Rio Grande**, as the Republic's Congress had declared in 1836. Mexico said that the border was the **Nueces** River, a good distance to the north.
🌐 FOREIGN LANGUAGE VOCABULARY
**Rio Grande** (REE-oh GRAHN-day). The great river that flows between Texas and Mexico to the Gulf of Mexico.
**Nueces** (noo-AY-ses). A river in South Texas that Mexico said was the southern border of Texas.

Each side had a case. Mexico pointed out that, under Spanish and Mexican rule, the Nueces had marked the edge of the **province** of Texas. Texas pointed to its own law and to the treaty signed by **Santa Anna** at **Velasco**. Neither argument settled anything, since each side had already decided what it believed.
🌐 FOREIGN LANGUAGE VOCABULARY
**Santa Anna** (SAN-tah AH-nah). Antonio López de Santa Anna, a Mexican army officer who became one of the most powerful men in Mexico.
**Velasco** (veh-LAHS-koh). A Texas port at the mouth of the Brazos River where treaties with Santa Anna were signed in 1836.

The land between the two rivers was a broad stretch of South Texas. It was thinly settled, and most of it was dry. But it was large, and it mattered to both sides. If the border was the Nueces, then American soldiers who crossed it were entering Mexico. If the border was the Rio Grande, they were at home.

The question was not settled by the annexation. The United States simply accepted the Texan claim, without asking Mexico. Mexico, which had warned that annexation meant war, broke off relations with Washington. The stage was set for a new conflict, and the border was the cause.

section: The answer to a long question
text: The answer to a long question

section: The answer to a long question
text: Step back and look at the whole story. Spain had claimed Texas for three hundred years but could not fill it. Mexico had invited **settlers** in and then lost them. Texas had won its independence but could not support itself. In the end, the land came under the flag of the nation whose settlers had come to dominate it.

section: The answer to a long question
text: The reasons were not simple, and none of them was certain. A different treaty, a different election, or a different choice by Texas leaders might have led to a very different result. But after 1845, the question of who would own this place had an answer, and the answer had a border still to be argued over.
💪 REMEMBER THIS QUESTION
Keep one question in mind: why did a nation that had won its independence choose to join another country? The answer is made of debts, dangers, elections, and hopes.

**treaty** (TREE-tee). A written agreement between countries.
📖 TODAY'S FOCUS
How can a country be rich in land and still be too poor to pay its bills?

The **Republic** of Texas had millions of acres of fertile land. It also had empty pockets. This lesson follows how the young nation tried to pay for itself, why its money collapsed, and how land became the one thing that Texas could offer to the world.

📚 PART 1 · A NATION WITHOUT MONEY
Debts from the start

The Republic began its life in debt. The war had cost money for soldiers, for supplies, and for ships. Texas had borrowed from banks and individuals in the United States, and it had promised to pay them back. But it had almost no income. There was no gold or silver mine, and few people to tax.

The debt grew year by year. By the early 1840s, the Republic owed millions of dollars, far more than it could ever raise from its small population. Interest piled up on top of the debt. A country that cannot pay its bills finds that credit dries up, and then even small needs become hard to meet.

Think about the size of the country. Fewer than forty thousand people lived in Texas in the first years of the Republic. They were farmers and merchants who had barely started to build their homes. They could not pay for an army, a navy, a government, and the roads and offices that a country needs.

The government tried several ways to raise money. It charged **tariffs** on goods coming in through the ports, but smugglers avoided them. It levied direct taxes, but they were hard to collect over so much distance. It sold **bonds**, but few buyers wanted them. Each fix brought in a little and left a large gap.
The collapse of the redbacks

When money ran short, the Republic printed more. Paper notes were issued in the late 1830s, and the later ones were known as **redbacks**, because of the color of the ink on the back. At first they were accepted at close to their face value. But the government kept printing, and people lost trust.

As more redbacks flooded the market, each one bought less. A note that was worth a dollar in 1839 might buy only a few cents' worth by 1842. Merchants refused to take it, or took it only at a deep discount. Soldiers and officials were paid in money that lost its value before they could spend it.

Think about a family holding these notes. A farmer sold a wagon of corn and received paper. When he went to buy tools, the merchant said that the paper was worth only half of what it claimed. By the time he could buy anything else, it was worth even less. Each day of waiting cost him more.

This is a common fate of a government that spends more than it earns. It is tempting to print money to **cover** the gap. But when money is printed faster than goods are made, the money buys less. Texas learned that lesson the hard way, and the damage fell on ordinary families who held the notes.
📚 PART 2 · LAND AS MONEY
What Texas could offer

If Texas had one real treasure, it was land. The country claimed an enormous area, and most of it was empty of settlers. The government could not pay its bills in cash, but it could pay them in acres. Land became a kind of **currency**, and the Republic used it for almost everything.

Soldiers who fought in the war received land, as a **bounty** for their service. Families who were already in Texas at **independence** received large tracts. Later arrivals received a smaller but still generous headright. A family could get over a thousand acres, and a single man could get several hundred.

That offer pulled in settlers by the thousands. Families from the southern United States crossed the Sabine with wagons and hopes. Some came to escape debts at home. Others wanted to farm on a scale that would have been impossible in the older states. Land was the Republic's best advertisement, and it worked.

Other costs came with the offer. The government had to survey land, record titles, and settle disputes among claimants. Many claims overlapped, and many titles were poorly drawn. Lawsuits over land would fill Texas courts for generations. A promise of land is easy to make and hard to keep clean.

But land had a weakness as money. It could not be spent quickly, it was hard to sell, and its value depended on how safe the country seemed. A buyer does not pay much for ground that **Comanche** **raiders** or Mexican armies might take. Land made Texas rich on paper, but it did not fill the **treasury**.

section: A new capital on the edge
text: A new capital on the edge

section: A new capital on the edge
text: The first capital had been the town of Houston, on Buffalo **Bayou**, a muddy new town that grew quickly. Officials complained of mud, mosquitoes, and high prices. When **Congress** voted to move, it was choosing the future of the country as much as the site of a town.

section: A new capital on the edge
text: In 1839, the Republic chose a new capital. Congress picked a spot on the **Colorado** River, in the rolling country where the settled farms ended and the Comanche range began. The new town was named Austin, in honor of the founder of the **colony**. It was a bold choice, and a dangerous one.

section: A new capital on the edge
text: 🌐 FOREIGN LANGUAGE VOCABULARY

section: A new capital on the edge
text: **Colorado** (kol-uh-RAD-oh). A river in Texas that flows to the Gulf of Mexico. It is not the Colorado River of the western mountains.

section: A new capital on the edge
text: The leaders hoped that a capital on the **frontier** would encourage settlers to push farther west. But the town was exposed. Government clerks worked with **rifles** close at hand, and travelers to Austin faced the risk of raids. For years, the capital sat at the very edge of the country that it governed.
📚 PART 3 · AN UNSETTLED CLAIM
The Cherokee in East Texas

One land question could not be solved by a headright. The Cherokee people, led by Chief Bowles, had lived in East Texas since the 1820s. They had come from east of the Mississippi, and they had settled the land with the permission of Mexican officials. They farmed and built homes, and they wanted to keep them.

In February 1836, as the war began, Houston had signed a **treaty** with the Cherokee and several other Native groups. It recognized their claim to a tract of land in East Texas, in return for peace during the war. Houston, who had lived among the Cherokee as a young man, hoped to keep them as friends.

But the treaty needed the approval of the **Senate**, and the Senate would not give it. Many **Texians** believed that the Cherokee land should be open to settlers, and some argued that the Cherokee had no right to it at all. The treaty was never approved, and the Cherokee claim sat in legal limbo.

That was where matters stood in December 1838, when Houston's term ended and a new president took office. The question of who owned East Texas was still open. A new president with a different idea about the Native peoples of Texas would soon decide to settle the question by force.
💪 REMEMBER THIS QUESTION
Keep one question in mind: when a government cannot pay its debts with money, what does it do? Texas paid with land, and land had a cost.

section: Spain brought the horse to America. Then the horse changed everything.
text: Horses did not live in the Americas before Europeans arrived. Spain brought them. Within a few generations, Native peoples on the plains had learned to ride and breed horses, and their way of life changed completely. One people, the **Comanche**, became so powerful on horseback that Spain could not defeat them. This lesson shows how that happened.

📚 PART 1 · HORSES SPREAD NORTH

section: A revolt that set horses loose
text: A revolt that set horses loose

section: A revolt that set horses loose
text: Spanish **settlers** and soldiers brought horses to the Americas, and they tried to control them. Native people were often forbidden to ride. But some Native workers learned to care for horses on Spanish ranches and at **missions**. They learned how to feed them, breed them, and ride them.

section: A revolt that set horses loose
text: A horse is not a simple gift. It must be fed, watered, trained, and bred, and a good horse takes years to raise. People who learned to care for horses were learning a whole set of skills at the same time. That is why the horse spread through knowledge as much as through animals. Where a people had skilled horse handlers, horses thrived. Where they did not, horses died.

section: A revolt that set horses loose
text: In 1680, the Pueblo peoples of New Mexico rose up against Spanish rule in a **revolt**. They drove the Spaniards out of the **province** for more than a decade. The Spaniards left many of their horses behind. In the years that followed, horses were traded and stolen across the plains. They passed from one people to the next, moving farther north every year.

section: A revolt that set horses loose
text: Think about the path a horse might take. A horse from a Spanish ranch could be traded to a Pueblo family. That family could trade it to a people farther north or east, who could trade it again. Each trade moved the horse a few hundred miles. Within a few generations, horses had passed through many hands and reached peoples who had never seen a Spaniard.

section: A revolt that set horses loose
text: Nobody planned this. Spain had brought the horse for its own use. It never meant to hand its **rivals** the power to defeat its **colonies**. History is full of results like that, when a tool is carried to a new place and used in a way that nobody expected.
📚 PART 2 · THE COMANCHE MOVE SOUTH

section: From the mountains to the plains
text: From the mountains to the plains

section: From the mountains to the plains
text: The Comanche once lived farther north, in the Rocky Mountains and the high plains, as hunters on foot. They got horses early, and horses opened a new life. Around 1700, groups of Comanche began moving south and east onto the plains of what are now Colorado, Kansas, Oklahoma, and Texas.

section: From the mountains to the plains
text: Why did the Comanche move south? Historians offer several reasons. The southern plains had huge herds of **bison** and wide grasslands that could feed many horses. There were also trading partners in the south, both Native peoples and Spaniards. And a people who could move quickly on horses could take advantage of new places that others had not yet claimed. The move was a choice, and it was a good one.

section: From the mountains to the plains
text: The Comanche were not alone. Other peoples on the plains, including the **Apache** and the Ute, also had horses. But the Comanche became the best horsemen and the best organized. By about 1750, they controlled much of the southern plains. Historians call their territory **Comanchería**. The Comanche called themselves the **Numunuu**, which means "the People."

section: From the mountains to the plains

text: **Comanche** (kuh-MAN-chee). A people who became the strongest power on the southern plains in the 1700s.

section: From the mountains to the plains
text: **Comanchería** (koh-mahn-cheh-REE-ah). The name historians use for the large territory the Comanche controlled on the southern plains.

section: From the mountains to the plains
text: **Numunuu** (NOO-moo-noo). The Comanche name for themselves. It means "the People."

section: From the mountains to the plains
text: The Comanche were also a flexible people. They were divided into many bands, and each band had its own leaders, who guided it for as long as people chose to follow. Bands could join together for a big hunt or a big **raid**, and then split apart again. This made them hard to fight. A Spanish officer could not defeat the Comanche by capturing one leader or one camp, because there was no single capital to take.
📚 PART 3 · THE APACHE PUSHED SOUTH

section: A new neighbor for Spanish Texas
text: A new neighbor for Spanish Texas

section: A new neighbor for Spanish Texas
text: The Apache had hunted bison on the plains for centuries. As Comanche power grew, many Apache groups were pushed south and west. One group, the **Lipan**, moved into Texas. That put them close to Spanish settlements, and some of them began to raid those settlements for horses and cattle.

section: A new neighbor for Spanish Texas
text: Other Lipan wanted peace with Spain. They hoped the Spaniards would protect them from the Comanche. Spain saw a chance to use that hope. As you will see, the plan did not turn out the way Spain wanted.

section: A new neighbor for Spanish Texas

section: A new neighbor for Spanish Texas
text: **Apache** (uh-PATCH-ee). A group of related peoples who lived on the plains and in the Southwest.

section: A new neighbor for Spanish Texas
text: **Lipan** (LIP-un). A group of Apache who moved south into Texas.

section: A new neighbor for Spanish Texas
text: The Apache did not simply give up. They fought, they moved, and they made new **alliances**. Their story shows that the Comanche rise was not a quick conquest of an empty land. It was a long struggle among peoples who each wanted the same grass, water, and herds. Spain was drawn into that struggle, whether it wanted to be or not.

section: PART 4 WHAT THE HORSE MADE POSSIBLE
text: 📚 PART 4 · WHAT THE HORSE MADE POSSIBLE
Bison, range, and raiding

On foot, hunters could kill a bison only by surrounding a herd or driving it over a cliff. On horseback, a hunter could ride beside a running bison and bring it down. That meant more meat, more hides, and more free time. The bison gave food, clothing, tents, tools, and goods to trade.

A horse also gave range. A mounted family could break camp quickly, follow the herds, and travel hundreds of miles. Horses themselves became a form of wealth. The more horses a family owned, the richer and more respected it was.

Horses also changed the work of the family. Hunting, moving camp, and caring for herds were shared tasks, and a skilled rider could do much more than a skilled walker. A person who could tame, train, and trade horses became important in the band. A family still needed everyone's help, but the horse made every hand more useful.

Raiding became part of this economy. Comanche groups raided Spanish and Apache settlements for horses, for goods, and for **captives**. They also traded with other peoples and with Spanish and French traders. Captives were sometimes adopted into Comanche families and sometimes traded away.

To the Comanche, raiding was not senseless violence. It was a way to gain horses, goods, and honor, and it was also a way to defend their territory from rivals. To the people who were raided, it was a terrible loss. A family that lost its horses might lose its way of life, and a family that lost a child might never see that child again. Both views are part of the story.

By the middle of the 1700s, all of this added up to something Spain had never faced in Texas. It was a large, mobile, well-armed people who needed nothing from Spain, and who could attack where Spain was weakest. The mission system could not hold them. Spanish soldiers could not catch them.
💪 WHAT TO CARRY FORWARD

The horse turned a few hunting bands into one of the great powers of North America. Spain had built its frontier for peoples it could gather and teach. The Comanche were a people on horseback who followed the bison and answered to no one. That mismatch is the key to what happened next.

section: What do you build first when you have just won a country?
text: After **San Jacinto**, Texas was free, but it had no money, no recognized borders, and no settled government. The people who had fought the war now had to write the rules for a nation. This lesson looks at the **constitution** they wrote, the **treaties** they signed with a captured president, and the first steps of the **Republic**.
