📚 PART 1 · WRITING THE RULES

section: A convention in a cold hall
text: A convention in a cold hall

section: A convention in a cold hall
text: The constitution of the Republic was written in March 1836, in the same rough hall where **independence** was declared. The delegates worked quickly because **Santa Anna** 's army was on the march. In two weeks, they finished a document that would shape the Republic for its whole life. They approved it on March 17, while their army was **retreating**.

section: A convention in a cold hall
text: 🌐 FOREIGN LANGUAGE VOCABULARY

section: A convention in a cold hall
text: **San Jacinto** (san hah-SIN-toh). A river and a battlefield on the coastal plain of Texas, near the modern city of Houston.

section: A convention in a cold hall
text: **Velasco** (veh-LAHS-koh). A Texas port at the mouth of the Brazos River where treaties with Santa Anna were signed in 1836.

section: A convention in a cold hall
text: **Santa Anna** (SAN-tah AH-nah). Antonio López de Santa Anna, a Mexican army officer who became one of the most powerful men in Mexico.

section: A convention in a cold hall
text: An interim government took over until a regular one could be elected. David Burnet became interim president, and Lorenzo de **Zavala**, a Mexican statesman who had joined the Texas cause, became vice president. Their jobs were temporary. They held the country together during the weeks of the war and the first months of peace.

section: A convention in a cold hall
text: 🌐 FOREIGN LANGUAGE VOCABULARY

section: A convention in a cold hall
text: **Zavala** (zah-VAH-lah). Lorenzo de Zavala, a Mexican statesman who joined the Texas cause and became its first vice president.

section: A convention in a cold hall
text: The delegates agreed on one thing quickly. Texas needed a government strong enough to wage a war and weak enough that no one man could rule it. Many of them had watched Santa Anna turn a republic into a one-man government. They did not want to repeat that story, and the constitution reflects their fear.

section: A convention in a cold hall
text: Think about how unusual the moment was. Most of the delegates had arrived in Texas within the last few years. Some had served in state legislatures or in **Congress** in the United States. Now they had to write a charter for a new country while a war went on outside the door.
What they borrowed

The delegates borrowed heavily from the United States. The constitution divided power among three branches: a president, a congress with two houses, and courts. It included a bill of rights that guarded free speech, trial by **jury**, and the right to bear arms. Anyone who knew the American system would feel at home.

They also changed some things. The first president served two years and later presidents served three, and no president could be elected again right away. The aim was to prevent one man from holding power for too long. Many delegates remembered Mexico's strongmen, and they wanted a government that could not be taken over by a single leader.

The constitution also gave the president real powers. He commanded the army and navy, he made treaties with the approval of the **Senate**, and he named many officials. The delegates believed that a young nation facing danger needed one clear leader, as long as the office had limits.

Some features came from Mexico, and they lasted. Texas kept the Spanish and Mexican rules for land **grants**. It kept the idea of community property, which says that what a husband and wife earn during marriage belongs to both of them. This was a legal tradition from Spain, and it protected the rights of wives in ways that many American states did not yet do.
Slavery written in

The constitution also protected slavery. It said that Congress could not pass any law to stop slaveholders from bringing **enslaved** people into Texas, that Congress had no power to free enslaved people, and that no owner could free them without the consent of Congress, unless the person was sent out of the country. It said that free Black people could not live in Texas without the consent of Congress.

This matters for understanding the people of the Republic. They did not all agree about slavery, and many **Texians** owned no enslaved people at all. But the law of the land protected the practice, and the economy of the cotton farms along the rivers rested on it.

This was a clear break from Mexican law, which had moved toward ending slavery. For many of the delegates, protecting slavery was part of what they wanted from independence. The Republic's founders did not hide the matter. They wrote it into the document. That fact would shape the later history of the state in many ways.
📚 PART 2 · A PRISONER PRESIDENT
The Treaties of Velasco

Meanwhile, the captured Santa Anna was held as a prisoner. In May 1836, at Velasco, he signed two treaties with the Texian government. In the public one, he promised to end the war, to order the Mexican army to withdraw south of the **Rio Grande**, and to free Texian prisoners.
🌐 FOREIGN LANGUAGE VOCABULARY
**Rio Grande** (REE-oh GRAHN-day). The great river that flows between Texas and Mexico to the Gulf of Mexico.

Think about what Santa Anna wanted. He wanted to save his life and return to power. Texians wanted him alive as a bargaining tool, though they did not trust him, and some of the soldiers wanted him hanged. Houston kept him safe. Santa Anna was released in the end, after a trip to Washington.

In a secret treaty, he promised to work to persuade Mexico to recognize the independence of Texas. The details of the border were left unclear. The agreement gave Texians something that they wanted. But it was a promise from a man who was a prisoner and who could easily say that he had signed under pressure.

That is just what the Mexican government said. It declared that a **captive** president had no power to give away Mexican land, and it refused to honor either treaty. Santa Anna was soon sent home. Mexico never accepted the loss of Texas, and for years it talked about winning it back.
📚 PART 3 · THE FIRST YEARS
Houston as president

In the fall of 1836, voters elected Sam Houston as the first regular president. They also voted on whether to seek annexation to the United States, and they voted yes by a huge margin. Texians saw union with the United States as the safest future. They did not expect Washington to delay.

Houston ran a very thin government. He kept the army small, because he knew that the country could not pay for a large one. He tried to keep peace with Mexico by avoiding **raids** across the border. At home he worked with Native peoples when he could, and he tried to avoid costly fights.

Houston also had to deal with the army. Soldiers who had won at San Jacinto were restless and hoped to march into Mexico. Houston sent most of them home on leave, because the country could not feed or pay them. It was an unpopular choice, but it kept the **treasury** from collapsing even faster.

In March 1837, the United States recognized Texas as a nation. It was a great relief. But Washington refused to take the next step. Many Americans in the North feared that adding Texas would add a huge slave state. President Van Buren did not want a war with Mexico. In 1838, Texas withdrew its offer.

Notice the position that this left Texas in. It had won its independence, but it still had no treaty with its main enemy and no promise from its main friend. It would have to survive on its own, and it would have to pay its own bills. That would prove to be very hard.
💪 REMEMBER THIS QUESTION
Keep one question in mind: what does a new nation owe to the people who lived under the old one, and what does it owe to itself?

section: San Antonio, La Bahía, and Nacogdoches
text: There were three towns in Spanish Texas. The first was San Antonio de **Béxar**, founded in 1718 beside its springs. It was the largest and the capital. The second was **La Bahía**, a fort and a **mission** that had moved several times and finally settled at the place now called **Goliad**. The third was **Nacogdoches** in East Texas. It began as a mission in 1716 and became a town in 1779, when **settlers** who had been moved out of East Texas moved back.

text: Each town had its own reason for being there. San Antonio guarded the road and held the springs. La Bahía watched the coast, where French or other ships might land. Nacogdoches stood near the French trading post at **Natchitoches**, so it watched the eastern border. None of them began because settlers wanted to farm or trade there. All three began as answers to a threat.

text: Notice how far apart the three towns were. San Antonio and La Bahía were about ninety miles apart, and Nacogdoches lay hundreds of miles to the northeast. The roads were rough, and the trip took many days. Each town stood almost alone on a very large map, and settlers in one could not easily help another.
📚 PART 2 · THE ARITHMETIC
How many people?

In the early 1800s, Spain took a **census** of the province. It showed only a few thousand Spanish-speaking people living in all of Texas. Most of them lived in San Antonio. Look at how many years that took. Spain had claimed the land since the 1500s. It had built missions and forts since 1690. Even so, the whole province held about as many people as a single large town in the United States.

To see how small this was, picture a school. A large middle school today might hold a thousand students. Spanish Texas, after three hundred years, would fill only a few of those schools. Compare that to Mexico City, which had well over a hundred thousand people. The difference between the capital and the northern **frontier** was enormous.

The numbers hide another problem. Many of the people counted were soldiers and their families, who could be sent elsewhere. Few had come to Texas to stay for generations. The population grew slowly, partly because the **Comanche** **raided** ranches and killed or captured settlers, and partly because the government could offer very few reasons to move there.
🌐 FOREIGN LANGUAGE VOCABULARY
**Comanche** (kuh-MAN-chee). A people who became the strongest power on the southern plains in the 1700s.

The census also leaves out the Native peoples who lived in and around Texas. The Comanche, the **Apache**, the **Caddo**, and many others made up most of the people who lived on this land. Spain counted only the people it ruled. That tells us something. For three hundred years, most of the land that Spain claimed was in fact held by other peoples.
🌐 FOREIGN LANGUAGE VOCABULARY
**Caddo** (KAD-oh). A group of peoples who lived in East Texas and farmed the land.
**Apache** (uh-PATCH-ee). A group of related peoples who lived on the plains and in the Southwest.

Meanwhile, the English colonies on the Atlantic coast had begun as a few small villages. By 1800, the United States had millions of people. The English model produced a very different result in the same amount of time.
📚 PART 3 · WHAT DID TAKE ROOT
Cattle, land, water, and names

Spain did leave real marks on Texas. The first was ranching. Spanish settlers brought cattle, horses, and sheep. The **cowboy** (*vaquero*), a horseman who worked with cattle, was born on these ranches. The skills, the tools, and many of the words of the American cowboy trace back to him.
🌐 FOREIGN LANGUAGE VOCABULARY
**cowboy (*vaquero*)** (vah-KEH-roh). A Spanish and Mexican horseman who worked with cattle. The word comes from vaca, which means cow.

The second was the land system. Spain gave out land in large **grants**, measured in **leagues** and in smaller parcels. That system, and the records that came with it, would shape land ownership in Texas for a long time. The third was water law. Spanish rules about sharing water from rivers and ditches also lasted. The fourth was names. Many Texas places, such as San Antonio, the **Brazos**, and the Trinity, have Spanish names, or names the Spaniards gave.
🌐 FOREIGN LANGUAGE VOCABULARY
**Brazos** (BRAH-zus). A major river in Texas that flows to the Gulf of Mexico.

Spanish ranching also gave Texas its first lasting business. By the late 1700s, large herds of cattle and horses grazed on ranches near San Antonio. Some animals escaped. Spanish horses that ran wild became the mustangs of the plains. It is worth noticing that these lasting marks came from ordinary ranchers and farmers, not from soldiers or priests. Their skills passed from family to family, and later ranchers, Mexican and American alike, adopted them. The things that lasted were practical, not grand.

Notice a pattern in what lasted. Priests, soldiers, and officials came and went, and their orders changed with every new king. Ranchers stayed in one place and passed down their land and their skills. A lasting thing is often one that ordinary people find useful in their own lives, even when no government is watching.
📚 PART 4 · AN ARGUMENT
Colony or garrison?

Historians still argue about what Spanish Texas really was. One side says it was a colony. It had towns, missions, ranches, and families who lived and died there for generations. They built lasting things, such as churches, ditches, and ranches.

The other side says it was a garrison. The province existed mostly to guard Mexico from **rivals**. Soldiers were the largest group, supplies came from far away, and few people lived there by choice. If the soldiers had left, the province might have vanished.

Evidence for the garrison side is easy to find. The Spanish government paid for most of what stood in Texas. Without money from Mexico City, the **presidios** would have run out of food and gunpowder. Evidence for the colony side is also real. Families married, raised children, and held land that their grandchildren **inherited**. Both lists are true, and that is what makes the question hard.
🌐 FOREIGN LANGUAGE VOCABULARY
**presidio** (preh-SEE-dee-oh). A Spanish fort where soldiers lived and guarded the frontier.
Which side do you find more convincing? Write a short argument in your notebook. Use at least two pieces of evidence from this lesson. You may find that the best answer says it was a little of both.

As you decide, think about what each reading explains. If Spanish Texas was a colony, why were there so few settlers? If it was a garrison, why did families build homes and ranches that lasted for generations? You may find that each side explains something the other cannot.
💪 WHAT TO CARRY FORWARD

Three towns, a few thousand people, and a handful of lasting traditions are what three centuries of Spanish effort left in Texas. The Spanish model had been built for a different kind of place. The question for the rest of this story is who or what would fill the empty space.
